"Boundaries need to be set, human beings do need a break sometimes."

News.title: BP profits highest in four years as Iran war pushes up oil price
News.content:
Profits at BP have surged to a four-year high after the war in the Middle East pushed up oil prices.

The oil giant reported a profit of $5.73bn (Â£4.26bn) between April and June. That was more than double the $2.35bn it made in the same period last year and the highest quarterly profit since the start of the Russia-Ukraine war in 2022.

The price of crude has jumped since the outbreak of the Iran war earlier this year due to major disruption to global supplies of oil and gas through the Strait of Hormuz.

Environmental and poverty campaigners blasted BP for "profiteering" off skyrocketing oil prices.

Despite the big rise in profits, BP chief executive Meg O'Neill said the company was not reaching its full potential.

The company, which employs nearly 14,000 people in the UK, confirmed plans to move further away from clean energy, revealing plans to sell off its US renewable natural gas business Archaea.

O'Neill said this was part of her plan to prioritise "value, not sentiment or history".

"We have to focus on the assets with the strongest potential to deliver competitive returns and long-term value," she said.

Last week, BP announced it was putting its North Sea business up for sale in a move that would end 60 years of production in the region by the company.

Crude oil prices shot up after the outbreak of conflict in the Middle East, which in turn pushed up petrol and diesel prices and domestic energy costs around the world.

BP said Brent crude - the global benchmark for oil prices - averaged $103.85 a barrel in the April-to-June quarter, up from $67.88 in the same period last year.

Angharad Hopkinson, from environmental campaign group Greenpeace, said the results showed that "corporate gains have become entirely divorced from the public good".

She said "the one point on which we agree with BP" is its decision to sell off its North Sea operations.

"Prolonging this parasitic relationship by trying to squeeze the last few drops of expensive oil out of the North Sea is sheer folly," Hopkinson said.

News.title: 'Rape list' part of misogyny girls face at school
News.content:
A group of teenage girls have said they feel "worthless" and "frightened" as a result of the extreme misogyny they regularly experience.

The students, from Tyneside, have spoken out after making a film about the language they endure at school and online.

Many comments are too explicit to share, but they include threats of violence and rape often masked as "banter". One girl described how disturbed she had been after a "rape list" was made by boys in her school.

The government said it was "taking bold and decisive action to halve violence against women and girls", with changes being introduced from September to help teachers challenge misogyny.

The North East has the highest rate of violence against women and girls in England and charities warned unchallenged attitudes could lead to abuse in early relationships.

Misogyny is defined as a contempt for, hatred of or prejudice against women.

One girl told the BBC she felt "worthless" after learning of the "rape list" made by boys in her school.

"Boys ordering girls, who they want to rape the most and then the least," she explained.

"It is frightening because you don't know people's real intentions."

News.title: Heatwaves are changing summer weddings - here's how to plan for one
News.content:
"As soon as I put my dress on, my makeup was just falling off my face."

Aimie Seale is one of hundreds of brides whose weddings landed in the middle of a heatwave this summer.

She had chosen a July weekend in the hope of avoiding any wet weather. Instead, she faced 30C heat with her ceremony in a sweltering West Yorkshire church, predominantly made of glass.

"It was just unbearably hot," says Aimie. "I remember looking at my husband at one point, and he was just dripping with sweat, so everybody kept passing him tissues halfway through the service."

Aimie and her now-husband Ryan had to book an emergency marquee to offer extra shade and an ice-cream van to keep their guests cool.

An additional cost on an already expensive day, with the average wedding in the UK costing more than Â£20,000., external

But this last-minute battle to cope with the heat is only going to get worse. Half of the years between 2015 and 2024 saw temperatures above 35C - up from one in ten - as climate change increases the risk of heatwaves.

News.title: 'Digital lifeline' - Gaza tech workers give glimpse of possible future
News.content:
"I was just in a trough, drowning in uncertainty," says Walaa Volidis, a Palestinian software engineer. "But deep inside, I made a decision: it will not be the end, no matter how hard it gets. I'll keep fighting for my dreams."

Wearing a headset and glued to her laptop, Walaa discusses AI on a video call with her mentor in California's Silicon Valley. The 24-year-old wants to keep her skills up to date.

But that is the least of her daily challenges as she lives in a tent in central Gaza supporting her displaced parents and four younger siblings.

"When the war started, I lost everything: my job, my university, even some of my family members. My sisters were injured," Walaa tells me from a co-working space in Deir al-Balah. She says her mental health was "totally destroyed", but she prioritised finding work.

Walaa is one of thousands of young Gazans now pursuing roles in the digital economy. "It's a kind of momentum," she says. "I have my main goal every single day to go to work, to finish my tasks. If you stop or cry about your situation, you will not do anything."

News.title: Half-price rail travel extended to 18-year-olds
News.content:
Eighteen-year-olds will be able to buy half-price train tickets for most services when railcard rules are changed later this month, the Department for Transport (DfT) has announced.

It's an extension of the 16-17 Saver railcard which currently expires when the holder turns 18. From 17 August, they will be valid for a full year from the date of purchase.

It means 17-year-olds will be able to buy the railcard up until the day before they turn 18, making it valid until the day before they turn 19.

The existing rule meant more than 70,000 students each year were an average of Â£175 worse off than those in the same academic year who hadn't yet had their 18th birthday, the DfT said.

The 16-17 Saver Railcard costs Â£35 per year and entitles the holder to 50% off most train fares.

Rail minister Lord Hendy claimed this "common sense change" is "exactly what passengers should expect from the railway".

He said the change would "lower the cost of travel at a critical time for teenagers, whether they're pursuing further education, vocational pathways or getting their footing in the jobs market".

Jacqueline Starr, chief executive of industry body the Rail Delivery Group, said the change demonstrates the sector's commitment to "offering better value fares and delivering a more joined-up railway".

Kaynat Ahmad, vice president for further education at the National Union of Students, described the railcard as "essential for young people reliant on trains to get to college, work or training".

Eighteen-year-olds were already entitled to a 16-25 Railcard, but that only entitles them to a third off the cost of travel.

The government said the measure would be paid for through increased train ridership, with more passengers as a result of more people being able to access the discounted fares.

The announcement comes after the government said the cap on most single bus fares in England will be cut from Â£3 to Â£2 next year.

News.title: France hits out at Reform UK plan to return migrants using Navy
News.content:
France has hit out at a Reform UK plan to return migrant boats using the Navy, saying the proposals would violate its sovereignty and breach international law.

Nigel Farage's party announced that if it was in power it would intercept boats crossing the English Channel and return migrants to French ports, even if France disagreed.

Opposition parties branded the plan unworkable, while a Labour minister said it would lead to "a lot of time arguing with France" instead of "actually getting to grips with the problem".

Responding to the French government, a Reform spokesperson said: "We will always stand up for British interests and protect our people, whether Emmanuel Macron likes it or not."

The spokesperson added: "Humanitarian missions do not violate maritime or international law."

Under the plans, which Reform said it would bring in if it entered government after the next election, military-crewed inflatable boats deployed from 10 Navy patrol vessels would be used to "come alongside" migrant boats crossing the English Channel.

Border Force officers and police stationed onboard would be tasked with arresting people in the boats, and they would then be returned to France or Belgium by Navy personnel or Marines.

The party said returns operations would be conducted by military personnel with Border Force officers on hand in case of "non-compliance", with a Bay Class landing ship providing "detention capacity at sea" for up to 700 people.

Speaking at a news conference on Monday, Reform's home affairs spokesman Zia Yusuf said the party would aim to get agreement to disembark arrested migrants at French ports.

He added: "If the Elysee Palace refuses, make no mistake - His Majesty's Royal Marines will disembark them safely on the very shore they left that morning".

Speaking alongside him, Farage played down the prospect of a diplomatic confrontation with the French, claiming that attitudes in France towards the idea were "softening".

But in a statement issued later on Monday, the French interior ministry said: "This would constitute a violation of French sovereignty, as well as a violation of the law of the sea and international law."

A spokesperson for the department added that measures agreed with the UK, as well as "operations deployed at the local level", had already led to a reduction in crossings so far this year compared to the same period in 2025.

News.title: Woman has pioneering womb surgery to fix 'miracle' baby with intestines outside its body
News.content:
Doctors have used ground-breaking surgery on an unborn baby to successfully correct a birth defect while he was still inside the womb.

His mother, Maisie Savage, from London, was operated on by doctors in the US while she was 26 weeks pregnant.

Baby Theo, who is now five months old and thriving, had gastroschisis, where the belly button does not develop properly, causing the intestines to grow externally.

Doctors partially exposed his mother's womb and then gently pushed his organs back inside his abdomen using keyhole surgery.

He was the third baby in the world to benefit from the first-of-its-kind clinical trial.

Maisie, 29, and Theo's father, Josh French, 36, both teachers, say they are incredibly relieved by the success of the pioneering surgery.

"He's a little miracle, isn't he?" Maisie told BBC News.

But they both know things could have been very different.

The serious birth defect affects one in 3,000 UK babies each year. In the best-case scenarios, babies can require weeks in intensive care and nutritional feeding through a tube or IV and corrective surgery.

For the most complex cases, like Theo's, outcomes are far more serious with up to six months in neonatal intensive care, multiple surgeries, IV nutritional feeding for up to two years, and a possible intestinal transplant.

Even with the highest level of medical care, one in 10 babies will die.

News.title: West Ham co-owner David Sullivan advised to stay away from home matches
News.content:
The recommendation from London Stadium comes after a joint investigation by BBC Panorama and The Times revealed that seven women have accused Sullivan of sexually exploitative and predatory behaviour. He has categorically denied the allegations.

He stood down as joint chairman of the club shortly before the investigation was broadcast, saying he wanted to focus on fighting what he called "factually incorrect and entirely false, decades-old allegations concerning my personal life". He remains the club's largest shareholder.

The investigation also revealed that Sullivan has been banned from contact with West Ham's women's and youth teams for three years due to safeguarding concerns. London Stadium were unaware of the restrictions until the BBC's report.

Sullivan was banned after a historic allegation about his conduct was raised with the Football Association in 2023. He has previously said the allegation was false and that because he had never met any academy or women's team players "1-2-1" during his 16 years at the club, he accepted what he saw as a "meaningless restrictionâ¦for a quiet life".

West Ham were relegated from the Premier League in May and are due to play their first home game of the new season, a Carabao Cup match against Portsmouth, on Saturday.

Sullivan was a regular attendee at the London Stadium last season, where he was photographed watching games from the directors' box.

A spokesperson for London Stadium, the operator of the publicly owned venue, said that "following media reports at the end of the season regarding a safeguarding matter being managed by the club, London Stadium sought further information to ensure it could fulfil its own safeguarding responsibilities".

It said that West Ham had told it that the "matter was investigated and that the club does not consider there to be an ongoing safeguarding risk associated with Mr Sullivan attending the stadium".

However it said that, despite this, it had recommended the businessman stay away from games because of the "potential for demonstrations and anti-social behaviour by some spectators".

Sullivan has previously faced criticism from fans over his running of the club, with thousands joining a protest in September last year calling for his departure.

West Ham declined to comment. It is understood that the club intends to work with the stadium operators to facilitate Sullivan's attendance at games.

Sullivan has not responded to a request for comment.

Meanwhile, presenter Tony Livesey left BBC Radio 5 Live on Monday after 16 years at the station, the corporation announced.

Livesey stepped back from his weekday late night talk show in June, following allegations made against Sullivan. He had previously worked as editor-in-chief of Sullivan's Daily and Sunday Sport publications.

One alleged victim said that Livesey had arranged a meeting between her and Sullivan in 1999.

Livesey said he had "no recollection" of introducing the young woman to Sullivan and that it was "not part" of his job to do so.

He added that he had "great sympathy for a woman who may have become a victim", but rejected any suggestion that he had played "any role whatsoever in that scenario" and said he found the allegation "abhorrent".

News.title: Newspaper columnist and broadcaster Rod Liddle dies aged 66
News.content:
Newspaper columnist and broadcaster Rod Liddle has died aged 66 after a short illness, his family has announced.

Liddle's children paid tribute to their father, who they described as their guide "on how to live an extraordinary life", while CEO of News UK, Rebekah Brooks, called him "an inimitable journalistic force."

Brooks added that "he challenged conventional thinking and left an indelible mark on British journalism."

Liddle, a columnist for the Sun and the Sunday Times, died at The James Cook University Hospital in Middlesbrough on Sunday evening.

A former editor of BBC Radio 4's flagship Today programme, he also had a weekly column in the Spectator, as well as a show on Times Radio.

His children, Wilder, Tyler and Emmy, said: "We're all very saddened and shocked at the sudden passing of our wonderful father.

"He raised us much as you might imagine, to be inquisitive, brave and always humorous.

"Even in hospital in the last few weeks, he consistently held the room and never let the awful situation show.

"He has left a legacy that we are all incredibly proud of, he will always be our guide on how to live an extraordinary life."

News.title: Author La Plante banned from driving for six months
News.content:
The court heard she already had nine points on her licence, from three speeding offences in June 2023 and then June and July 2025.

She told the court she believed she would have to have the dog rehomed if she was unable to drive him to his daily walks, saying: "I think the emotional turmoil of that would truly damn my career as a writer.

"It's very, very solitary and I work exceptionally hard and I would just stop."

La Plante, who is best known for creating Prime Suspect's no-nonsense Det Ch Insp Jane Tennison, admitted driving at 24mph twice, 25mph, 26mph and 27mph in the latest offences, which all happened as she was on her way to take her dog for his daily walk.

Giving evidence, La Plante said she got her dog Theo after suffering the devastation of the untimely death of another dog, Hugo.

Fighting back tears, she said she "lost it" when Hugo died and she "didn't know what to do with [her] life".

She added her new dog had helped her through the grieving process.

News.title: Farage says he discussed return to politics months before general election
News.content:
Nigel Farage has told the BBC he discussed the "potential liabilities" of returning to politics before the 2024 general election.

It comes after The Sunday Times, external reported Farage had negotiated a deal in March and April 2024 with then-Reform leader Richard Tice to return to lead the party.

Farage confirmed he spoke with Tice in spring 2024 to scope out what would happen to Reform's finances if he returned but said it "wasn't a deal, it wasn't an agreement", adding that talks came "quite some time after" he received a Â£5m gift from a billionaire donor.

Labour said Farage's remarks had "blown a gaping hole" in his argument for not declaring the gift after becoming an MP in July 2024.

Farage has repeatedly argued the Â£5m from British cryptocurrency investor Christopher Harborne was an "unconditional gift", was intended for his personal security, "wasn't political in any sense at all" and he was not an MP when he received it.

Reform's opponents have said he should have declared it in the MPs' register of interests when he was elected to Parliament.

The Parliamentary Standards Commissioner was investigating whether Farage broke the rules, but the process was suspended when he stood down as Clacton MP last month to force a by-election.

Farage said he took this decision as the "people of Clacton should be the judges of my actions". The investigation will be resumed if Farage wins the by-election, which is taking place on 13 August.

Farage left frontline politics in 2021 and embarked on a broadcasting career.

In May 2024, Farage was serving as Reform's honorary president but announced he would not be standing as a candidate in the general election in July of that year.

He reversed this position at the beginning of June and took over the leadership of the party.

Appearing at a press conference on Monday, Farage was asked if he had negotiated a deal on what would happen to Reform's finances if he came back as leader - in light of the report in The Sunday Times.

He replied: "I had no intention of returning to politics or as leader of Reform, but in the spring of that year I did talk to Richard Tice about what the liabilities would be if I was to come back to that position.

"And you'd be a bit of a mug, wouldn't you, to walk into a job and not find out what the potential liabilities were, and they were substantial.

"But without Richard, the party wouldn't have even survived, so that was useful for me to know. But it wasn't a deal, it wasn't an agreement, it was subject to if I came back."

He added: "If you want clarification on this, that came quite some time after the gift, which is perhaps the important point."

Bridget Phillipson, chair of the Labour Party, said: "Nigel Farage has blown a gaping hole in his excuse for why his secret Â£5m 'gift' from a crypto billionaire did not need to be declared."

The Commons code of conduct states that new MPs "must register all their current financial interests, and any registrable benefits (other than earnings) received in the 12 months before their election within one month of their election".

The rules say "purely personal gifts or benefits" from family or commercial loans would not normally have to be registered.

The rules also say "both the possible motive of the giver and the use to which the gift is to be put should be considered", adding "if there is any doubt, the benefit should be registered".

News.title: Police dog sniffs out man hiding behind fake wall on 300-plant cannabis farm
News.content:
A man has been jailed for six months after being found by a sniffer dog behind a fake wall on a cannabis farm.

Albert Hysaj, 42, pleaded guilty to producing cannabis and was sentenced at Cardiff Crown Court on Friday.

Hysaj was caught after a police dog named Asko located him in the commercial property on the Bowen Industrial Estate, in Aberbargoed, Caerphilly county, in May.

Gwent Police found 313 cannabis plants inside two linked units over three rooms, which included a living area with kitchen and bathroom.

A former far-right activist, who has a string of convictions including harassing a Jewish MP, has been selected to stand as a Conservative candidate in upcoming local elections.

Joshua Bonehill-Paine has said he was “tremendously proud” to have been selected by the party to stand as a candidate for Crewkerne South in next year’s Somerset Council elections.

Mr Bonehill-Paine, who now runs a political satire account on social media posting AI videos, is a former neo-Nazi activist who has several convictions, including posting anti-Semitic material ahead of a planned neo-Nazi rally.

In 2016 he was found guilty of harassing former MP Luciana Berger in a string of anti-Jewish rants, posting articles online calling her a "dominatrix" and "an evil money-grabber" with a "deep-rooted hatred of men".

open image in gallery Joshua Bonehill-Paine claimed Labour MP Luciana Berger was responsible for Jesus's death ( Social media )

In one, he claimed the number of Jewish Labour MPs was a "problem" and illustrated his posts with offensive pictures, including the anti-Jewish cliche of a rat with Ms Berger's face superimposed on it.

The Conservative Party said his past actions were “indefensible” but insisted he has “sought to make amends through counter-extremism work”.

“He was rightly punished and served his sentence,” a spokesperson said. “Mr Bonehill-Paine has explained that he has sought to make amends through counter-extremism work.

open image in gallery Joshua Bonehill-Paine has said he was “tremendously proud” to have been selected by the party to stand as a candidate for Crewkerne South in next year’s Somerset Council elections ( Joshua Bonehill-Paine/Facebook )

“The Conservative Party believes in rehabilitation and that people can change, but all members must adhere to our code of conduct and our values.

“Ultimately the decision to elect him will be one for the public.”

Mr Bonehill-Paine now runs the Crewkerne Gazette, a satirical social media account with thousands of followers, and has shared videos of himself speaking publicly against antisemitism.

open image in gallery Joshua Bonehill-Paine posted articles describing the MP as a ‘dominatrix’ and ‘an evil money-grabber’ ( PA )

He told The Independent he is “very proud to be a changed man from the one that I was over 10 years ago”, and said: “For the last 8 years I have worked in counter extremism delivering seminars and talks to the police, probation, schools and universities.”

He added: “My only hope is that more people like me, who have made terrible mistakes change their life around and turn around from the path they are on, this especially is concerning antisemitism.”

Announcing his candidacy on social media, Mr Bonehill-Paine vowed to “fight for local people first” and put Crewkerne “on the map”.

“I founded the The Crewkerne Gazette and put our town on the map. Now it is time to put Crewkerne first at County Hall,” he wrote.

open image in gallery It comes as Kemi Badenoch clamps down on candidate selection for the next general election, having reportedly blocked former Conservative Party co-chairman Sir Grant Shapps from standing as an MP ( PA )

“No more weakness. No more excuses. No more decline. No more being forgotten.”

It comes as Kemi Badenoch clamps down on candidate selection for the next general election, having reportedly blocked former Conservative Party co-chairman Sir Grant Shapps from standing as an MP.

She wrote in the Telegraph that there would be “no special treatment for former MPs”, adding: “Just because someone was a minister does not mean they automatically come back as a minister again. Just because someone had a seat before does not mean the party owes them another one.

“Everyone starts from scratch. Everyone has to earn their place.”

News.content:

An In-N-Out Burger employee killed in a mass shooting outside one of the fast food chain’s Idaho restaurants was killed while working her first-ever job, according to reports. ​

The shooting unfolded in Twin Falls on Saturday, with three victims being killed during the attack. According to the Twin Falls Police Department, the suspect in the shooting was identified as 24-year-old Chad Williams, who died from a self-inflicted gunshot wound. ​

However, the family of late In-N-Out employee Ashley Garibay told The California Post that working at the chain was her first job and that she “fell in love” with it.​

“She proudly traveled to open new stores, and her dream was to one day manage an In-N-Out store,” the family said. “She was passionate about serving customers and left this world doing what she loved to do.”​

A statement given by the family to The Los Angeles Times revealed that they have been left “heartbroken and devastated” by 23-year-old Garibay’s death.

open image in gallery Ashley Garibay was killed during a shooting outside an Idaho In-N-Out while working her first ever job ( Supplied )

​“She was a friend to all, and no matter what difficulties she was facing, she always found a way to help others find the light in the darkness,” Garibay’s family said. ​

A GoFundMe campaign launched to raise money for funeral services has raised over $23,000 as of August 4.

Twin Falls police say that they first received reports of a shooting on August 1 at around 2.29 p.m.​

Authorities also confirmed that seven victims were injured, two of whom were treated and released and three of whom are in stable condition.

Two others are in critical condition.​

Williams, the deceased suspect, is believed to have acted alone. ​

In a statement shared online, In-N-Out CEO Lynsi Snyder said that Williams attacked victims both on and off In-N-Out’s property and ended his life shortly after shooting “innocent people who never saw it coming.”

​“In-N-Out will be mourning with the families and praying for them as they tread through a very painful season,” Snyder wrote. ​

Jordan Salinas, a 35-year-old private citizen, told ABC News that he confronted the shooting after he spotted Williams aiming a rifle at passing vehicles.

open image in gallery Twin Falls police say that they received reports of a shooting at 2.29 pm on August 1 ( AP )

"He seemed unusually comfortable aiming that rifle at those cars," Salinas said. "As soon as some rounds started coming at him, everything changed immediately. All that bravado he had immediately crumbled."

During a Sunday news conference, Twin Falls Police Chief Matthew Hicks said that Salinas and an armed off-duty Idaho State Police trooper confronting the suspect helped drive Williams away from the scene and saved lives.

A second victim was identified to The Associated Press as Christopher Claunch by his sister, Kimberley Castaneda. ​

Garren Taylor, one of Claunch’s friends, said the late man was known by friends as “Toph” and had dedicated his life to helping people get sober. ​

“He helped hundreds of people,” Taylor told the publication. “He was just a gift to anyone he came in contact with. It wasn’t about the paycheck; his attitude was: ‘I get to help someone today.’”​

The In-N-Out location where the shooting took place opened just weeks ago on July 24, according to a company press release.

Britain has experienced a scorching summer, creating ideal conditions for outdoor cooking enthusiasts to fire up their grills.

Jon Finch, Weber brand engagement manager for EMEA and co-author of Grillstock: The BBQ Book, notes the exceptional duration of the season.

"Oh, it’s been endless. Absolutely," he remarked. "I barbecue all-year round, rain or shine.

“Christmas turkey on the grill, all that good stuff. But to be able to sit out, be warm and comfortable whilst grilling, and not having to worry about the weather, is fantastic."

Finch further highlighted the persistent heat: "And it’s not really showing any signs of letting up either," he added. "It seems to be heatwave after heatwave – we’re bouncing between them."

This continuous grilling might tempt many to overlook the chore of cleaning their barbecue, especially when anticipating another session the following day.

However, experts stress that a clean grill is paramount not only for ensuring food safety but also for significantly extending the appliance's lifespan.

As Finch points out: “Quite often, when you’re cooking on the grill, you’ve got friends and family round, you want to hang out with them; or you’ve got food ready to cook and just want to get on with that.

“So I think it’s hard to do it there and then [clean], but quite often a little bit of maintenance straight after you grill; and then a bit of maintenance either well in advance of cooking, or just before you put food on, really pays benefits.”

The live-fire cooking expert shares his top tips to keeping your barbie spick and span.

Get rid of debris

“I think the enemy of the inside of a barbecue is moisture,” warns Finch.

So when you finish cooking, he says if you generally either close the lid on your gas grill, or close off the air vents on a charcoal grill, there won’t be any airflow.

“And any moisture that’s trapped in there is not doing any good. Bits of food are going to go mouldy. Any exposed bits of metal or steel could tend to oxidise a little bit, unless it’s coated or enamelled.

open image in gallery The food and any built-up gunk on your grill will come away so much quicker and easier if your grill is hot ( Alamy/PA )

He continues: “So we really want to keep soap and water, and moisture in general, outside of the internal working parts of the grill.

“The outside of the grill is fine for for soapy water because that dries off really quick and easy; but inside just stick to scraping it, brushing it and getting rid of as much debris as you can.”

Clean whilst hot

This is a really basic one, suggests Finch. The food and any built-up gunk on your grill will come away so much quicker and easier if your grill is hot.

“So the easiest thing to do, and I know it’s one extra step, especially if you’re entertaining… but when you finish cooking, crank your grill up to hot and give it a good scrub down.

“Especially the grill grates because they’re the bits food has had contact with, and make sure you get off as much of that residual burnt-on food and grease as you can.

“But the flip side is you don’t want to be too rigorous at that point, because a light coating of oil across the grill grates helps protect it from the elements, moisture, anything like that.”

It’s about getting any bits of food off the grill whilst it’s still hot, and then if you want to give it a deep clean, wait until the grill cools down.

“Take the grill grates out, then take a plastic spatula once it’s cold and scrape out the body,” he advises. “The underneath of where you’ve been cooking your food, making sure that’s all clear of grease and any bits of food and debris as well.”

open image in gallery The food and any built-up gunk on your grill will come away so much quicker and easier if your grill is hot ( Vonhaus )

Clean before you cook, not after

“So it’s good to give a good scrub down of your grill grates when you finish cleaning,” underlines Finch.

“But alternatively, if you want to keep that layer of oil on the grill grates, leave it like that. Just get the food off, and then next time you cook, get it nice and hot, and give it a really good clean a second time.

“So that’ll keep it in the best possible condition.”

Top-down cleaning

It’s important to begin at the top of the grill and work your way down.

“When the grill’s cold, start with the grill grates and give those a good clean. Then lift the grill grates out, and go down to the next layer.

“Clean the inside of the body, then clean the charcoal grates down the bottom… so everything’s funnelling right down to the bottom of the grill,” explains Finch.

This ensures you’re working everything… “the grease, the debris, right down to the bottom; so it’s into the into the trap that’s designed to collect it all,” he adds.

open image in gallery It’s important to begin at the top of the grill and work your way down when cleaning a BBQ ( Weber )

Leave off the chemicals

“Wherever possible, avoid using chemicals on the grill at all,” advises Finch.

Heat and a bit of elbow grease should do the job, but if you must, “look specifically for grill grate cleaners designed to be used on surfaces that food’s going to be in contact with.”

But if you want to get a really nice shine on the outside of the grill, he suggests using a specialised enamel or stainless steel cleaner without aggressive chemicals.

“A well-maintained grill will keep on going for decades, and the number one rule is keep it clean, and it will serve you well,” says Finch confidently.

More than 1,700 people have died in eastern Congo in the fastest-growing outbreak of the Ebola virus, new data reveals.

The latest government update confirms 3,802 cases and 1,707 fatalities as of Tuesday. Dr Jean Kaseya, Director-General of Africa CDC, expressed uncertainty regarding when the outbreak might peak during a visit to Bunia, near the epicentre.

He cautioned that a significant 80 per cent of new infections are now stemming from community spread rather than traceable contacts.

Declared on 15 May, this particular outbreak is linked to the Bundibugyo virus, for which no approved vaccines or treatments currently exist. The response has been severely hampered by a confluence of factors, including delays in contact tracing, difficulties accessing affected regions, deep-seated community mistrust, and persistent violence from armed groups and some residents.

The disease is predominantly concentrated in eastern Congo’s remote Ituri province, accounting for nearly 90 per cent of cases, though it has also spread to five other provinces, including the major city of Kisangani. Neighbouring Uganda, however, declared itself Ebola-free in mid-June after its last patient was discharged.

open image in gallery The Ebola outbreak is spreading at record speed ( Reuters )

The crisis is further exacerbated by the fact that patient zero remains unidentified, and ongoing displacement due to armed conflict and illegal mining makes tracing thousands of contacts incredibly difficult.

Healthcare workers, crucial to the containment effort, have faced immense challenges. In Mongbwalu, staff issued an ultimatum over unpaid wages, threatening to escalate action if demands were not met within 24 hours.

Previously, workers in Bunia went on strike over pay and dangerous conditions. The World Health Organization (WHO) reports that over 100 healthcare professionals have been infected since the outbreak began.

This current outbreak has claimed more lives at a quicker pace than any previous one, including the 2014-2016 epidemic which saw over 11,000 deaths from 28,000 cases.

That earlier outbreak took approximately eight months to reach 1,000 fatalities, highlighting the accelerated nature of the current crisis. A significant funding gap, attacks on health centres, and the ongoing conflict in eastern Congo continue to impede effective intervention.

Amid these grave challenges, a glimmer of hope has emerged with the recent commencement of a highly anticipated study in Ituri, testing two potential Ebola treatments.

For the first time in more than 100 years, a total solar eclipse is coming to mainland Spain.

Throw in a crescendoing meteor shower and a six-planet parade on the same day, and stargazers will be treated to a view like no other.

Daytime darkness will descend August 12 across the Iberian Peninsula close to sunset — plus slivers of Greenland and Iceland — as the sun, moon and Earth align perfectly in the sky.

Starting near the North Pole before tracking south, totality will last up to two minutes and 18 seconds, an appetizer for an even longer solar show next year — a 6 and a half minute extravaganza that will sweep from Spain to North Africa and the Middle East.

open image in gallery An information panel displays measures on how to safely view an upcoming solar eclipse on a street in Palma de Mallorca on July 31, 2026 ( AFP/Getty )

It will take 1 and a half hours for the umbra, or moon’s sun-blocking shadow, to race along the 5,130-mile (8,260-kilometer) course, most of it over an empty Atlantic. Maximum totality will occur off Iceland’s west coast. By the time it reaches a small patch of Portugal and then Spain with its massive crowds, totality will have dwindled to a minute or so. The spectacle will end in the Mediterranean.

Eclipse chasers gear up for the solar spectacle

Hundreds of millions more on the sidelines are in for a treat as well.

A partial eclipse will delight as far away as Alaska and Siberia, enveloping Canada, the northern U.S., and much of Europe and West Africa.

The closer to totality’s course, the more the sun will vanish behind the moon – 94% coverage in Dublin and 83% in Oslo, Norway. Montreal will see an 18% bite out of the sun, tapering to 9% in New York and 2% in Norfolk, Virginia.

Special eclipse glasses are crucial. even if a morsel of sun is showing.

open image in gallery A woman is looking at the sun through a pair of special cardboard glasses designed to protect her eyes while watching the solar eclipse on August 12 in Saint-Pol-de-Leon, in the Finistere department of Brittany in western France, on August 1, 2026. (Photo by Nicolas Guyonnet / Hans Lucas / AFP via Getty Images) ( AFP/Getty )

Adding to the cosmic wonder, the day begins with six of our neighboring planets forming an arc in the sky before dawn and end with the Perseid meteor shower peaking after nightfall under the new moon. Streaking meteors could photobomb totality, with some of the brighter planets and stars visible in the background.

Eclipse mapmaker Michael Zeiler is chasing an even more elusive interloper: the northern lights.

For his 13th total solar eclipse, Zeiler will be on a cruise ship in a Greenland fjord, sailing as a guest lecturer. He’ll point a video camera toward the north to capture any aurora forming during totality. A massive outburst from the sun would be the icing on his eclipse cake.

“What gets me excited is viewing rare phenomena,” Zeiler said in an email.

He’s not the only one revved up.

See who's hosting solar eclipse watch parties and science experiments

The European Space Agency will host a live webcast from Spain’s Astrophysical Observatory of Javalambre and a public celebration in Leon. NASA will provide its own coverage, as will the Italian-based Virtual Telescope Project and others.

“For me, it’s not just a scientific moment. It’s not just an incredible alignment of heavenly bodies. It’s also a very human moment,” said ESA’s director of science Carole Mundell. “It’s a real human connection between us with our feet planted on the Earth and the cosmos.”

open image in gallery This image provided by NASA and captured by the Artemis II crew from lunar orbit, April 6, 2026, shows the Moon eclipsing the Sun. ( (NASA via AP, File )

Two of ESA’s space telescopes will observe the eclipsed sun and its corona, or outer atmosphere. Proba-3, the space agency’s artificial eclipse-making satellite duo, will be in the wrong part of its orbit during totality as seen from Earth, but will try to sneak in some before-and-after shots.

U.S. college research teams are also pitching in, launching more than 60 high-altitude balloons from Spain and Iceland to study Earth’s atmosphere and other changes during the eclipse when the temperature momentarily drops. They launched 10 times as many balloons during the 2024 total solar eclipse that captivated North America.

“A couple of minutes isn’t a lot of time, but it’s still plenty to affect the atmosphere and to make that cold, dark shadow of the moon on Earth,” said Montana State University’s Angela Des Jardins, who leads the NASA-funded balloon project.

Southwest Research Institute’s Amir Caspi also expects a scientific bonanza from his study aboard a NASA high-altitude plane. Four cameras will record the corona in nine wavelengths as the jet chases the eclipse at 460 mph (740 kph), extending totality to nearly three minutes in the air. Caspi anticipates thousands of images gathered from each camera during those precious 180 seconds.

"It’s true the eclipse is short, but it’s still incredibly valuable," he said.

And there's more to come

An exceptionally long total solar eclipse is in store for 2027, yielding nearly three times more observation time.

The southern tip of Spain will take center stage on Aug. 2, 2027, with up to six minutes and 23 seconds of totality extending into Morocco, Algeria, Libya, Egypt, Saudi Arabia, Yemen and Somalia.

open image in gallery In this image provided by NASA the Artemis II crew, counterclockwise from top left, Mission Specialist Christina Koch, Mission Specialist Jeremy Hansen, Commander Reid Wiseman and Pilot Victor Glover pose with eclipse viewers during a lunar flyby on April 6, 2026. ( NASA via AP, File )

Then on Jan. 26, 2028, a ring-of-fire eclipse will round out Spain’s celestial trifecta — “a lucky coincidence,” according to ESA’s Mundell.

It’s all the more extraordinary considering Spain’s last full solar eclipse — not counting the Canary Islands — occurred two days before the Titanic’s sinking in 1912. Because that rare hybrid eclipse toggled between a ring-of-fire and just a few seconds of totality for Spain, some consider 1905 for the country’s last pull-out-all-the-stops solar eclipse.

The Royal Observatory of Belgium’s Andrei Zhukov can’t get enough of them regardless of their length or origin. His Proba-3 science mission has created more than 60 simulated total solar eclipses over the past two years, with the longest lasting five hours and 38 minutes from two satellites flying in formation.

“We’re looking forward to more eclipses,” Zhukov said, “natural or artificial.”

News.title: 10 best armchairs for relaxing in style, reviewed by an interiors expert
News.content:
Your questions about armchairs answered

What is the best armchair?

I rate Habitat Dawson fabric swivel chair as the best overall. Excellent value, it's a comfy swivel design that is neutral enough to suit a living area, kitchen, office or bedroom space. It comes with a matching footstool for an extra £60, so you can put your feet up and relax.

My best budget buy is the Nyla accent chair from Dusk. At 81.5cm high, it’s a relatively compact armchair that can be easily transported around the home and it’s neutral enough to work with most colours and finishes. You could use it to add extra seating around a sofa, as a space to sit in an open-plan kitchen and living room or in a corner of your bedroom.

Also worth a mention is Loaf’s slow riser, which is simply dreamy and its design works well in both classic and more contemporary set ups. While it comes with a premium price tag, I think it’s a design that will age gracefully through the years, so well worth the spend.

How I tested armchairs

To find the best armchair, I called in a selection of attractive designs from well-known brands. I placed the armchairs up around my house – carrying out the odd bit of DIY to set them up when necessary – and have taken time out to try them out personally. I’ve rated them on the following criteria:

Design: I’ve rated each armchair on its aesthetics and how attractive it looks. I’ve honed in on its materials – be it wood or metal – and fabric options – be it faux leather, velvet or linen. I’ve assessed how durable I think each chair is and whether I think its craftsmanship has the quality to stand the test of time.

I’ve rated each armchair on its aesthetics and how attractive it looks. I’ve honed in on its materials – be it wood or metal – and fabric options – be it faux leather, velvet or linen. I’ve assessed how durable I think each chair is and whether I think its craftsmanship has the quality to stand the test of time. Comfort: I tested out each armchair personally, and asked family members and guests to give their opinion too. I took into consideration firmness and support – softer cushions feel comfy at first, but firmer ones can offer more support over time, for example. While style is important, comfort is undeniably what will ensure the chair becomes a permanent fixture in your home, after all.

I tested out each armchair personally, and asked family members and guests to give their opinion too. I took into consideration firmness and support – softer cushions feel comfy at first, but firmer ones can offer more support over time, for example. While style is important, comfort is undeniably what will ensure the chair becomes a permanent fixture in your home, after all. Ease of cleaning and durability: An armchair will get a lot of wear and tear, so choosing a design that is practical and easy to keep looking box fresh is important. I’ve rated each design on how easy the materials are to care for and how easy the design is to clean.

What should you look for in a good armchair?

“Think about how you intend to use the armchair as this will dictate what kind of style you choose,” says interior designer Andrew Dunning of London Contemporary. “Is it for reading? Then you’ll probably want something with a higher backrest for supporting your head and neck. Or if you intend to use it while watching TV, perhaps you’ll want to opt for a design with a matching footstool. If it’s to furnish an empty stretch of wall or corner of your living space, a bold, colourful design or one with a unique shape will add the wow-factor to your design scheme. But no matter what design you choose, comfort is key as the best armchair should be cherished, used daily and just get better with age.”

How do I clean a wood and leather armchair?

“When cleaning an armchair with a leather seat and wooden frame, it's important to treat each material separately to avoid damaging the finish,” says Emma Mannion, cleaning expert at Astonish.

Wipe down the leather seat with a dry microfibre cloth to remove any dust and surface dirt. For a deeper clean, use a slightly damp cloth with a small amount of diluted mild soap, wiping gently over the surface before drying it straight away with a clean cloth. For the wooden arms and legs, use a soft cloth to remove dust, then wipe with a barely damp cloth and a mild cleaning solution, always following the direction of the wood grain. Finish by drying the wood thoroughly to prevent moisture from affecting the finish.

How do I clean a fabric armchair?

“Your vacuum's upholstery attachment is your best friend for this,’ says Catherine Green, sustainable cleaning expert at Smol.

Clean away loose crumbs, dust, or pet hair with a good vacuum. Pop any removable cushion covers in a cool wash. For fixed upholstery or a general refresh (this method works wonderfully for velvet sofas and chairs too), mix half a litre of warm water with half a teaspoon of washing-up liquid to create some suds. With a microfibre cloth, apply a small amount of the suds, and gently rub the fabric in circular motions. Once the dirt has lifted, wiping the area with another clean, slightly damp cloth. The golden rule here is to make sure cloths aren't too wet; soaking the fabric can lead to water-logging and nasty, musty smells building up. If you just have a few isolated marks, spot cleaning with a bleach-free stain gel is a fantastic alternative. To tackle any lingering odours, a sprinkle of bicarbonate of soda left on the fabric for at least 30 minutes before vacuuming acts as a brilliant natural deodoriser.

Why you can trust IndyBest reviews

Emily Peck is a lifestyle journalist with more than 20 years of experience writing about homes and interiors, gardens, gadgets, wellbeing, fitness and modern living. Her work has appeared in publications including Ideal Home, GQ, Livingetc, The Telegraph and Wired.

Over the years, she has trialled a wide range of products – from dining chairs and beehives, to ice baths and hair dryers – to make her an expert in product testing. Follow her on Instagram @emilypeckwriter or connect with her on LinkedIn.

News.title: Forget 10,000 steps a day: This is how many you really need
News.content:

You’ve probably heard that hitting 10,000 steps a day is the key to health and longevity. This magic number feels like a medical rule, handed down by doctors across the globe.

But where did it come from? And is it even true?

Let’s step back to Japan in 1964

Believe it or not, but the infamous 10,000 steps a day recommendation didn’t come from a research laboratory. In fact, it is not scientific at all. It came from a Japanese pedometer called the manpo-kei which translates to “10,000-step meter”.

This pedometer went on sale just after the 1964 Tokyo Olympics, at a time when there was a growing worry people in Japan weren’t moving enough.

The number was mainly chosen was because it was catchy and easy to remember. The Japanese kanji character for 10,000 – 万 – even looks a little like a walking person, which may have played a role in deciding on the number.

Believe it or not, but the infamous 10,000 steps a day recommendation didn’t come from a research laboratory ( Getty/iStock )

So 10,000 was a slogan to sell a step-counter, not an evidence-based recommendation.

So many ideas about what makes us sick, or keeps us well, sound plausible. Early studies might sound promising. But then something gets twisted. In this series, we investigate how a grain of truth ends up as a common health myth. And we untangle what went wrong along the way.

So what does the research say?

Getting 10,000 steps a day can be a useful goal, and it will have a positive impact on your health. But you can reap health benefits from even less.

A recently published systematic review combined the results of 57 studies and more than 160,000 adults to examine the relationship between daily steps and health. Interestingly, they found 7,000 steps a day was where health benefits were maximised.

Reaching 7,000 steps a day was linked to a 47% lower risk of dying early, a 25% lower risk of cardiovascular disease (heart disease and stroke), a 14% lower risk of type 2 diabetes, a 38% lower risk of dementia, a 22% lower some of depression and a 28% lower risk of falls.

Some health benefits started well before 7,000 steps.

The researchers found going from about 2,000 to 4,000 steps a day makes a real difference. These health benefits then increase again slightly from 4,000 to 7,000 steps a day, after which the benefits start to plateau.

These results align closely with other research looking at all types of physical activity, where going from being inactive to moderately active yields the largest health improvements. Moving from a moderate to high level of activity does provide additional benefits, but these are much smaller in magnitude.

Why walking is good for you

Walking is a form of “aerobic” exercise. It raises your heart rate and places stress on your respiratory, muscular and cardiovascular systems.

If you do it regularly, it can improve your heart and metabolic health, and reduce your bodyweight.

Walking can also reduce stress and improve mental health, possibly due improvements in feelings of self-esteem and self-efficacy that comes with regular movement.

Steps versus minutes

There is some additional nuance that needs to be considered when discussing how far you walk each day: how hard you walk.

Most people choose a walking pace that pushes them into the realm of “moderate intensity” exercise. However, the health benefits of exercise scale up with exercise intensity: you get more bang for your buck from more intense exercise.

So, if you pick up the pace and move towards a vigorous exercise intensity (where it’s hard to maintain a conversation), you will get larger health benefits in less time. This is why official exercise guidelines treat 75 minutes of vigorous activity as roughly equal to 150 minutes of moderate activity.

With this in mind, rather than focusing on steps, you might be better off focusing on the number of minutes you accumulate each week.

About the author Hunter Bennett is a Lecturer in Exercise Science at Adelaide University. This article was first published by The Conversation and is republished under a Creative Commons licence. Read the original article.

Recent research even suggests short bursts of high-intensity exercise spread across the day can have surprising health benefits.

So, if you’re short on time, walking faster is one of the simplest ways to get more out of that same walk.

But walking alone isn’t enough

Walking covers the “aerobic” side of fitness well. However, it doesn’t really address the “anaerobic” side.

Anaerobic fitness refers to your muscle mass, muscle strength, and power. Having higher anaerobic fitness is linked to having a better quality of life and lower risk of mortality as you get older.

This is why most health authorities recommend muscle-strengthening activities (such as lifting weights) at least two days a week.

This will also help reduce your risk of type 2 diabetes, while also helping you avoid falls and stay independent for longer as you get older.

If you can aim to hit 7,000 steps each day, and add in weight training twice per week, you’re going to have most of your bases covered from a health perspective.

News.title: World’s first seahorse hospital fights to protect them from extinction
News.content:
With careful precision, marine biologist Linda Albonetti extracts a 10cm-long injured seahorse – a heavily pregnant male – from an aquarium tank to apply healing ointment to its wound.

Linda, 29, coordinator at the world’s first specialist seahorse hospital, is currently caring for around 50 of these tiny creatures, all of which were brought in by local fishing crews after becoming snagged in their nets.

The seahorse will be kept for a few more days before it is released back into the Adriatic Sea, giving it time to recover from the cut to the soft, bony plates that form its outer carapace.

What the team here are doing is a literal drop in the ocean, a small attempt to fight back against the potential extinction of these remarkable fish.

In Europe and around countries like Indonesia, they are being poached in their millions for sale to a voracious Asian traditional medicine market where they are consumed as an aphrodisiac and alleged cure for impotence, asthma and kidney problems.

“There is definitely a downward trend in the overall seahorse population because they are being collected for the Asian market,” says Linda. “Technically, they cannot be exported to countries such as China, but there is no specific law preventing that trade. They do not have the same protections as sea turtles, for example.

“It is not happening in this part of Italy yet, but it is further south, off the Mediterranean coast. That is why it is so important that we monitor their numbers and maintain a good relationship with the local fishermen.”

News.title: The 13 best castle hotels in England
News.content:
Few places capture the imagination quite like a castle, and England is home to some of the most remarkable places to spend the night. If it’s not the romance of waking up in a canopied four-poster bed, or losing ourselves in centuries-old tapestries and visceral oil paintings, we are lured by tales of brave knights and plotting dignitaries, duplicitous royals and ghosts parleying secrets in the hallways.

Part of the magic is spending an afternoon wandering grounds and gardens followed by evenings in front of a roaring fire, or dining in a banquet hall that may have hosted medieval kings and queens. While not every castle has crenellated battlements, glistening moats or royal connections, each stony stronghold on our list has something special that makes it worth travelling for. In this modern age that might include a spa, fine-dining restaurant or extra touches like free admission to exhibitions and museum tours. Here’s our pick of the best castle hotels in England.

News.title: Careless Liverpool concede same goal twice in second-half capitulation against Leeds
News.content:
Soldier Field in Chicago hosts an all-Premier League tie encounter as Liverpool take on Leeds as both sides bring their US tours to a close. Both Premier League encounters between these sides last season ended in draws; a 3-3 draw at Elland Road was followed up by a 0-0 stalemate at Anfield. The draw at Elland Road was immediately followed by Mohamed Salah speaking to the media, claiming he had been thrown under the bus.

It is a new era at Liverpool as former Bournemouth boss Andoni Iraola has replaced Arne Slot at Anfield. They kicked off the Iraola era in Nashville, Tennessee, with a 4-2 win over Sunderland, following that up with another victory in New York on Wednesday night, beating Wrexham 1-0, and will be aiming to make it three wins from three on their US tour.

“I think it [the US tour] has been really, really useful,” Iraola said in an interview on the official Liverpool website. Obviously, you spend a lot of time with the players, with the staff, you get all the information you can. And I think there is also an evolution, it has to be. We start to understand each other better, what we need to do. Every game, I hope we can get closer and closer and put ourselves in a position where the few players that still are not here start to train also, they are helped by the others.”

Virgil van Dijk and Cody Gakpo resumed training back on Merseyside whilst Alexis Mac Allister, Alisson and Victor Munoz are yet to return to training following their World Cup exploits. The trio of Florian Wirtz, Alexander Isak and Ryan Gravenberch are all set to feature for the first time this pre-season.

Leeds’ pre-season campaign began with a 3-2 loss to Championship Wrexham in Tampa, Florida before beating Sunderland 1-0 in New Jersey courtesy of a long-range strike from Lukas Nmecha. Former Liverpool man Harry Wilson joined Leeds on a free from Fulham this summer.

“Really tough but that is expected,” Wilson said. That is what pre-season is for, building up a base for when the season starts, making sure you are in the best physical position you can be to attack the season. It has been good. I played against them [Leeds] twice last year when I was at Fulham. Both games were really, really tough games.

“I think when the fans have got a good team to support, I think that [the atmosphere at Elland Road] goes up a notch. I think the size of the club was a massive part of me coming. Then speaking to the guys, the chairman, the sporting director, and seeing kind of the plans and the aims for the club, it is something I wanted to be a part of.”

Team news to follow shortly.

News.title: Oil plummets as Trump calls off Iran strikes
News.content:
Oil prices have plunged after Donald Trump called off strikes and said the US and Iran would hold further peace talks.

Brent crude, the international benchmark, sank as much as 9.5pc early on Monday to less than $82 a barrel after the US president said he had halted plans for “disastrous” strikes.

Mr Trump said: “Obviously, they don’t want to be attacked. They knew the extent of the attack because they saw it forming.

“Now what we’re doing is we’re talking to them in the form of a negotiation. It begins tomorrow afternoon.”

Mr ‌Trump also ordered oil companies to lower petrol prices for American ‌consumers ‌and criticised ⁠Chevron’s chief executive for not crediting his administration for supporting the fossil fuel industry.

The president said that he had been asked by Iran as well as US partners Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates and Qatar to hold off on strikes. He halted plans for a major attack against Iran on Saturday, which he said would have been the biggest since the Second World War.

Mr Trump claimed the sides were on the “perimeter” of a peace deal.

Oil’s sharp fall also sent the cost of government borrowing lower on Monday over hopes that it would ease inflation.

The yield on 10-year UK gilts, a benchmark for what the Treasury pays to borrow money, dropped from 5.05pc to 4.98pc, while the equivalent US bonds dropped from 4.74pc to 4.69pc.

Stock markets in Europe also rose, with the FTSE 100 up 0.2pc, the Cac 40 in Paris up 0.3pc and the Dax in Frankfurt climbing 0.1pc.

News.title: Inside the trial for a vaccine to end malaria
News.content:
A small group of brave volunteers were given an experimental vaccine in Oxford this week in a bid to bring to an end the centuries-old scourge of malaria.

“I’m on my second vaccine now. Then I’m due to have my third vaccine soon, and then in November, I’ll be given malaria,” said an upbeat Mike Luciw, a 32-year-old local who works in recruitment.

“The hope is to help find something that could save millions of people.”

There are already two licenced vaccines for malaria but the new Oxford “RH5” shot is not like anything that has come before.

The existing jabs only act against malaria as it moves towards the liver in the early stage of infection, and provide only partial protection.

The new combination vaccine, in contrast, is designed to fight it off both at the liver stage and in the wider bloodstream, effectively knocking it out altogether.

The project is being run by the husband and wife team of Simon Draper, Professor of Vaccinology and Translational Medicine at the University of Oxford, and Professor Angela Minassian, an infectious disease specialist and clinical lead for their malaria programme in Oxford’s Department of Paediatrics.

“The dream for malaria … has been to have these two lines of defence, liver and blood, so if the first line fails, you’ve got a second,” says Prof Draper, who leads on the science.

“Our dream is to have a vaccine that gives over 90 per cent efficacy in African children,” adds Prof Minassian, who heads the clinical trials for the new jab.

News.title: Dowman weaves his magic and new signing shines as Arsenal hit ground running
News.content:
Hello and welcome to our live coverage for this pre-season friendly between Girona and Arsenal at Estadi Montilivi in Catalonia.

With the transfer speculation surrounding Vinícius Júnior’s and Bruno Guimaraes’ potential moves to Arsenal ramping up, the reigning Premier League champions are in action against Girona as they step up their preparations ahead of the upcoming campaign.

Unlike other Premier League heavyweights, Arsenal have kept their pre-season tour relatively local with a selection of games in Spain, Ireland and England, before they face Manchester City in the FA Community Shield on August 16 at the Millennium Stadium in Cardiff.

Arsenal beat League One side MK Dons 3-0 in a behind-closed-doors friendly on July 25 at the Sobha Realty Training Centre, thanks to goals from Reiss Nelson, Ethan Nwaneri and Ceadach O’Neill.

After featuring in this victory and setting up Nelson for the opener, Christos Tzolis will be looking to continue his positive momentum with his new club, after joining Arsenal for £34m earlier this summer. Many fans will be keeping a close eye on the recently-signed winger given that various core members of last season’s Premier League-winning squad are yet to return from their post-World Cup breaks, having progressed deep in the competition.

Tournament winners David Raya, Martin Zubimendi and Mikel Merino, Norway captain Martin Odegaard, as well as England internationals Bukayo Saka, Declan Rice, Eberechi Eze and Noni Madueke are all missing for this game, while France’s William Saliba is out injured and set for an extended period on the sidelines.

Those who exited the World Cup earlier than the aforementioned players, including Gabriel Magalhaes, Gabriel Martinelli, Piero Hincapie, Kai Havertz, and Viktor Gyokeres, have all joined up with the squad in northern Spain.

Mikel Arteta’s men will play a wounded Girona, who suffered relegation from the top flight of Spanish football last season due to a 19th-place finish.

Kick-off is at 19:00, with team news arriving shortly.

News.title: Josh Kerr turns ‘race of the century’ into one-sided show of power
News.content:
“It means everything – absolutely incredible,” said Kerr, who joined the rendition of Flower of Scotland before closing his eyes to soak up the moment in a stadium where he had competed as a child in even the shot put.

“To do it in front of a Scottish crowd, where I learned how to race, doesn’t get any better,” he added. “I came here week after week growing up as a kid. This was the championship of my season with the world indoors and going after the record. This was on the calendar before any of that. I think a British crowd deserved more from me and I owed them that.”

Of the tactics compared to his world record, where he had to hold an even pace throughout, Kerr stressed the importance of staying calm and not being tempted into pushing too soon. “London was a big stress, pushing my body to the extreme limit,” he said. “Doing a championship race is a nice clean slate; using your brain instead of your body. It’s how I love to race.

“When you’re running that slow, your job is not to waste energy and I did that. I knew an opportunity would open up. Then it was about staying awake and alive and trying to get some space. felt like I had plenty of gears left in me.”

Kerr had emerged to a huge home ovation and, with the Proclaimers booming out as the runners completed the first two laps, he was content to stay in the pack even as Myers followed. There was then only one brief moment of concern as the runners began gathering themselves during the penultimate lap and Kerr became momentarily boxed in.

News.title: Exciting young talent JJ Gabriel makes debut as Man Utd beat Atletico Madrid
News.content:
Manchester United 2 Atletico Madrid 1

JJ Gabriel showed glimpses of his potential as he made his Manchester United debut in their 2-1 win over Atletico Madrid in Stockholm.

The 15-year-old may have been introduced with only eight minutes remaining, but, given how highly rated he is, it was a significant move by Michael Carrick to give him game time in the senior team.

There were hints of why Gabriel is so well regarded during those eight minutes, as he found space in the centre of the pitch and linked well with Leny Yoro. But he was also on the receiving end of some physical challenges – something he will have to grow accustomed to the more he plays at senior level.

Yoro, who himself made his senior debut as a 16-year-old for Lille, was impressed by Gabriel and said: “He’s a really good player. He is still really young and still has a lot to learn and a lot to improve on but he’s really humble and still working, so I’m happy for him to get his first minutes. I hope, for him, it’s going to continue like that.”

VIRAL England fan Andy Milne has revealed that he was DETAINED by police at the World Cup final for a bizarre reason.

Milne has become a familiar face for viewers at major international tournaments over the years.



The supporter has followed England around the world for over 40 years and is regularly spotted on TV in the crowd.

Most recently, he travelled to the United States for the World Cup and even managed to get a ticket to the final.



However, he almost missed the match between Spain and Argentina completely after being stopped by police.

Recalling the unusual situation on The Pezzadox Show recently, Milne explained: “I’ve been to eight previous World Cup finals and I’ve got my tickets for all of those World Cup finals. It means a lot to keep those.

“I’ve also got a few other tickets. I’ve got a 1966 World Cup final ticket that’s signed by Geoff Hurst.

“So this time, of course I want to keep my World Cup final ticket, but they’re all electronic so they won’t issue a paper ticket.

“So I hatched a plan and I went to a ticket resolution centre. I told them that I’d lost my phone, is there anything I could do about it. They gave me a paper ticket.

“I planned this in advance and I thought, when I get that, and I’ve got shorts, and it’s sweaty and everything out there, it’s going to get ruined.

“So I decided to take a paperback book to put it inside to keep it nice and flat and pristine, which I did.

“I’m going into the ground and security is high, Donald Trump is there, you’ve got police everywhere and loads of security guards.

“You’ve got to put what’s in your pockets there and walk through the thing that goes beep.

“So I walked in, put my paperback book down, and this policeman was saying: ‘What is that?’



“I said: ‘It’s a book,’ and he told the security guy: ‘Search it,’ so the security guy picked it up and rifled through it.

“They pointed to the book. He picked up the book, had a look at it and just turned round to those two officers and said: ‘F***ing idiots.”

USA superstar Folarin Balogun has been offered to Tottenham.

It comes amid Tottenham manager Roberto de Zerbi being on the lookout for a quality striker to compete with Dominic Solanke and provide squad depth.



And his prayers may have been answered in the form of a World Cup wonder – and former Arsenal star.

SunSport understands that Balogun has been offered to Tottenham via intermediaries.

Sports.title: Arsene Wenger makes decision on future as Arsenal hero is named in Uefa’s legal letter to under-fire Fifa boss Infantino
Sports.content:
UEFA are cranking up the pressure on Fifa big shot Arsene Wenger – but the Arsenal hero is refusing to quit, according to reports.

Wenger has been name-dropped in a letter from Uefa threatening legal action against Fifa.



European football‘s governing body has been among the most vocal critics of Gianni Infantino‘s money-grabbing plan to sell stakes in the World Cup to private investors – which was scrapped on Saturday after fierce backlash.

And now they have called on Fifa’s head of global football development, Wenger, as well as 13 other top executives, to gather all the documentation they can find on the sell-off plan as they weigh up making it a legal matter.



Uefa’s letter, which was seen by The Times, read: “Uefa hereby gives formal notice that it is actively considering legal action, arbitration, and/or regulatory complaints arising out of and in connection with the FFE [Fifa Forward Enterprise] plan proposed by Fifa and all related matters.

“You and Fifa are required to take immediate steps to identify, locate, and preserve all documents and electronically stored information described in this notice that are in your or Fifa’s possession, custody, or control.”

Fifa president Infantino is hanging by a thread as rival governing bodies look to oust him immediately.

But Wenger, 76, has no intentions of going with him.

The same report states that the former Arsenal boss of 22 years feels he has a ‘mission to help youth football across the world’.

Wenger took the Fifa post in 2019, a year after leaving the Gunners, to oversee the growth and development of football globally.



BEST ONLINE CASINOS – TOP SITES IN THE UK

His role also gives him sway during reviews into Fifa rule changes and tournaments.

Powerful football figures are determined to get rid of Infantino, who has lost support from a number of key players in recent days.

The English and Welsh FAs are among those to have turned on the 56-year-old.

And after threatening to boycott the World Cup if the sell-off plan went ahead, chiefs from Uefa, Concacaf and the Asian Football Confederation are now ready to stage their own breakaway version of international football’s biggest tournament if Infantino remains in post.



The greedy Fifa boss was eyeing an astronomical salary jump from £2.6million to as much as £47m if the plan had come off.

He was also panned for suspending a one-match ban handed to USA striker Folarin Balogun at America’s home World Cup after a phone call from his pal Donald Trump.
