A Washington state man was arrested Monday on a first-degree arson charge in connection with the Old Trails Fire, one of several wildfires that have destroyed hundreds of structures and forced tens of thousands of people to evacuate the Spokane area, authorities said.

Aaron F. Farinacci, 37, was taken into custody after Spokane County Sheriff’s Office detectives and Washington Department of Natural Resources investigators developed probable cause to arrest him, according to the sheriff’s office.

Citizen tips and information from Airway Heights police officers and Spokane County sheriff’s deputies who responded to the initial call and conducted evacuations helped lead investigators to Farinacci, the sheriff’s office said.

Authorities described Farinacci as a convicted felon from Arizona but said they had found no documented criminal history involving fires.

Investigators have not connected Farinacci to the two other major blazes burning in the area, the Autumn Lane and Fairview fires, officials said.

PALISADES FIRE SUSPECT ALLEGEDLY DRIVEN BY 'SOCIETAL REVENGE,' BEHAVIORAL ANALYST TESTIFIES IN COURT

"We will be looking into any other crimes Mr. Farinacci may have committed in the past," Spokane County Sheriff John Nowels said during a news briefing.

Nowels said first-degree arson was the charge supported by probable cause at that stage of the investigation and cautioned that the case could change as authorities gathered additional evidence.

Detectives obtained an arrest warrant for Farinacci and a search warrant for his residence in the 2800 block of West Elliott Drive, according to the sheriff’s office.

Deputies served the warrant Monday and arrested Farinacci without incident. Authorities said detectives found a butane lighter and waterproof matches while detaining and searching him.

SPENCER PRATT REACTS TO SPOKANE DEVASTATION WITH BLUNT WILDFIRE WARNING AND MESSAGE OF FAITH

Farinacci was booked into the Spokane County Jail and was being held on $1 million bond.

The Old Trails Fire was first reported Saturday near North Old Trails Road and West Euclid Road. It became the largest of three destructive fires burning around Spokane and remained uncontained Monday, according to authorities and wire reports.

The three fires had collectively destroyed at least 700 structures and prompted evacuation orders affecting approximately 67,000 people as of Monday, according to The Associated Press. More than 1,000 firefighters were battling the blazes.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson declared a statewide wildfire emergency Saturday amid drought, unusually high temperatures and strong winds. The declaration also imposed a statewide prohibition on most outdoor and agricultural burning through Sept. 30.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

A Pennsylvania school bus aide was arrested after he allegedly inappropriately touched a 14-year-old girl with special needs and appeared to take photographs and videos of her with his cellphone, according to police.

Ali Khan, 62, was charged with endangering the welfare of a child, corruption of minors, indecent assault and related offenses, the Bensalem Township Police Department said.

Khan was being held at the Bucks County Correctional Facility after failing to post 10% of his $500,000 bail.

The girl’s parents contacted police on Thursday, July 30, to report that their daughter had allegedly been inappropriately touched by a bus aide earlier that day, according to investigators.

HIGH SCHOOL COUNSELOR PLEADS GUILTY TO MULTIPLE SEX CRIMES INVOLVING TEEN SHE WAS MEANT TO HELP

Police said their investigation determined that Khan allegedly touched the Bensalem High School student multiple times on Wednesday, July 29, and Thursday, July 30, while she was riding a bus to the school’s extended school year program.

Investigators said surveillance footage from inside the bus showed Khan directing the girl to a specific seat before allegedly touching her inappropriately while securing her seatbelt and after she was seated.

Police said the footage also appeared to show Khan engaging in sexual conduct and using a cellphone to photograph or record the girl.

"Bensalem Police would like to commend the victim of this assault for having the courage to come forward and report the assault," police said. "Additionally, Bensalem Police would like to thank the Bensalem School District for their assistance with this investigation. The safety and well-being of our students continues to be the top priority of both the Bensalem Township Police Department and the Bensalem School District."

The Bensalem Township School District said the employee was immediately removed from service and from the district pending the outcome of criminal and administrative investigations.

"The safety and well-being of our students is our highest priority," the district said in a statement. "Whenever concerns involving student safety are brought to our attention, we act immediately to protect students, support families, and cooperate fully with law enforcement. We are committed to conducting a thorough administrative review while respecting the integrity of the criminal investigation."

CALIFORNIA MIDDLE SCHOOL ASSISTANT PRINCIPAL NABBED IN CHILD SEX STING

World.title: Lindsay Clancy defense scores ‘extremely helpful’ psychosis concession as expert flags next hurdle

This story discusses suicide. If you or someone you know is having thoughts of suicide, contact the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline at 988 or 1-800-273-TALK (8255).

Lindsay Clancy’s attorney sought to blunt prosecutors’ portrayal of the Massachusetts mother as organized and calculating, pressing a hospital psychiatrist to acknowledge that a person can communicate, make plans and carry them out while experiencing psychosis.

"People can communicate and plan and act on plans even if they’re in the middle of a psychosis, right?" defense attorney Kevin Reddington asked Dr. Sejal Shah Monday.

HEATED LINDSAY CLANCY COURTROOM EXCHANGE OVER 911 CALL, CRIME SCENE PHOTOS SETS STAGE FOR MOM’S MURDER TRIAL

"Yes," Shah replied.

Reddington then asked whether someone must be "drooling and stumbling and unable to walk and talk" to be psychotic. Shah said no and agreed that a person in psychosis can still communicate with others.

Clancy is charged in the deaths of Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, 8 months, inside the family’s Duxbury home. Her defense maintains she was suffering from postpartum psychosis. Prosecutors argue she acted deliberately and understood what she was doing.

LINDSAY CLANCY’S EX-HUSBAND DETAILS ‘BIG SPIRAL’ AS EXPERT SAYS ONE PART ‘SCARED ME’ IN MOM’S MURDER TRIAL

Seth J. Zuckerman, a celebrity criminal defense attorney, former New York City prosecutor and founder of Zuckerman Legal Group, said the case will turn on Clancy’s mental state at the precise time the children were killed.

"What was in her mind at the exact time that she killed her children?" Zuckerman told Fox News Digital.

He said prosecutors have focused on Patrick Clancy’s trips to CVS and a local restaurant, along with his communications with his wife, to portray her as lucid during the critical time frame.

WATCH: Psychiatrist calls Lindsay Clancy an 'honest' patient

LINDSAY CLANCY’S EX-HUSBAND DETAILS PILL USE AS EXPERT SAYS EVIDENCE COULD SHAPE MURDER TRIAL

Shah, an associate chief of psychiatry and medicine at Brigham and Women’s Hospital, first evaluated Clancy five days after the killings.

She testified that Clancy was confused, made mistakes during a cognitive assessment and had experienced visual hallucinations after spinal surgery.

Shah diagnosed delirium and said possible causes included anesthesia, oxygen problems and an elevated heart rate. The symptoms resolved by the following day, Shah said.

During later evaluations, Clancy appeared calm and cooperative, displayed organized and goal-directed thinking and denied hallucinations and suicidal or homicidal intent.

Reddington used cross-examination to argue those observations did not establish Clancy was free of psychosis at the time of the killings.

"Was she, in your opinion and your experience, an honest patient telling you what her symptoms were, if any?" Reddington asked.

"Yes," Shah said.

FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X

"She didn’t go off and try to exaggerate to you and say, ‘I’m seeing visions and I’m hearing voices,’ and suicidal ideation and homicidal ideas," Reddington said. "She didn’t say any of those things to you, did she?"

"Correct," Shah said.

SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS

"So this is not, in your opinion, someone who was trying to exaggerate her conditions for some legal reason, correct?" Reddington asked.

"No," Shah replied.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE

Zuckerman called that concession "extremely helpful to the defense," although not decisive.

"They want to portray her as someone who wasn’t manipulative, who didn’t have some grand plan," he said.

SEND US A TIP

On redirect, prosecutors challenged the defense’s portrayal by focusing on Clancy’s medication history.

Shah agreed Clancy was not taking every psychiatric medication discussed at the same time and said she had not known some prescriptions were barely used or untouched.

GOT A TIP?

Shah also confirmed that Clancy requested do-not-resuscitate status after surviving her fall from a second-story window. The hospital did not immediately change her status because of the reported suicide attempt.

Shah said Clancy later agreed her mental health should be stabilized before reconsidering the request.

LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

Zuckerman said Monday’s cross-examination helped the defense by supplying testimony that Clancy could appear lucid at some moments while experiencing severe psychiatric symptoms at others.

Still, he said its value will depend on whether the defense can connect those symptoms to the moment the children were killed.

GET BREAKING NEWS BY EMAIL

"The burden is on the prosecutors to show that she was criminally responsible at the time of the deaths," Zuckerman said. "That is unique to Massachusetts, and I think it’s beneficial to the defense here."

Clancy, a former labor and delivery nurse at Massachusetts General Hospital, has pleaded not guilty to three counts each of murder and strangulation. Judge William Sullivan told jurors that the Commonwealth must prove beyond a reasonable doubt that Clancy was criminally responsible when the children were killed.

Coby Bryant’s Chicago Bears tenure is not off to the start he wished, as he was emotional after being carted off the training camp field during Monday’s practice.

There is a bright side to Bryant’s situation, though, despite needing to miss time.

Bryant was very upset as he got himself onto the cart after suffering a knee injury, expecting the worst just days into his Bears career one season after winning the Super Bowl with the Seattle Seahawks.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

Bryant was facing tight end Cole Kmet during a 1-on-1 drill where he went down and immediately clutched at his leg. But Bryant’s injury got a better diagnosis than he initially believed.

It won’t be season-ending for Bryant, as ESPN reported the safety will miss eight-to-10 weeks after suffering a hyperextended knee, bone bruise and small fracture.

PANTHERS DEFENSE TAKES MAJOR HIT AS STAR PASS RUSHER SUFFERS MAJOR INJURY ON FIRST DAY OF CAMP: REPORTS

Bryant signed a three-year, $40 million deal to join the Bears this offseason, bolstering a secondary that was overhauled following multiple departures.

He figured to be a mainstay after proving his worth with the Seahawks during his rookie deal, where he tallied seven interceptions and helped his team win the Super Bowl.

Bryant may not be available during Week 1, but since that’s five weeks away, he shouldn’t be gone for long when the regular season finally kicks off.

"It always sucks to see," second-year tight end Colston Loveland said about Bryant’s injury, per the New York Post. "That’s part of it. You know, he’s tough, he’s a dog. He’s going to be fine."

As Bryant will attack rehab, the Bears’ depth chart will be tested. They spent their first-round draft selection on Oregon standout safety Dillon Thieneman, who was always considered the team’s starting free safety next to Bryant. But Cam Lewis, who was at slot cornerback after Kyler Gordon suffered a previous injury, will likely move to safety to fill the gap there.

Lewis is another free agent signee for the Bears, who lost Kevin Byard, Jaquan Brisker, Nahshon Wright, C.J. Gardner-Johnson and Jonathan Owens this offseason. Lewis spent the past six seasons with the Buffalo Bills.

This is the time of year when teams are hoping for health, but the NFL knows all too well that depth determines just how far a team goes come February.

World.title: GOP senators clear Todd Blanche’s AG path after ‘anti-weaponization’ fund scrapped
World.content:
Republicans on the Senate Judiciary Committee on Tuesday are expected to advance Todd Blanche’s attorney general nomination after it had been delayed over concerns from two Republican senators on the panel.

Blanche’s path to confirmation had been on hold after Sens. John Cornyn of Texas and Thom Tillis of North Carolina — both of whom are leaving Congress in January — raised concerns about the “anti-weaponization” fund that the Trump administration tried to establish back in May to give taxpayer-funded payments to Trump allies, potentially including Jan. 6 rioters who, Trump pardoned on his first day back in office.

If the committee approves Blanche’s nomination, it would advance to a vote before the full Senate, where Republicans hold 53 seats.

Blanche said Sunday that he had reached a deal to amend the settlement that Cornyn and Tillis later said satisfied their concerns. Trump had recently defended the “anti-weaponization fund” and said he would revive the fund if Blanche’s nomination were blocked.

In a statement Monday, the two lawmakers said they were “pleased that the Department of Justice has issued a formal order terminating the anti-weaponization fund.”

“We look forward to voting to advance his nomination out of the Senate Judiciary Committee soon,” they added.

Blanche, who served on Trump’s legal defense team during his hush money trial, was confirmed as deputy attorney general last year. He was nominated for the position after Trump fired former Attorney General Pam Bondi in April amid reports that he was frustrated with her for not pursuing legal action against his political foes more aggressively.

The “anti-weaponization fund” would have been established with a symbolic $1.776 billion in connection with a lawsuit Trump and his family members brought against the government he controls over the leak of his tax returns.

Even with the carveouts in the Blanche documents that would block the “anti-weaponization fund” from moving forward, the Justice Department has ways to make payouts to Trump allies through the long-established Judgment Fund.

Hundreds of pardoned Jan. 6 rioters have made claims against the government and it’s not clear how the Justice Department will handle those claims moving forward, even though the government would have an easy method to get them dismissed because they weren’t filed in a timely manner. The Justice Department moved to dismiss one of the lawsuits Monday.

World.title: Man accused of arson in the biggest of 3 major fires in Spokane, Washington
World.content:
A 37-year-old Spokane, Washington, resident with a previous manslaughter conviction was arrested Monday in connection with the largest of the region’s three wildfires, which have displaced thousands of people and destroyed hundreds of structures, authorities said.

Aaron Farinacci, 37, was taken into custody without incident with the help of a SWAT team after a judge signed a warrant based on an allegation of first-degree arson, Spokane County Sheriff John Nowels said at an evening news conference.

Farinacci was being held on $1 million bond, he said. It was unclear whether he has been formally charged or has a lawyer, and the Spokane County public defender’s office did not immediately respond to a request for comment Monday night.

Farinacci was arrested after police said a witness reported seeing a man near the Old Trails Fire shortly before it started around 10 a.m. Saturday, Nowels said. The witness told police the man was looking into the trees and was later seen crouching at the side of a road near some grass, before he “stood up and looked very nervous” and walked away, Nowels said.

People watch the Old Trails Fire in Spokane on Saturday. Young Kwak / AP

Deputies detained Farinacci the same day about a half-mile from where the fire started and questioned him, but he was ultimately released, Nowels said. He had waterproof matches and a butane lighter, which could have been used to spark the fires, Nowels said.

On Sunday, major crimes detectives were able to link the suspect to the fire “and determined that the origin of the fire was indeed exactly where the witnesses had seen Mr. Farinacci kneeling in the grass,” Nowels said.

Farinacci was known to walk in the area before and had been questioned about “arson-related behavior” in the past, though he was never arrested or convicted for that, Spokane County Prosecuting Attorney Preston McCollam said.

Farinacci has a criminal record in Arizona, McCollam said, including a conviction for manslaughter. Public records indicate he was convicted of manslaughter in 2012 for a killing in Maricopa County in 2010.

At 3,619 acres, the Old Trails Fire is the largest of three major blazes burning in the Spokane region.

The fires have taken out an estimated 700 structures and caused the evacuations of 67,000 people in the Spokane area, federal incident commander Tom Clemo said Monday. They have collectively burned through more than 8,000 acres and were 0% contained Monday night.

Nowels said there is no evidence connecting Farinacci to the other two major blazes in the region. He is scheduled to appear in court Tuesday, McCollam said.

World.title: What we know about the victims of the Idaho shooting
World.content:
One was a young worker at the popular In-N-Out burger chain in Twin Falls, Idaho, with dreams of managing her own store one day. Another was a man who had gotten sober and worked to help others with substance problems improve their lives. And another was simply charging his vehicle after another day of work.

All three were among the victims of a 24-year-old gunman who opened fire Saturday afternoon outside the restaurant in the town of around 50,000 people.

Three people were killed and seven were injured. The families of Ashley Garibay, 23, and Christopher Claunch confirmed they were killed.

An off-duty state trooper and a civilian fired on the gunman and diverted him from the restaurant, the police chief said.

The gunman, Chad Williams, fatally shot himself, police said. Investigators were working Monday to determine more about the shooting and a possible motive.

Here is what we know about some of the victims:

Christopher Claunch. Courtesy Claunch family

Christopher Claunch, killed in shooting, helped others with sobriety

Christopher Claunch, known as “Toph,” worked at the treatment facility in Rupert where he had gotten sober, which a family friend said was a joy in his life.

Claunch “was always successful out there, but doing this was definitely the bright spot of his day, of his life, helping others find recovery,” said Garren Taylor, a spokesperson for the Claunch family.

Claunch worked at the Renaissance Ranch, where he had gotten sober, Taylor said. When he was finished, the center wanted him to work there.

“His big, open, giving heart, he was able to help so many people in a short amount of time in those two years,” Taylor said.

Claunch touched many lives, and he helped those struggling with alcoholism or other types of addiction, people whom society can sometimes see as “throwaways,” Taylor said.

“Toph was the kind of guy that — he was a magnet to those people, and he could open them up and share with them in a way that made a difference,” Taylor said.

Claunch’s partner of 25 years, Teresa Sperry, found out that Claunch had been killed when the sheriff’s department arrived at her house at 12:30 a.m. Sunday.

Ashley Garibay. Courtesy Garibay family

Ashley Garibay, slain In-N-Out associate, was ‘amazing, beautiful soul’

Ashley Garibay was a 23-year-old associate at In-N-Out, “and she fell in love with it,” her family said in a statement Monday.

“In-N-Out Burger was Ashley’s first job, and she fell in love with it. She proudly traveled to open new stores, and her dream was to one day manage an In-N-Out store,” her family said.

They said she loved serving customers “and left this world doing what she loved to do.”

Garibay was “a devoted daughter, sister, auntie, cousin and friend,” her family said.

“Ashley was an amazing, beautiful soul who loved living life. She was adventurous, outgoing, smart and driven, never letting obstacles get in her way,” the family said.

“She lit up a room with her bright smile and a laugh that was contagious. She was a friend to all, and no matter what difficulties she was facing, she always found a way to help others find the light in the darkness,” they said.

Lynsi Snyder, the president of In-N-Out Burger, said Sunday that she was heartbroken.

“She was taking care of our most important asset — our customers, and her life was taken by a disgusting human who doesn’t value the lives of others or his own,” Snyder said.

“He shot both on our property and off and ended his life shortly after he took the precious lives of our associate and customers, innocent people who never saw it coming,” Snyder said.

The wounded

Taxi driver Terry Dudley was charging his Tesla in anticipation of the end of a shift when he was shot “in the back, around the neck area,” his son, Michael Dudley, said Sunday.

“He was just in the car,” Michael Dudley said. “He got shot, and then the car next to him got lit up, as well.”

Terry Dudley was sitting in the driver’s seat when he was hit, his son said.

Michael Dudley said his father was conscious until paramedics arrived. Terry Dudley called 911, which was busy, and then called his friend and said he’d been shot, Michael Dudley said.

“He’s in pretty rough shape, but it’s to be expected,” Michael Dudley said. “But they’re doing everything they can. He seems to be stabilizing, so hopefully he stays on the upturn.”

At first, imaging “looked like it missed everything, right? Like somehow, someway, like miracle,” he said. But further examination detected bleeding, and he required surgery, Michael Dudley said.

James Palmer, who owns the taxi service Terry Dudley works for, said the driver called him to tell him he had been shot after he couldn’t get through to 911. He said Dudley was flown to a hospital in Boise and remained there Monday with serious injuries.

“It’s a lot, man,” Palmer said. “It’s daunting, to say the least, to even try to gather the scope of all this. It’s been absolute chaos.”

He said Dudley was “kind of like my right hand.”

Marcus Scott said on Facebook that his son Austin “A.J.” Scott was critically wounded and faces a long recovery. He said his son was shot after he moved “toward the danger” when he heard gunfire in an effort to protect others.

“We are incredibly thankful that God spared his life and that his wife and friend were there to provide immediate care until he could get to the hospital,” he wrote.

Marcus Scott said in a message to The Associated Press on Monday that his son used to work as an officer for Twin Falls police and the Idaho State Police. He declined to comment further on his son’s actions, saying it is his son’s story to tell.

World.title: Feds charge ‘frustrated’ FBI agent they say stole nearly $1 million in crypto from Russia
World.content:
WASHINGTON — An FBI supervisor detailed to the U.S. intelligence community faces two federal charges accusing him of transferring nearly $1 million from cryptocurrency accounts tied to an adversarial nation into his personal cryptocurrency wallet.

Patrick Yaroch was charged with interstate transportation of stolen goods and receipt of stolen goods after he told a Justice Department employee that he became “frustrated” the FBI “could not or would not act against adversarial cryptocurrency accounts,” according to court documents. Yaroch is reported to have said he was upset he could not do more to disrupt cryptocurrency use by an adversarial nation during an investigation.

The adversarial nation was Russia, two sources familiar with the matter told NBC News.

A federal public defender representing Yaroch declined to comment.

Yaroch said he made some very poor decisions, according to an FBI affidavit: “Yaroch said that he went into FBI systems and found keys needed to transfer money from wallets to himself.”

He made up to a dozen transfers, which added up to just under $1 million, the affidavit says.

Yaroch confessed because he was ashamed and it was “eating him up inside” and he wanted to get it off his chest, the affidavit says.

Yaroch also submitted an online FBI self-report form and voluntarily met with personnel at FBI headquarters to discuss his actions — he told headquarters personnel he wanted to disclose something because he had “screwed up.”

The affidavit, however, says Yaroch “never interacted with anyone associated with the adversarial accounts, including foreign entities.”

When the FBI searched his home, Yaroch handed over his FBI credentials and details of his cryptocurrency wallets.

The total value of all transferred funds was about $925,426.07.

U.S. Magistrate Judge Lindsey R. Vaala of the Eastern District of Virginia ordered Yaroch temporarily detained Monday. A hearing is set for Tuesday.

The FBI said Monday that it “immediately took action” as soon as it became aware of the allegations.

“The individual has since been fired from the Bureau. We hold our employees to the highest ethical standards, and this conduct is not tolerated at the FBI,” a spokesperson said. “We are conducting a thorough investigation in the aftermath, and as this is an ongoing matter, we will have no further comment.”

World.title: Man charged with setting one of the 3 devastating Spokane area wildfires
World.content:
A 37-year-old man was arrested Monday for allegedly starting the largest of the three devastating Spokane, Washington-area wildfires that are leaving some residents with nothing.

Aaron Farinacci, 37, a Spokane resident, was booked on suspicion of first degree arson in connection with the Old Trails Fire and was being held on $1 million bond, the Spokane County Sheriff's Office said.

Authorities began investigating Farinacci after a witness saw him kneeling near grass where the fire began, Spokane County Sheriff John Nowels told a press conference late Monday.

"We believe it was matches or a lighter. When he was detained ... he was found to be in possession of some waterproof matches and a butane lighter," the sheriff said, adding that Farinacci was only arrested in connection with the Old Trails Fire.

He has a prior manslaughter conviction, Nowels said.

With some 67,000 people under evacuation orders amid the three blazes, hundreds could be coming home to total losses.

"All of our memories are gone," said Anna Andreachi, a Spokane resident whose home was lost in the blaze. "My dad just died, and all of his stuff was still in there, too."

More than 700 buildings in the Spokane area have been destroyed, and another 400 have yet to be assessed, officials said Monday.

"It's a nightmare situation," Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson said. "This is likely the worst natural disaster in Spokane history."

Joe Cvancara and his family managed to save their home by digging a fire line. But his neighbor's home and at least eight others in the area were destroyed.

Cvancara said he's grateful but that it feels like "almost survivor's guilt, in a way. Like, wow. So we're going to open our home to our neighbors. I know it's going to take a long time to rebuild."

A partially melted street sign sits in front of a burned out residential home in the Balboa neighborhood of Spokane, Washington, on August 2, 2026. Erick Doxey / AFP via Getty Images

The fires began Saturday, when extreme drought, bone-dry brush, high heat and wicked winds combined to create a dangerous environment for fires to spread quickly. Firefighters went door to door trying to save as many homes as they could, but were soon overwhelmed.

As of Monday, no deaths had been reported. Spokane County Sheriff John Knowles told reporters on Monday there were 14 people authorities were trying to get in touch with, but stressed that he didn't want to qualify them as missing.

"These are people who may have called for help or for help evacuating, and many of them likely did get evacuated," he said. "You know, with poor cell phone coverage, people's cell phone batteries die or they get to some place where they do find shelter and we haven't been able to reach them by phone. So, that's the task ... for those 14 people that we haven't been able to talk to."

The Old Trails Fire and the Fairview Fire are both still burning, but the main focus for firefighters on Sunday and Monday was the Autumn Lane Fire.

The heat and wind that initially fueled the fires had died down by the beginning of the week, but the dangerous conditions are expected to return by Wednesday.

Daniel Ramey, a spokesperson for the California Interagency Incident Management Team 7, which is taking part in the firefighting efforts, told CBS News that the next few days could be critical for firefighting efforts.

"It looks like Wednesday into Friday we're going to be seeing a heat trend up to the 90s, so it's really time for us to put in the work ... on this fire up north and continue the efforts with getting the communities back into their homes as soon as possible below us," he said.

Three members of the Spokane Fire Department sit on a curb in front of burned down homes in the Balboa neighborhood of Spokane, Washington, on August 2, 2026. Erick Doxey / AFP via Getty Images

Ramey said that while the three fires aren't particularly big compared to other notable wildfires, the issue is that they have occurred in what's known as the wildland-urban interface — areas where human structures sit on the edge or within the wilderness.

"There's always a chance when you live next to trees and grass and the beautiful nature that you're going to have a potential for fire like we saw," he said. "We didn't have rain for the whole month of July in this area, so everything was extremely dry. Everything was susceptible to those new starts, like we saw."

For the Pacific Northwest, this has been one of the worst fire seasons in three decades. At least 16 major fires are burning in Washington state. In Utah, a fire has burned nearly 70,000 acres after doubling in size Monday. The Big Rock Fire in southeastern Idaho has burned more than 2,500 acres and forced evacuations.

Ramey warns things could get worse, with California still relatively quiet so far but firefighting resources already stretched thin.

World.title: Trump raises concerns in call with Rep. Max Miller amid abuse allegations
World.content:
President Trump called Rep. Max Miller on Monday and raised concerns about the Ohio Republican's reelection campaign following allegations Miller assaulted his ex-wife, Emily Moreno, and their 2-year-old daughter, two sources directly familiar with the call confirmed to CBS News.

Miller, who has adamantly denied the allegations, told the president he has no plans to leave the race, according to one of the sources. Miller pointed to his campaign's internal polling, telling Mr. Trump it showed his campaign in a strong position for reelection.

The call was first reported by Axios.

A source close to the Miller campaign told CBS News the campaign's internal polling has shown Miller ahead, despite the allegations that have engulfed the campaign in recent weeks. CBS News has not independently verified the polling.

In a statement to CBS News, Miller said:

"If I dropped out of this race, it would mean we as a nation have fallen so far from our American values. I will not validate false claims by removing myself just to please the court of public opinion. I am innocent of all of the allegations that have been attributed to me. I have done well representing my constituents' interests. Why would I drop out?"

Moreno, who is the daughter of GOP Sen. Bernie Moreno of Ohio, has accused Miller in court papers and police reports of throwing her against a wall during a February custody exchange and causing their daughter to suffer a clavicle fracture and handprint-shaped bruise. She also alleged that Miller threw hot water at her in 2024 and pointed a gun at her last year.

Emily Moreno asked a court last week to issue a restraining order blocking Miller from contacting her lawyer. She alleged in court filings that Miller has repeatedly had physical and verbal altercations with her attorney amid an ongoing custody fight over their young daughter. Miller and Moreno, who were married between 2022 and 2025, have court-ordered restraining orders against each other.

Miller has denied the allegations and accused his ex-wife of defaming him and abusing their daughter herself. In a livestream Sunday on X, he suggested the timing of the allegations was meant to impact the ongoing custody battle. He argued his ex-wife has engaged in a pattern of reporting "serious and destructive allegations with absolutely no evidence."

"These are incredibly serious criminal accusations, and if these accusations were true, I would be in jail," Miller said Sunday. He pointed to an April letter from county investigators closing a probe into whether he physically abused his daughter in February, calling the allegation "unsubstantiated."

Stefan Mychajliw, a spokesman for Emily Moreno, called Miller's livestream "shameful" and "lie-filled."

"There is a documented trove of evidence that Miller has a history of violent and dangerous behavior and no amount of victim shaming will change that," Mychajliw said in a statement. "Miller can lie and spin on X, but he cannot do so under oath in a court of law. We are confident that justice will prevail in court."

Miller is seeking a third term in Congress. He ran unopposed in the Republican primary for his district and is set to face off against Democratic nominee Brian Poindexter in the general election in November.

Sen. Moreno said over the weekend his ex-son-in-law should no longer serve in Congress over the allegations.

"If there are any basic standards of character required to hold elected office, Max Miller fails them," the senator said Sunday in a post on X. "He should not serve in the House of Representatives."

Sen. Moreno said he had hoped to keep the matter private, but that "Max Miller's increasingly erratic and dangerous behavior has made that impossible."

The senator said that Miller "needs serious psychological help" and called him a "danger to my daughter."

"I believe Max Miller needs to seek professional help to end the clear pattern of abuse he has left in his wake," Sen. Moreno wrote. "I believe he should not be free to continue endangering others until he does."

World.title: Sen. Moreno says ex-son-in-law Max Miller shouldn't serve in Congress
World.content:
Washington — GOP Sen. Bernie Moreno of Ohio said on Sunday that his former son-in-law, Rep. Max Miller, shouldn't serve in Congress amid swirling abuse claims, as Miller vowed to stay in the race for another term and strongly denied all allegations of misconduct.

"If there are any basic standards of character required to hold elected office, Max Miller fails them," Moreno said in a post on X. "He should not serve in the House of Representatives."

Miller's reelection campaign has been plagued in recent weeks by allegations of abuse against his ex-wife — the senator's daughter Emily Moreno — and their child that have emerged in legal filings. The second-term Ohio Republican responded to the accusations in a livestream on X earlier Sunday, in which he said allegations that he abused his daughter or his ex-wife were false.

The statements came after Miller's ex-wife asked a court to issue a restraining order last week blocking the Ohio Republican from contacting her lawyer. Emily Moreno alleged in court filings that Miller has repeatedly had physical and verbal altercations with her attorney amid an ongoing custody fight over their young daughter. Miller and Moreno, who were married between 2022 and 2025, have court-ordered restraining orders against each other.

The restraining order request followed months of allegations leveled by Emily Moreno against Miller. In court papers and police reports, she has accused Miller of throwing her against a wall during a February custody exchange and causing their daughter to suffer a clavicle fracture and handprint-shaped bruise. She also alleged that Miller threw hot water at her in 2024 and pointed a gun at her last year.

Miller has called the allegations untrue and pointed to the fact that he still has joint custody of his daughter, while accusing his ex-wife of defaming him and abusing their child herself. In Sunday's livestream, he cast doubt on the timing of the allegations against him, suggesting that they were made to sway the custody fight. He argued his ex-wife has engaged in a pattern of reporting "serious and destructive allegations with absolutely no evidence."

He also released documents that he argued would clear him of allegations that he injured his child or abused his former wife, saying: "These are incredibly serious criminal accusations, and if these accusations were true, I would be in jail." He pointed to an April letter from county investigators closing a probe into whether he physically abused his daughter in February, calling it "unsubstantiated."

A spokesman for Emily Moreno, Stefan Mychajliw, called Miller's livestream "shameful" and "lie-filled."

"There is a documented trove of evidence that Miller has a history of violent and dangerous behavior and no amount of victim shaming will change that," Mychajliw said in a statement. "Miller can lie and spin on X, but he cannot do so under oath in a court of law. We are confident that justice will prevail in court."

In his post on X Sunday, shortly after Miller's video, Sen. Bernie Moreno called the last two years "pure hell" for his family. And while he noted that he hoped to keep the matter private, Moreno said: "Max Miller's increasingly erratic and dangerous behavior has made that impossible."

Moreno claimed that Miller "needs serious psychological help" and called him a "danger to my daughter."

"I believe Max Miller needs to seek professional help to end the clear pattern of abuse he has left in his wake," Moreno posted. "I believe he should not be free to continue endangering others until he does."

Miller responded to his former father-in-law on X, saying: "If my daughter said the same thing to me, I personally wouldn't wait two years before holding him accountable."

"You know this isn't true and the only reason you are speaking out now is to hide from your own media circus," Miller said. "This is all political."

World.title: Trump says Jeanine Pirro "choked" in dropping Reflecting Pool cases
World.content:
Washington — President Trump on Monday publicly rebuked Jeanine Pirro, his handpicked U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia, for dropping the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool vandalism cases, but ignored questions about whether he intends to fire her.

The Justice Department submitted a court filing Friday moving to dismiss vandalism charges against 67-year-old former Olympian David Hearn, saying the Interior Department incorrectly attributed damage in the pool's lining to vandalism and that evidence showed "contractor error" and a "botched installation" were to blame.

That move did not rest well with Mr. Trump, who said Pirro "choked" and "made a mistake."

"I was disappointed with Jeanine Pirro," Mr. Trump told reporters in the Oval Office on Monday. "Really disappointed with Jeanine Pirro. She folded like an umbrella."

"Frankly, I think she choked," he said. "...I guess she choked. I don't know what the hell happened."

According to court filings reviewed by CBS News in D.C. Superior Court, since Friday, Pirro's office also moved to dismiss or said it would drop its prosecutions against three more people who were charged with vandalizing the Reflecting Pool. All three had been facing misdemeanor charges.

The president snapped at one reporter who asked if he's reconsidering Pirro's role as U.S. attorney and ignored another question from a reporter about whether he'll fire Pirro.

The president had previously voiced his displeasure on Truth Social, writing Saturday, "I disagree 100%" with Pirro's decision on the Reflecting Pool case. But Monday's comments in the Oval Office went further.

Asked if the president is considering removing Pirro from her post, the White House referred CBS News to the president's comments in the Oval Office.

Multiple sources later told CBS News that Pirro's job is safe for now. Pirro spoke with the president on Monday in the Oval Office, but didn't quit or ask if Mr. Trump wanted her to step down, sources with direct knowledge said. Mr. Trump is "pissed" about Pirro dropping the vandalism charges, but did not fire her, the sources said.

Hearn, who lives in nearby Bethesda, Maryland, said he stopped by the pool on June 19 while on a 64-mile bike ride, and authorities arrested him after he reached down to touch it. He was accused of ripping a piece of sealant from the pool, but he denied any wrongdoing.

Attorneys for Hearn said in a statement Friday that the case "should never have been brought" and that the government "owes Mr. Hearn an apology."

Moving to drop the charges was an about-face for Pirro. She held a news conference when the case against Hearn was first announced, saying: "One of the most offensive images that I hold in my mind are the images of national monuments that are being debased, roped, torn down, graffitied, and damaged by individuals. This unchecked vandalism and civil disorder turns into criminal behavior, and that's why we are here today."

Editor's note: This story has been updated to correct a reference to the additional charges that were dropped; they were all misdemeanors.
