World.title: 55 hours in the water: Polish swimmer crosses Baltic Sea from Sweden to home country
World.content:
The swimmer set off from Sweden on Friday, making a fifth attempt to take on one of the toughest challenges of his career. On Sunday evening he reached the Polish coast, where crowds of supporters were waiting for him. For the feat to be officially recognised, Kubkowski had to leave the water under his own steam and could not receive assistance from a boat at any time. That condition was met.

 

Once on shore, the athlete admitted that the sheer exhaustion meant he was not yet able to grasp the full extent of his achievement. For more than two days he remained in the water, with no sleep and no real break, racking up thousands of strokes.

During the crossing, his main foe was not only the distance but also physical exhaustion. After several dozen hours without sleep, he went through crisis periods marked by concentration problems and loss of lucidity. The team accompanying Kubkowski monitored his safety and navigation and ensured a regular intake of energy and fluids.

Years of preparation and a battle to make a dream come true

This success in the Baltic Sea is the result of several years of attempts and preparation. Kubkowski first took on the challenge in 2022, but had to stop after 115 kilometres. Over the years he gradually improved his performance and gained the experience needed to complete such a demanding route.

He came closest to his goal in 2025, when he covered around 159 kilometres and spent 53 hours in the water. He was then only about 15 kilometres short of the Polish coast. That attempt was called off because of extreme exhaustion.

This time, the athlete drew on all his previous experience. His preparation included hours of swim training, endurance exercises, work on mental resilience and a carefully planned nutrition strategy.

Kubkowski dedicated his success to the beneficiaries of the Cancer Fighters foundation, for whom a fundraiser was organised during the challenge. For years the swimmer has combined extreme sport with charity work.

The Pole holds the world record for 24-hour swimming, has won multiple medals at national and international events and is the initiator of the Ultra Baltic Swim project. Crossing the Baltic Sea, however, has been the biggest challenge of his career to date.

At the same time, Karolina Szczepaniak also set out to try to swim across the Baltic. The Olympic swimmer, who competed at the Beijing and London Games, holds a Guinness World Record for 72 hours of uninterrupted swimming. Her goal was to reach Pobierowo and support the treatment of 14-year-old Piotr Małolepszy. Her attempt ended after 58 hours in the water, when she was still about 40 km from the Polish coast.

Strength, endurance and determination

Swimming across the Baltic is regarded as one of the toughest challenges in long-distance swimming. The swimmer must face not only a considerable distance but also changeable weather, cold water, waves and mounting physical fatigue.

The Pole's historic success has earned widespread recognition in the sporting world. His feat is not only the fulfilment of a long-held dream; it also testifies to his perseverance and determination to reach his goal despite past failures.

After five attempts and thousands of hours of training, Bartłomiej Kubkowski can add one of his most striking achievements to his record: swimming solo across the Baltic.

World.title: Suspected heatstroke kills three lions at Japan zoo, spokesperson says
World.content:
Three lions at a Tokyo zoo have died from suspected heatstroke and others are under treatment, a spokesperson said on Tuesday, with the big cats struggling with high humidity.

 

Japan sweltered through its hottest summer on record last year and parts of the country have hit 40C in recent weeks, qualifying for the new designation "cruelly hot day," with thousands of people hospitalised.

Ten of the 16 lions in Tama Zoological Park have suffered symptoms such as "loss of appetite and decreased activity" since mid-July, and three lionesses died, the zoo said in a statement.

One three-year-old female died on Tuesday, another aged 11 died on Friday, and the third on Sunday aged 15.

The Tama Zoological Park said the lion enclosure, where visitors can normally be driven around in zebra-pattern "safari" buses, was closed to the public until further notice.

Students use portable electric fans to cool themselves in Kumagaya, 21 July, 2026 AP Photo

"According to our veterinarian, the cause of the deaths is suspected to be heatstroke" because dehydration and multiple organ failure were observed, a spokesperson told the AFP news agency.

"Even though lions are thought to be resistant to heat, zoo keepers have been strengthening countermeasures to cope with Japan's summer heat in recent years. Heat here comes with high humidity; that is different from heat with dry air in Africa," she said.

The spokesperson said the heat "arrived suddenly" this summer after the rainy season ended in late July.

"We are strengthening measures against the heat (further), sprinkling water, improving ventilation and installing spot air conditioners," she said.

Several lions are still being treated, she added.

Animals for profit

Animal rights group PETA said the lions named Mugi, Ichigo and Luena "were born, lived, and died in confinement, deprived of everything that makes life worth living for a wild animal."

"Zoos are not rescues or sanctuaries; they exist to display animals for profit, not to put animals' needs first," PETA said in a statement.

Close to 18,600 people were taken to hospital for heatstroke between 20-26 July, with 45 of them pronounced dead on arrival, according to the fire and disaster management agency.

Japan experiences about 1,300 heat-related deaths annually and is aiming to halve that number by 2030.

Scientists say human-induced climate change is increasing the frequency and intensity of extreme heat events in Japan and elsewhere.

Its highest recorded temperature of 41.8C was registered on 5 August 2025, in Isesaki, north of Tokyo.

Authorities have adjusted the timing of several cultural and sporting events in recent years because of the heat, including the World Cosplay Summit in Nagoya, which held its final summer edition last weekend.

World.title: Identity of new 007: 'Good bet' that next actor to play James Bond announced this year says producer
World.content:
The guessing games are over soon...

 

Following the news that the casting for the new James Bond was in its final stage, with director Denis Villeneuve and producers Amy Pascal and David Heyman having reportedly notified actors for the final round of August auditions, Pascal has revealed that we will soon get to know the identity of the next 007.

During an interview for Spider-Man: Brand New Day, which she also produced, Pascal told Deadline that "the end of the year is a good bet" when it comes to the timing of the announcement.

“I would say the end of the year is a good bet,” said Pascal. “We are being really, really methodical. Having worked with Barbara Broccoli at the studio, I mean, Daniel Craig is a hard act to follow. And it’s got to be something really different that is stirring and exciting and different.”

The rumour mill has been working overtime ever since Daniel Craig drank his last vodka martini in 2021’s No Time To Die, which concluded his 15-year run as Bond.

Since the last Bond movie, the 007 franchise was sold to Amazon MGM Studios, who took creative control from long-serving producers Barbara Broccoli and Michael G. Wilson.

Names such as Aaron Taylor-Johnson, Callum Turner, Jacob Elordi, Jack Lowden, Louis Patridge and Tom Francis have been circulating as potential candidates for the role of Bond, but until an announcement is made, nothing is certain. The audition process is ongoing and traditionally, once a name is out there, the chances are it’ll be another actor who gets the role.

The odds are that Amazon will bank on a relatively unknown actor in his late 20s rather than someone who is already in demand. Time will tell, and not long to find out...

Bond 26 will be directed by Denis Villeneuve and is being written by Peaky Blinders creator Steven Knight. Production is expected to kick off in 2027, with a release planned for 2028.

World.title: Gravity-defying dogs and brooding bovines: Meet the winners of the International Pet Photography Awards
World.content:
As anyone who has ever tried photographing their pet will attest, capturing the perfect shot is easier said than done. The winners of this year’s International Pet Photography Awards make it look effortless.

 

Founded in 2019 by Australian photographers and educators Charlotte Reeves and Craig Turner-Bullock, the annual competition has grown into what the organisers describe as the world’s largest professional pet photography awards.

This year’s edition attracted more than 4,200 entries from photographers in 48 countries.

From that field, a panel of 27 judges named Australian photographer Callie Soden International Pet Photographer of the Year, the competition’s highest honour. Soden also won the Creative and Studio categories.

The competition celebrates everything from split-second action shots to carefully composed portraits across 12 categories, including Action, Canine Portrait, Feline Portrait, Documentary, Pets & People and Rescue. Four new categories also debuted in 2026: Commissioned Portfolio, In-Camera Artistry, Phone and Studio.

Each winner’s selection is tallied from their three highest-scoring photos rather than a single shot. The International Pet Photographer of the Year, meanwhile, is decided by combining the highest scores across five images spanning any category.

From dogs held in heavenly poses and statuesque cats to horses, frogs, owls, rabbits and a photogenic cow, here are some of our favourite shots from this year’s competition.

Callie Soden's 'Amazing Grace' helped earn her Pet Photographer of the Year honours Callie Soden / The International Pet Photography Awards

This shot of Linda Glomb's rescue dog cemented her win in the Action category Linda Glomb / The International Pet Photography Awards

“Many of my artistic images feature my rescue dog, Schnuffi. She's a little whirlwind and happily goes along with every crazy idea I have,” Glomb says of the image above, part of her portfolio in the Action category. She took it using her car headlights for light.

Mark Vandijck won the Canine Portrait category with his sweeping shots of dogs in nature Mark Vandijck / The International Pet Photography Awards

Looking for "honest moments and genuine emotion," Laura Brockhoff won the Equine Portrait category Laura Brockhoff / The International Pet Photography Awards

Belinda Richards' mosaic of the cat Moosha won the Feline Portrait category Belinda Richards / The International Pet Photography Awards

Belinda Richards’ playful portfolio began as a lighting test with a friend’s cat, Moosha, and ended with a series of shots displaying Moosha’s mercurial attitude. “She gave me so many expressions and poses that I had to put together something showcasing her complete personality,” Richards says.

The award for In-Camera Artistry went to Germany's Andrea Zachrau Andrea Zachrau / The International Pet Photography Awards

Jennifer Chassagnol's Open category portfolio includes this close-up of a calf with stylish bangs Jennifer Chassagnol / The International Pet Photography Awards

Baby lambs cuddle together in this winning shot in the Open Portrait category Jennifer Chassagnol / The International Pet Photography Awards

“These images were created to inspire deeper respect and appreciation for all animals, especially those we so often overlook,” says Open Portrait winner Jennifer Chassagnol.

Sandra Ferwerda captures a close-up with an owl for the Pets and People category Sandra Ferwerda / The International Pet Photography Awards

To see more endearing pet shots – including a video showcasing the top 100 highest-scoring photos this year – visit The International Pet Photography Awards' winners page.

World.title: Sri Lanka closes schools as heavy rains trigger floods and mudslides, killing at least five
World.content:
Sri Lanka closed schools in its tea-growing mountainous regions on Tuesday as heavy rains triggered floods and mudslides that left five people dead and three wounded, officials said.

 

Heavy downpours over the last two days have wreaked havoc in many parts of the country, flooding homes, fields and roads.

The mountainous areas in the country’s central region are the worst affected by the severe weather, according to the government’s Disaster Management Centre.

So far, five people have died after being buried in mudslides that overran two houses in the central region, while three others were wounded and two people have gone missing, said Pradeep Kodippili, the centre's spokesperson.

Kodippili said rains and floods damaged 129 houses and that nearly 2,000 people were evacuated.

People walk across a mud covered road following heavy rain in Nawalapitiya, 4 August, 2026 STR/Copyright 2026 The AP. All rights reserved.

Navy and army troops have been deployed to rescue people trapped in the floods and help them move to safe places.

Local television channel Hiru TV showed troops and civilians rescuing people trapped in their homes because of the floods and facing the risk of being buried by mudflows.

Local channels also showed huge rocks, mudslides and fallen electric posts on several main roads in the central region, blocking traffic in some parts of the area.

The latest disaster comes as the country is still trying to recover from the devastation in November caused by Cyclone Ditwa that killed nearly 640 people, affected 2 million people and caused an estimated $4.1 billion (€3.5 billion) in damage.

People walk across a mud covered road following heavy rain in Nawalapitiya, 4 August, 2026 AP Photo/undefined/Copyright 2026 The AP. All rights reserved.

The Central province was the hardest hit by that cyclone and the government is struggling to rebuild roads, railways and houses in the region.

Mudslides and floods are among the most destructive natural disasters, causing severe damage to lives and property in Sri Lanka every year.

Heavy monsoon rains mostly trigger mudslides in the central hill region while flooding low-lying areas, forcing thousands of people to evacuate their homes.

World.title: Greek firefighters hope to contain blaze near Athens as easing winds enable use of waterbombing aircraft
World.content:
Firefighters in Greece were hoping to contain a wildfire on the outskirts of Athens on Tuesday that is burning for a fifth day, with easing winds enabling the use of vital aircraft.

 

"Today, more than 30 aircraft will be deployed in the area," enabling access to difficult mountain terrain, fire department deputy spokesperson Yiannis Artopios told state TV ERT.

Over 500 firefighters were deployed in villages around Mount Kithairon, some 60 kilometres northwest of the capital according to the fire service.

"We want to keep the fire in a controlled situation," Artopios said.

Large areas affected by the fire still contained active or smouldering hotspots requiring constant monitoring, as even a strong gust of wind could trigger fresh outbreaks, the spokesperson said.

"It's a huge area and there could be a flareup again at any moment," he said.

Firefighters approach towering flames on Mount Kithairon near Porto Germeno, 3 August, 2026 AP Photo

The greater Athens area and the neighbouring island of Evia remained under near maximum fire risk on Tuesday according to the civil protection ministry.

The wildfires have claimed the lives of five firefighters since last week.

On Sunday, two Bell helicopters collided while operating on the western outskirts of Athens, killing a Danish pilot and his Greek co-pilot.

Three other firefighters died in Crete and the Peloponnese last week.

Other fires across the country, including one on the Ionian island of Cephalonia, had largely been contained, the Greek fire service said.

"I would say that it is definitely one of the worst fire crises I've seen in the past, maybe eight to 10 years," Theodore Giannaros, a senior wildfire meteorologist at the National Observatory, told the AFP news agency.

A firefighting helicopter drops water over a wildfire on Mount Kithairon near Porto Germeno, 3 August, 2026 AP Photo

Winds at the end of July were the strongest in 15 years, the observatory has said, adding that more than 13,000 hectares of forest and agricultural land have been affected in the fire near Athens, which broke out on Friday.

Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis has warned that Greece faces "extremely difficult" days ahead as high temperatures and dry conditions continue to fuel fires.

Like much of the Mediterranean, Greece has experienced increasingly frequent and intense wildfires that scientists link to climate change.

World.title: Iran: Is Reza Pahlavi's political star fading?
World.content:
Once seen as a leading opposition figure, Pahlavi now faces questions about his political relevance in Western capitals and inside Iran.

An investigation by Reuters news agency into Reza Pahlavi, the son of the last shah of Iran, has raised a question: has Iran's most prominent opposition figure abroad lost credibility and influence among Western policymakers and Iranians?

Reuters reported in July that Pahlavi's candidacy had "sputtered" after appearing to reach its high point earlier this year.

Although he has repeatedly declared his readiness to lead Iran through a transitional period, senior US officials have publicly distanced themselves from the prospect of a US-backed effort to bring Pahlavi to power.

The Reuters report notes that critics accuse Pahlavi of relying too heavily on foreign military intervention and failing to build a lasting political coalition.

A shift in Pahlavi's rhetoric

During periods of heightened tensions, Pahlavi welcomed international pressure on the Islamic Republic.

In January 2026, he told Iranians that the international community had entered the stage of action and echoed US President Donald Trump's message that help was "on its way."

"Great nation of Iran, the eyes of the world are upon you. Take to the streets, and as a united front, shout your demands," Pahlavi wrote on X.

After the military conflict failed to bring about the collapse of the Iranian government and criticism intensified over the consequences of war, Pahlavi said that "the final victory will still be forged by our hands" and that it was the Iranian people who would "finish the job."

The main responsibility, he said, remained with the Iranian people themselves. Some critics argued that this emphasis on the role of the Iranian people marked a retreat from his earlier messaging about international help.

How the West views Pahlavi

Mojtaba Najafi, a researcher focusing on political and social movements in Iran, argues that Western governments have never regarded Pahlavi as a truly viable option.

Calls for regime overhaul boost exiled heir to Iran monarchy To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"A serious alternative would need the capacity to gain and manage power, influence existing power structures and offer a realistic prospect of structural political change," Najafi said. "Western governments have never considered Pahlavi to have met these criteria."

Najafi distinguishes between Europe and the United States. "European governments primarily approach Iran from the perspective of stability," he said, pointing to migration, geopolitical and security concerns, and the containment of radicalism and terrorism.

The researcher argues that, in the United States, pragmatic forces favor an accommodation with elements of the Islamic Republic.

"Their main concern is ending the regime's anti-American orientation and protecting US interests," Najafi said. "From this perspective, Washington is not necessarily seeking a transition led by a figure such as Pahlavi."

Israel's position is different

Israel's approach differs from that of the United States and Europe because Israel and the Islamic Republic have been enemies for the past few decades.

Najafi argues that some Israeli officials may view an opposition movement such as Pahlavi's as a useful source of pressure on the Islamic Republic.

Arash Azizi, a researcher at Boston University, is more critical. He argues that Pahlavi has failed to demonstrate the political skills necessary for his ambitions.

"Pahlavi has failed to demonstrate the political skills necessary for the ambitions he has set for himself," Azizi said. "His strategy has relied heavily on foreign powers that have shown little willingness to support him decisively."

"Pahlavi has cultivated ties with Western and, more recently, Israeli figures, but these efforts have not translated into decisive political backing," Azizi added.

Washington remains divided

Amir Taheri, a Paris-based political activist and supporter of constitutional monarchy, offers a more favorable assessment. He argues that Pahlavi leads a movement that has managed to connect different groups within the opposition and has been the most visible Iranian opposition figure abroad over the past year.

At the same time, Taheri acknowledges that Washington's position is divided. While parts of the Republican Party support Pahlavi, another faction favors accepting the existing political reality in Iran and seeking a new order from within the current system.

Taheri also considers Pahlavi's meetings with right-wing politicians in Europe a strategic mistake. Such contacts, he says, have not been well received by governments and traditional political forces.

His popularity in Iran remains uncertain

Pahlavi's popularity inside Iran is difficult to measure reliably. Iranian society remains highly volatile, with many people facing repression, economic hardship and inflation.

Could Reza Pahlavi play a role in Iran's future? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The consequences of war, Najafi argues, have shown that simplistic assumptions about political change through foreign intervention can bring suffering to the Iranian population. If the conflict does not result in political change, it could seriously damage Pahlavi's popularity.

Taheri also sees a decline in Pahlavi's political trajectory. His association with conservative and right-wing parties in the United States and Europe, as well as his support for a war that many Iranians regard as unjust, have damaged his position, he argues.

From a personal to a systemic alternative

The experts offer no unified answer to who could replace Pahlavi if his political standing continues to weaken.

Azizi and Najafi emphasize the limitations of his movement and the cautious attitude of Western governments. Neither identifies a specific alternative, instead stressing the importance of civil society and domestic forces within Iran.

Mehrdad Bozorg, a Germany-based political analyst and supporter of Reza Pahlavi, argues that Pahlavi's credibility among Iranians has actually increased, particularly following a brutal clampdown on anti-government protesters.



"After this crackdown, Iranians understood more clearly than ever that the Islamic Republic must go," Bozorg said. "At the same time, Reza Pahlavi has been the only opposition figure who has sincerely and consistently worked toward achieving a transition away from the Islamic Republic."

Bozorg said Pahlavi's legitimacy comes from the trust of the Iranian people rather than from other countries and argued that Western hesitation to acknowledge this hampers the Iranian people's aspirations for freedom.

Why Iran and Israel are enemies To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"Israel, for various reasons, shares the Iranian people's view and, at least regarding the need for the Islamic Republic to leave power, is aligned with the national revolution movement," Bozorg said.

"It therefore sees the reality on the ground and understands that the Iranian people have chosen Reza Pahlavi as the leader of the transition. For this reason, it is realistic for Israel to view Reza Pahlavi as the only alternative."

Taheri argues that Iran should move beyond personality-driven politics and toward a "systemic alternative." In his view, the 1979 revolution's transfer of power to a single figure, Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini, should not be repeated.

Reza Pahlavi remains the most widely recognized Iranian opposition figure, according to many analysts. Yet there is no consensus over his political influence or his ability to unite opponents of the Islamic Republic.

While Arash Azizi and Mojtaba Najafi believe his position has weakened, Amir Taheri still considers him a major opposition actor.

Whether Pahlavi regains or further loses political weight will depend largely on Iran's evolving political landscape and the position of international powers.

Edited by: Keith Walker

World.title: South Korea: 16 dead amid record heat wave, President Lee urges action
World.content:
President Lee Jae Myung called on officials to take prompt action as extreme weather conditions became "normal." Authorities extended their first-ever heat wave warning ⁠for all of Seoul on Tuesday.

At least 16 people have died in South Korea, as a record heatwave hits the country. President Lee Jae Myung has called for increased support for those affected amid warnings that extreme weather was becoming more frequent.

Between May 15 and August 2 this year, a total of 2,025 people have suffered heat-related illnesses, the interior ministry said in a statement.

What did President Lee say?

"We need to make efforts for a fundamental overhaul of the national crisis system, ​since this extreme weather is becoming normal," President Lee said at a cabinet meeting, where he urged officials to accelerate measures to protect the daily lives of people. He also called for inspections of ‌power systems as demand for air ‌conditioning rises.

South Korea's southeastern island city of Yangsan recorded a temperature of 42.5 degrees Celsius (108.5 degrees Fahrenheit) on ‌Sunday, the highest measured in 122 years of ​observations, the national weather agency said.

President Lee Jae Myung urged officials to increase support for those affected as extreme weather becomes more frequent. Image: Kim Hong-ji/REUTERS

After authorities issued their first-ever heatwave warning ⁠for parts of Seoul and Gyeonggi on Monday, the Korea Meteorological Administration extended it to the entire capital city on Tuesday. This was the first such advisory since the designation was introduced this year to alert the public about extreme temperatures.

South Korea grapples with historic heat wave

Temperatures in the capital hit 38 degrees Celsius at midday and were expected to fall only to about 29 degrees overnight. Residents were urged to stay indoors and drink plenty of water. The city has also designated about 4,000 public facilities as cooling centers.

While Seoul has a population of 9.6 million people, the wider metropolitan area is home to more than 25 million residents, which is about half of the country's population.

Scientists have warned that extreme weather events like heat waves are becoming increasingly frequent and more intense as a result of climate change.

Europe wildfires continue as new heatwaves hit France, Spain To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In Japan, cities have experienced "cruelly hot days" this summer, a new meteorological term the country uses to designate days with intense heat above 40 degrees. Tama Zoo in Tokyo announced Tuesday that three lions have died in the past week due to suspected complications from heatstroke as Japan swelters.

Europe has also faced a sweltering summer, with Germany's heat-related death toll for 2026 already surpassing every full-year total since 2016 — and expected to climb as another spell of extreme temperatures takes hold.

World.title: Three lions die of heatstroke at Tokyo zoo
World.content:
The zoo said that 10 of its 16 lions have been ill. Japan has been experiencing an extreme heat wave since late July.

Tama Zoo in Tokyo announced on Tuesday that three lions have died in the past week due to suspected complications from heatstroke as Japan swelters.

On its website, the zoo said that it was suspending the entire lion exhibit "due to the emergence of several lions requiring treatment for poor health, primarily characterized by loss of appetite, fatigue, and decreased activity... Some lions became severely ill, exhibiting symptoms such as inability to stand and loss of consciousness," before passing away.

Ten of the organization's 16 lions are currently unwell, they said, adding that although lions have evolved to deal with dry African heat, Japanese humidity presents additional challenges.

The zoo said three of its lionesses had died in since July Image: Dreamstime/IMAGO

'Cruelly hot' days

Japan has seen temperatures of 40 degrees Celsius (104 Fahrenheit) in recent weeks, leading to the government to adopt the term "cruelly hot day" for policy-making purposes.

Nearly 18,600 people were treated for heatstroke in Japanese hospitals in late July, national health officials have confirmed, saying that 45 of the victims had already died before they could be treated.

This summer has seen a series of extreme weather events across the globe, which are becoming more frequent as climate change worsens.

Nearby South Korea has also seen a substantial heat wave in recent days, with President Lee Jae

Myung urging authorities to step up support for the population after some 16 people died from heat-related causes.

World.content:
08/04/2026 August 4, 2026 German breweries continue to disappear

Breweries like this are becoming rarer in Germany Image: Helmut Meyer zur Capellen/imageBROKER/picture alliance

The number of beer breweries in Germany is continuing to sink, a trend possibly reinforced by the falling numbers of people who consume the beverage, new statistics have shown.

In figures released on Tuesday following Friday's International Day of Beer, the Federal Statistical Office (Destatis) said there were still 1,415 existing breweries in 2025.

That is 53 fewer than in 2024 and a whole 137 fewer than in 2019, the year in which the most breweries in three decades were registered.

Destatis said declining beer sales were a factor in this development.

They said beer sales had gone down by 15.7% in comparison with 2019.

In 2025, some 7.8 billion liters (2.06 billion US gallons) were sold, down from 8.3 billion liters in 2024 and 9.6 billion liters in 2016.

Of the German states, Bavaria had the most breweries (588), followed by Baden-Württemberg (190) and North Rhine-Westphalia (131).

However, with the exception of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern and Saxony-Anhalt, all states have seen the number of breweries decline.

World.title: India: Dhaka presses Delhi on stance ahead of Hasina speech
World.content:
08/04/2026 August 4, 2026 BJP accuses opposition of disrupting Indian parliament

The ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) on Tuesday accused India's leading opposition party, the Indian National Congress (INC), and its allied parties of disrupting parliamentary sessions and wasting taxpayer money.

"Due to the Congress party's continuous uproar and disruption of the house proceedings, two important bills related to public welfare had to be passed without discussion," BJP national spokesperson Sambit Patra said in a press conference from the party's headquarters.

He was talking about the Registration of Births & Deaths (Amendment) Bill and the Bankers' Books Evidence Bill.

"Both these bills are directly linked to the interests of the public," he said adding that detailed discussions did not take places for either due to the disruption. The bills, however, were passed in the lower house of the parliament.

"Hardly any bill is being discussed. The reason behind this is the conduct of the Congress party and some of its INDIA alliance partners. I am genuinely surprised by their double standards," he told reporters, referring to a broad multiparty alliance led by the iNC, the National Developmental Inclusive Alliance (INDIA).

The BJP's press conference comes amid growing attacks from the opposition regarding the government's response to student protests in July and an alleged theft of donation money from a grand temple in Ayodhya in northern Uttar Pradesh.

Over the last two weeks, parliamentary sessions have regularly been adjourned due to protests from the opposition bloc or sloganeering in house.

The BJP spokesperson called for INC President Mallikarjun Kharge said India's Home Minister Amit Shah to come to parliament on Monday to explain the reported police brutality on students in last month's protests.

He also called on Prime Minister Narendra Modi to answer how donation money from the temple was stolen when the temple's trust was "under the PM's oversight."

World.title: Venezuela earthquake death toll crosses 6,000
World.content:
The updated death toll comes weeks after the 7.2 and 7.5 magnitude quakes hit on June 24, causing massive damage to people and property.

The twin earthquakes that struck Venezuela in late June killed 6,125 people, the latest figures revealed by top lawmaker Jorge Rodriguez on Monday showed.

The updated numbers come weeks after the 7.2 and 7.5 magnitude quakes hit on June 24, unleashing massive damage on people and property, and triggering national emergencies. Unofficial estimates say between 17,000 and 29,500 people are still unaccounted for.

The previous death toll was 5,546.

What was the scale of the damage?

The quake led to nearly 200 buildings collapsing, mostly in the coastal state of La Guaira, which was hit the worst.

Rodríguez said that clean-up operations continued, clearing almost 350,000 tons of debris, which is about 16.5% of the 2.1 million tons of total wreckage estimated by the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP).

Authorities classified over 16,200 structures as unsafe, pushing many to leave. Thousands of people are now living in makeshift shelters in La Guaira and Caracas.

Several structures were deemed unsafe in the aftermath of the earthquake Image: Jimmy Villalta/JNA Press/Sipa USA/picture alliance

On Friday, lawmakers in the country unanimously approved a law that makes it easier to rent properties, a measure aimed at helping displaced victims. It repeals an anti-rental legislation passed by former leftist administrations.

Venezuela's Acting President ​Delcy Rodriguez came to power after US forces kidnapped her predecessor Nicolas Maduro in January and took him to New York, where he is facing trial. She has defended the government amid criticism ​that officials did not do enough to help ⁠quake victims, including people trapped in the rubble.

World.title: Cuba: Further blackouts disrupt energy restoration attempts
World.content:
Authorities say unfavorable weather in the Caribbean has hampered efforts to restore power to Cuba's national grid amid repeated blackouts. Many Cubans now have power only for a few hours a day.

Cuba's efforts to restore electricity after a series of blackouts were hampered again on Monday when a second nationwide power cut in a day, the sixth this year, struck its national grid.

Power began returning to parts of Havana and several provinces in central and western Cuba during Monday and, by midday, authorities said about half of the capital had electricity again.

However, the state electricity provider later warned that unfavorable weather had again interrupted the restoration process.

Cuba blackouts: What have authorities said?

"In the process of reestablishing the [National Electric System], existing weather events caused disruptions to the grid, directly affecting the generator units that were online," the provider said in a statement posted to social media on Monday afternoon, without specifying the extent of damage or how many areas were affected.

"We continue to work intensively to revert the situation and achieve the system reset as soon as possible."

By early evening, authorities were reporting some progress, saying four generating units at Energas Jaruco were operating and several transmission substations around Havana had ​been re-energized.

Cuba faces most severe energy crisis in decades To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Cuba: Life amid blackouts

Repeated blackouts ⁠since the start of the year have ​disrupted businesses, public services and life in general across Cuba, a Caribbean ​island of roughly 10 million people.

Most Cubans now have power only for a few hours a day at best, making normal life nearly impossible.

The government, which is already battling shortages of food, fuel ​and medicine and a long economic downturn, blames decades of United States sanctions and embargoes which limit access ​to fuel, financing and ⁠spare parts needed to maintain its power system.

The Trump administration has this year tightened sanctions and enacted an oil embargo, further choking the Caribbean country.

Washington claims the outages reflect failures of ⁠the country's state-run economic model.

World.title: España reprochará en Bruselas la reacción europea a la crisis de Ceuta
World.content:
Tal vez sea una hipérbole calificar la migración como arma de destrucción masiva; probablemente los ceutíes no lo vieron de la misma manera el pasado fin de semana. Pero no es ningún exceso retórico argumentar que la política migratoria es a día de hoy el asunto más espinoso en la UE, con la ultraderecha cargando las tintas y la derecha, e incluso el centroizquierda escandinavo, sumándose a esa ola que tiene poco que ver con los valores que Europa dice defender. Una de las grandes excepciones es España, que está aplicando una regularización para cientos de miles de migrantes y políticas de apertura que explican, en parte, un avance del PIB muy por encima de las métricas europeas. Pero más de 60.000 personas han atravesado irregularmente las fronteras españolas —que son las de Europa— hace apenas unas horas, provocando una crisis de primera magnitud, y han reafirmado la soledad de España en esa agenda tan controvertida. Hasta 22 países capitaneados por una populista italiana, Giorgia Meloni, y la socialdemócrata danesa, Mette Frederiksen, cargaron con fuerza contra la España de Pedro Sánchez tras la avalancha ceutí con una mezcla extraña de hechos alternativos y amnesia de los valores europeos. La gélida reacción de la presidenta de la Comisión Europea, Ursula von der Leyen, dio pábulo a esos ataques, aunque este lunes –con la crisis en vías de solución— la alemana cambió el paso y adoptó un tono más conciliador. El Gobierno español, a pesar de los errores, resolvió el grueso del problema en 48 horas. Y este martes llega su turno: España, según las fuentes consultadas, reclamará en la cumbre de ministros del Interior solidaridad a los socios y afeará a los más duros lo que Pedro Sánchez ha calificado de “reacción egoísta, polarizadora e ilegal”, guiada por “prejuicios, fake news, ignorancia o interés político”.

“Esa va a ser la posición española”, resumen las fuentes consultadas en el Ejecutivo, que aplauden el cambio de postura de Von der Leyen y vaticinan que algunos socios se desmarcarán de la posición de Meloni y Frederiksen tras la brusca reacción inicial. “Hay decepción por la reacción inicial de los socios, pero a la vez el nivel de críticas se ha atemperado respecto a las primeras horas. La carta de Sánchez fue contundente, por la sincronización entre EE UU, la ultraderecha y una parte del centro derecha europeo, y esa es la línea de la posición española, pero teniendo en cuenta que el tono general ha mejorado”, explican fuentes de La Moncloa.

La solidaridad, al menos verbal, habría empezado a llegar en la reunión de embajadores que se celebró este lunes para preparar el encuentro virtual de los ministros, según fuentes diplomáticas conocedoras de lo sucedido en este encuentro. Las mismas fuentes hacen hincapié en el tono constructivo de esa reunión, aunque apuntan que España ha mostrado su frustración con la reacción de los socios y ha subrayado, a modo de reproche, las diferencias entre el caso de Ceuta frente a otros similares en el pasado, como los de 2021 en las fronteras de Polonia y Lituania con Bielorrusia. Aquellos fueron tildados de “ataques híbridos” y toda Europa, incluida España, los condenó y ofreció su solidaridad; lo de Ceuta ha sido, en cambio, una “crisis migratoria inadmisible” cuyo responsable es España, según la misiva que firmaron 22 países.

Aunque en esa primera cata el tono haya sido positivo, también ha quedado claro que las diferencias políticas de fondo persisten: el ejemplo citado en público y en privado siempre es la regularización masiva. Fuentes del Gobierno esperan para este martes una reunión “tensa y larga”, y admiten que varios socios insisten en el papel de la regularización en la crisis de Ceuta, “a pesar de que todo apunta a que fue nulo”.

España ha sido el país europeo más duro en las críticas a Israel y a Trump en los últimos tiempos; al cabo, la lucha contra la ultraderecha es probablemente el argumento central del presidente Pedro Sánchez en la próxima convocatoria electoral. En algunas agendas, como Gaza, el consenso tiende hacia las posiciones españolas. Pero por el camino Sánchez se ha ganado un enemigo peligroso, Donald Trump, y las críticas cada vez menos veladas de los socios europeos más preocupados por la guerra de Ucrania, por la negativa española a gastar el 5% del PIB en defensa. Esa enemistad con el trumpismo ha vuelto a sentirse este miércoles: el embajador estadounidense ante la UE, Andrew Puzder, ha respaldado en un mensaje en la red social X la carta impulsada por Italia y Dinamarca.

La crisis de Ceuta –en el fondo más crisis geopolítica que migratoria— pone de manifiesto la actual falta de apoyos de Sánchez en Bruselas. Solo Francia, Portugal, Irlanda y Luxemburgo se negaron a firmar la carta de Meloni y Frederiksen. Y aun así, tras los excesos de las primeras horas, las aguas van volviendo a su cauce. La presidenta de la Comisión Europea, Ursula von der Leyen, que se sumó al principio a ese coro de voces críticas, moduló su mensaje, en lo que fuentes españolas califican como un “cambio de postura brutal”.

Von der Leyen completó este lunes un giro respecto a su posición inicial en una misiva dirigida a Sánchez. Reclamó “solidaridad”, algo que solo había hecho hasta ahora el presidente del Consejo Europeo, el portugués António Costa. Felicitó a España y a Marruecos, “un socio importante para controlar el tráfico de personas y la inmigración ilegal”; es curioso cómo casi nadie en la UE ha puesto el grito en el cielo con Rabat. Y dejó atrás los reproches públicos del viernes (“no podemos permitir que nadie venga a nuestra Unión sin respetar nuestras normas”) para limitarse a pedir a España que refuerce las infraestructuras críticas, algo que el Gobierno español ya ha hecho, de momento sin solicitar ayuda a Europa.

El ministro de Exteriores, José Manuel Albares, ofreció el lunes a primera hora una primera aproximación de la posición española. España “exigirá” a los socios “solidaridad”, según Albares. “Ceuta y Melilla son dos ciudades españolas, pero también europeas y frontera de la UE”, declaró en TVE. “España es a día de hoy la ruta mediterránea con el menor número de entradas irregulares por cualquiera de las rutas”, defendió el ministro en esa comparecencia. Los datos de Frontex confirman esa tesis. En el primer semestre entraron 16.643 irregulares por el Mediterráneo oriental (Grecia), y casi 15.000 por el Mediterráneo central (Italia), frente a las 7.860 por el Mediterráneo occidental (España) y poco más de 3.000 por la ruta canaria. Las cifras cayeron un 42% en el conjunto de 2025, según Frontex. Y registran un descenso del 25% adicional en lo que va de año (con datos hasta el 16 de julio), según Interior.

El ministro Fernando Grande-Marlaska enarbolará esos números ante sus homólogos, según las fuentes consultadas, poniendo énfasis en el compromiso con el control de fronteras y el aprobado de España en la aplicación del Pacto de Migración de Asilo (frente a las carencias de Italia, por ejemplo). “No se puede dudar del compromiso de España con sus obligaciones europeas o cuestionar la diligencia española en política migratoria”, según fuentes de Interior, pero es exactamente lo que han hecho 22 países por escrito y lo que un grupo de socios argumentarán en la reunión. En ella, España defenderá que ha logrado controlar los flujos procedentes de Mauritania, Senegal, Gambia y también de Marruecos. A pesar del exquisito celo diplomático de Sánchez, Albares y Grande-Marlaska, la cooperación o al menos connivencia de Rabat en la avalancha de entradas del pasado fin de semana es cada vez más evidente, como sugirió la ministra de Defensa, Margarita Robles, y han denunciado numerosos analistas.

En el fondo, el foco migratorio es solo el espantajo de una brecha mayor en el seno de la Unión. En el salto de 2021, mucho menos numeroso, la reacción unánime fue de solidaridad; ahora no. “La diferencia es que ahora Sánchez está solo, es el único líder socialista de peso en Europa; la danesa Frederiksen no está en ese bando en materia migratoria”, subraya Margaritis Schinas, exvicepresidente de la Comisión y ahora ministro de Agricultura en Grecia. Tanto los escandinavos como los bálticos están dolidos con España por lo que entienden como falta de compromiso en el gasto militar. Y el resto de Europa, a izquierda y derecha, por la regularización: la percepción es que el país que ha aprobado esa medida es a la vez incapaz de controlar las fronteras. “Los hechos dicen otra cosa. Pero en política mandan más las percepciones que la realidad. Hay una profunda división política, con cada socio a lo suyo, y un malestar general con España, y eso se refleja en el episodio de Ceuta y la reacción europea”, según fuentes del Ejecutivo de uno de los países de la zona euro.

Josep Borrell, exjefe de la diplomacia europea, critica que Italia y otros Estados miembros hayan “abusado del ordenamiento jurídico de la UE en flagrante violación del principio de cooperación leal que les vincula con España”. Luis Simón, investigador principal del Instituto Elcano, añade que la reacción española “fue tardía y refleja lagunas en inteligencia”. Destaca, además, que las medias tintas con Rabat, tanto en España como en Bruselas y el resto de las cancillerías, “inducen a pensar que tenemos un potencial problema grave de seguridad en la frontera sur”. Lejos de defenderse, España tiene previsto pasar hoy al ataque en Bruselas, con escasos apoyos, la Comisión Europea de perfil y 22 países (o algunos menos, según la versión española), de uñas.

“Es el momento de elevar el asunto al nivel de jefes de Estado y de Gobierno para reforzar los mecanismos de alerta y las respuestas europeas a una crisis de este calado, y de estrechar la cooperación en materia de fronteras”, lanzan fuentes diplomáticas, sabedoras de que es uno de los puntos destacados del próximo Consejo Europeo el próximo octubre. Tanto Von der Leyen como António Costa y Pedro Sánchez han dado las primeras muestras de que ese puede ser el próximo alto en el camino.

World.title: “En el rap, destaca el que tiene más ingenio. Lo que hacemos tiene un verdadero peso cultural”
World.content:
Arkano, el adolescente que descubrió su identidad gracias al rap. Conversaciones sobre la educación que queremos | Pensemos el mañana (Episodio 2)

Arkano, rapero y referente del ‘freestyle’ en España, se sienta a conversar con Bohemia, una joven promesa de la improvisación, sobre cómo el error forma parte del aprendizaje, cómo gestionar las críticas y cómo la educación colabora en crear mejores artistas urbanos

Guillermo Rodríguez 'Arkano' Artista de rap Su trayectoria reúne algunos de los grandes hitos del freestyle desde que, con 15 años, se proclamó campeón de España de la Red Bull Batalla de los Gallos de 2009. Incluso batió un récord Guinness al improvisar durante 24 horas y 34 minutos seguidos. Paralelamente, impulsa y participa en iniciativas sobre salud mental y colabora en campañas contra el acoso escolar Isabel Arrabal 'Bohemia' Estudiante de 3º de ESO Y ‘freestyler’ A sus 15 años, compagina los estudios en el IES Averroes (Córdoba) con sus primeras competiciones de freestyle. Empezó a improvisar con 14 años, tras descubrir el rap en YouTube, y forma parte de una nueva generación de jóvenes que ha encontrado en la cultura urbana un lugar donde desarrollar su confianza

Dice Arkano (Alicante, 32 años) que el rap le transformó, que incluso le salvó la vida. A los 15 años, cuando aún lo conocían más como Guillermo Rodríguez y todavía cursaba la ESO, ganó en España la Red Bull Batalla de los Gallos, la competición de improvisación más importante del país. “Yo era un chaval muy tímido, no tenía habilidades sociales, lo pasé bastante mal en la época del instituto y descubrir el rap fue como encontrar una voz propia”, cuenta. La cultura urbana le alumbró, le infundió más confianza.

“El 'freestyle' se basa en lanzarse al vacío, no podemos aspirar a que todo sea perfecto. Tenemos que estar preparados para el error”

Isabel Arrabal, conocida como Bohemia, tiene la misma edad que tenía Arkano cuando se coronó como una joven promesa. No es su única coincidencia; esta cordobesa también ha ganado seguridad en sí misma después de atreverse a rapear. En Pensemos el mañana, el proyecto de Fundación Unicaja y Grupo Prisa sobre la educación del futuro, reflexionan sobre cómo han podido desarrollarse gracias a sus inquietudes artísticas y a esos entornos sociales fuera de las aulas, no convencionales.

"El rap me ayudó mucho a relacionarme con mis compañeros, a tener más seguridad en lo que hago, porque antes era muy tímida. Me ha ayudado a confiar más en mí”

Bohemia y Arkano charlan, además, sobre lograr que el miedo a equivocarse no les inmovilice, la relación entre educación y rap (y la importancia de tener “un lenguaje más rico”, como precisa Arkano) o la gestión de críticas y redes sociales. Aunque sea una asignatura pendiente para algunos adolescentes, Bohemia ha aprendido a manejar esos mensajes anónimos y ofensivos: “A mucha gente le puede llegar a afectar, y el consejo que les daría es que piensen en quiénes son ellos realmente”.

Pensemos la educación del futuro ‘Pensemos el mañana’, un proyecto de Fundación Unicaja, busca fomentar el conocimiento, los valores de la educación, un aprendizaje sostenible y responsable y dar respuestas a los grandes desafíos de la educación del futuro. El proyecto pivota sobre seis ejes: 1 Aprendizaje y sentido vital 2 Bienestar y salud mental 3 Futuro y empleabilidad 4 Sostenibilidad y sentido colectivo 5 Tecnología y ética 6 Carácter y ciudadanía ¿Qué está ocurriendo en estos tiempos de cambios profundos y transversales? ¿Cuáles son los grandes retos para afrontar la transformación que viene? ¿Qué educación necesitamos? Diferentes personalidades de todos los ámbitos nos ayudarán a responder a estas y otras preguntas destinadas a impulsar cambios, dinamizar ideas y apoyar propuestas con impacto pedagógico y social. ‘Pensemos el mañana’ es un proyecto inspirador para las futuras generaciones llamadas a conquistar nuevas cotas del saber en un mundo complejo y cambiante.

World.title: Pistas para un viaje de verano a Portugal: de las playas del Algarve a los azulejos de Lisboa
World.content:
Ciudades y pueblos llenos de encanto, pistas para comer bien y barato y algunos trucos para descubrir el país

Año tras año, Portugal es un destino de vacaciones recurrente. Pero decir Portugal puede tener muchos significados: están las playas del Algarve que acogen a los amantes del surf, los pueblos del centro del país llenos de encanto y calles empedradas o los paisajes que dejan el Duero y el Tajo a su paso por el país vecino. Además del magnetismo de Lisboa y Oporto, dos ciudades llenas de vida y de historia.

Esta es una guía de destinos para quienes este verano viajen a Portugal.

Además, dos pistas gastronómicas para saber dónde comer y qué pedir en Lisboa y Oporto. Así como una visita cultural imprescindible en la capital lusa.

Y la experiencia viajera en primera persona de Paco Nadal, dispuesto a regresar una y otra vez al país.

World.title: Rabobank profit flat as it braces for loan losses
World.content:
Rabobank made no profit growth in the first half of this year, reporting a net profit of nearly €2.7 billion, the same as in the first six months of 2025, after setting aside €562 million for loans that might not be repaid.

That is more than four times the €136 million it set aside a year earlier, the bank said in its results statement.

Chairman Stefaan Decraene told reporters the provisions related to two cases in South America but declined to name the companies or projects involved, broadcaster NOS reported.

Business in the Netherlands grew. Deposits at the Dutch retail arm stood at €375.1 billion, and lending at €293 billion.

Takeover talk

Decraene said Rabobank was open to buying another bank, telling NOS that scale is becoming more important.

Rabobank also said it will invest up to €2 billion in strengthening its data and IT systems and scaling up its use of artificial intelligence. Reuters reported that the spending will be spread over the next three years.

The bank’s return on equity was 9.5% and its core capital ratio 20.2%, which it said makes it one of the best-capitalised banks in Europe.

World.title: Man who held prison staff hostage given suspended jail sentence
World.content:
A man who held three prison staff hostage at knifepoint for several hours has been given a further suspended sentence of a year.

Corné H. seized and handcuffed his victims for several hours on December 5 last year at the jail in Vught after threatening them and five other colleagues with kitchen knives.

The 30-year-old had served a nine-month term for holding four staff at a bar in Ede, Gelderland, against their will in March the previous year.

At the time of the incident he was being detained in Vught’s psychiatric unit waiting to be given a place in a clinic under the Dutch compulsory treatment system (tbs).

The sentence was suspended to allow H. to continue his treatment, which began in June, meaning he will only have to go back to prison if he commits another offence.

The court in Den Bosch heard that H. suffered as a result of conditions including PTSS, schizophrenia and autism, which influenced his behaviour. A psychiatric assessment also said he had “anti-social and borderline personality traits”.

The judge said his victims feared for their lives and the incident “must have been dreadful for them”, but accepted H. had diminished responsibility and imposed a sentence that met the prosecution service’s demands.

At the earlier trial, H. was cleared of taking the bar staff in Ede hostage but convicted of depriving them of their liberty and threatening them.

Police sealed off the venue after he went in at closing time with guns and explosives and threatened to blow up the building, leading to a stand-off lasting more than eight hours.

World.title: Police raise concerns over sharp rise in weapon seizures
World.content:
Dutch police seized 5,165 gas and alarm pistols, air weapons and pepper sprays last year, up from 4,080 in 2022, according to figures given to broadcaster NOS – a rise of almost 27%.

Police said they did not know whether the increase indicates that more people are carrying such weapons, or if it reflects boosted efforts to find and confiscate them.

Gas and alarm pistols are the main worry because they are hard to tell apart from real firearms, police spokesman Martin van der Meij told NOS. Alarm pistols make a loud bang but fire no projectile, while gas weapons can release tear gas.

They are cheap, easy to obtain and relatively simple to convert into working firearms, he said. A converted pistol was used to kill the crime reporter Peter R. de Vries in 2021.

Buying these weapons in Germany or Belgium and bringing them into the Netherlands is a criminal offence, though people do not always realise it.

Herman Oldenkotte, who runs a gun shop in Gronau just over the German border from Enschede, told NOS that he estimated 80% to 90% of his customers were Dutch. In Germany the weapons can be bought without a licence by anyone over 18.

Police also say more weapons are arriving by post. The Netherlands has pressed the EU for years to bring in a licence requirement or a ban.

Pepper spray is banned for civilians under Dutch weapons law. The justice ministry said in June it planned to allow permits for people at particular risk, such as stalking victims, while ruling out legalising it for everyone.

World.title: Limburg wildfire spreads across 100 hectares overnight
World.content:

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

The wildfire in the Boschhuizerbergen nature reserve in northern Limburg has burned through about 100 hectares overnight and is still not under control, according to authorities, who have issued an NL-Alert warning to the surrounding area.

The Limburg-Noord emergency services authority (VRLN) said the fire had spread rapidly since Monday afternoon, when the area affected was 21 hectares, broadcaster NOS reported.

A spokesperson for the VRLN said on Tuesday morning that the fire had grown further overnight but was no longer spreading. Around 300 firefighters and emergency workers are tackling it, with crews sent from across the country.

Parts of the burned area have been put out, but the fire is still going elsewhere. Authorities have not yet said when it can be fully extinguished, saying it depends on conditions.

Two military helicopters dropped water over the site on Monday but had to stop at nightfall and are due to resume on Tuesday morning.

The NL-Alert warned that people should stay out of the smoke and close windows, doors and ventilation.

That alert remains in force, and NOS reported that a new one covering a wider area was expected on Tuesday morning because the wind has shifted.

A camping site, De Oude Barrier, has been evacuated and guests taken to a nearby hotel. Drones have also been banned from the area.

No trains are running between Boxmeer and Venray. Rail network operator ProRail expects the line to stay shut until at least 6pm on Tuesday.

The fire spread quickly because the wind strengthened and temperatures were high. The Netherlands is in an official water shortage after weeks with little rain.

Bomb disposal specialists were called to a house in Rotterdam on Monday evening after a device was found during a police search.

Officers responded to reports of a person with a gun at the house in Voorne, in the Feijenoord district.

No weapons were found, but police cordoned off the area after explosives were found in the garden.

The disposal service EOD took the item away and destroyed it safely in the Kralingse Bos, Rotterdam’s largest urban park.

Police did not give any details of what the device was. Investigations are continuing.

World.title: Shell sells Dutch solar farms in retreat from renewables
World.content:
Shell is selling every solar farm it owns in the Netherlands. The five sites, plus a combined wind and solar park at Pottendijk near Emmen, are going to the French oil company TotalEnergies.

The deal covers all of Shell’s wind and solar projects on land across Europe (its offshore windfarms are not included) and the company will not disclose what it is being paid.

The Dutch sites can produce up to 254 megawatts between them, enough to power tens of thousands of homes. They are at Moerdijk, Heerenveen, Emmen, and Sas van Gent and Koegorspolder near Terneuzen.

Some were built on land Shell had already used for oil and gas, and the company used them as proof it was changing. The Emmen farm stands on the site of an old gas treatment plant, part of a project Shell said could be an example for the rest of the country.

The sale needs approval from regulators and is expected to be completed at the end of 2026.

Retreating from transition

Wael Sawan, Shell’s chief executive, has shifted spending back towards oil and gas and away from low-carbon projects. TotalEnergies has moved the other way, buying renewable assets across Europe.

The Hague district court ordered Shell in 2021 to cut its emissions by 45% by 2030. The company dropped Royal Dutch from its name and moved its headquarters to London the following year, and won its appeal in November 2024.

Milieudefensie has taken that case to the Supreme Court and launched a second action last year over the company’s 700 oil and gas projects that are still in development.

Shell is not leaving Dutch renewable energy altogether. It keeps its stakes in North Sea wind farms, its Holland Hydrogen 1 plant at Rotterdam and its carbon capture work.

World.title: Doctors want more hospitals to offer late-term abortions
World.content:
The Dutch association of gynaecologists, the NVOG, and the healthcare inspectorate IGJ want more hospitals to carry out late-term abortions – between 22 and 24 weeks – saying access to the care is not currently assured for all women.

Abortion is legal in the Netherlands up to 24 weeks. Terminations up to 22 weeks usually take place in abortion clinics, while those between 22 and 24 weeks are carried out in hospitals, of which only a small number currently do so.

Sanne Gordijn, head of obstetrics at the UMCG in Groningen, one of the few hospitals already providing the care, said some women were travelling to Spain, Britain or parts of the United States because they could not get a termination here.

She told broadcaster NOS that a late abortion is emotionally difficult for staff and never becomes routine, which is why the work needs to be shared out. The risk of medical complications after 22 weeks is why the procedure takes place in hospital.

Amsterdam’s OLVG has said it has been asked to take part but that reports it has already begun doing so are incorrect.

Gordijn said the grounds for a termination are usually a combination of factors, that the pregnant woman’s need comes first, and that no distinction is made between medical and non-medical grounds.

The UMCG said staff and medical social workers discuss the situation with women, including alternatives such as adoption, and that psychological support is available. Just over 39,000 abortions were carried out in the Netherlands in 2024, of which 331 were between 22 and 24 weeks.

Abortion clinics have reported a rise in attacks and intimidation in recent years, and MPs voted last year to bring forward a review of the abortion law, on a motion from NSC and the ChristenUnie.

World.title: Three terror suspects kept in custody as inquiries continue
World.content:
Three teenagers who were arrested in dawn raids last week on suspicion of planning terrorist attacks have had their detention extended while police inquiries continue.

A 19-year-old man named as Muhammad K. was detained at his home in Eindhoven last Wednesday, at the same time as a 16-year-old youth from Rotterdam and a 17-year-old from De Rijp, a village near Alkmaar.

K. was sentenced to 112 days in prison and banned from travelling out of the Netherlands two years ago after a court convicted him of plotting attacks on nightclubs and police stations in Belgium. No attacks actually took place.

The other two suspects were among a group of 14 people aged between 14 and 30 who were arrested in April last year for allegedly inciting others to carry out terrorist attacks, using the social media platform TikTok.

The public prosecution service said the arrests were carried out by the special interventions service (DSI), acting on information from the intelligence agency AIVD. It added that no weapons were found during the raids and there were no signs that a specific attack was being planned or a target had been identified.

A magistrate in Rotterdam agreed last Friday to detain the trio in custody for a further 14 days.

World.title: Pole becomes first person to swim 160km Baltic Sea route between Sweden and Poland
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Polish swimmer Bartłomiej Kubkowski has become the first person in history to swim across the Baltic Sea between Sweden and Poland, covering a distance of just over 160 kilometres (99 miles). On Sunday evening, an exhausted Kubkowski clambered onto the beach in the town of Dziwnów on Poland’s northern Baltic coast, around 56 hours after he had set off from Kaseberga in Sweden on Friday. The achievement marks a personal triumph for Kubkowski, for whom this was the fifth attempt to complete the route. His effort this year has raised over 715,000 zloty (€166,000) for children’s cancer treatment so far, with donations to his fundraiser still coming in. View this post on Instagram A post shared by PURELY ATHLETICS (@purelyathletics) During the crossing, Kubkowski was unable to sleep and, although a support boat accompanied him and provided food and drink, he was not allowed to touch the vessel itself. His journey of around 160km was not far off the longest-ever continuous, unassisted open-water swim ratified by the Marathon Swimmers Federation, which was the 168.3 km swum by American Sarah Thomas in 2017 in Lake Champlain, between the US states of New York and Vermont. Kubkowski has been attempting to swim the route between Sweden and Poland since 2022, getting progressively closer to achieving the goal. Last year, he came within 11km of the Polish coast before extreme exhaustion and deteriorating weather forced him to give up, reported Eurosport. However, Kubkowski, a former competitive swimmer who now devotes himself to ultraswimming, did last year manage to break the world record for the longest distance swum in a swimming pool over 24 hours, after he managed to cover 103.6 km (64.5 miles). Another Polish swimmer, Karolina Szczepaniak, is also currently attempting to swim from Sweden to Poland along a slightly different route to Kubkowski’s. At the time of writing, she is around 110km into the 172km journey, and has raised almost 400,000 zloty for charity. Szczepaniak, a former Olympic swimmer, also attempted the feat last year, but was forced to give up after 57 hours amid worsening weather. However, the 146.7km she swam set a new record for the longest distance covered by a female swimmer in the Baltic Sea and a Polish record for open-water swimming by a woman. A Canadian multinational operator of convenience stores, Alimentation Couche-Tard, has announced plans to acquire Poland’s Żabka Group, which runs Europe’s largest chain of convenience stores. The company has offered 32 zloty per share, valuing Żabka at 32.6 billion zloty (€7.56 billion). Żabka’s main shareholders have agreed to sell their stakes, with final approval still required from stock market investors. If the transaction is completed, Żabka is likely to be delisted from the Warsaw Stock Exchange just two years after its market debut. Właściciel Circle K chce przejąć 100% Żabki. Cena w wezwaniu ma wynieść 32 zł za akcję =>https://t.co/61XEGuQnnB via @PawelBiedrzycki https://t.co/61XEGuQnnB — Strefa Inwestorów (@strefainw) July 31, 2026 The acquisition will be carried out through Alimentation Couche-Tard’s Polish subsidiary, Circle K, which runs petrol stations, and will cover all of Żabka Group’s more than one million shares. Alimentation Couche-Tard has already secured commitments to acquire at least 57.2% of the company. Heket, an entity linked to CVC Capital Partners owning 37.6% of Żabka’s shares, and PG Investment Company, holding 10%, have agreed to sell their entire stakes. A group of major individual shareholders, together controlling 9.6% of Żabka’s shares, has also agreed to sell its holdings to the Canadian buyer. The investors include members of the company’s management and former executives. They have also agreed to reinvest part of the proceeds from the sale into Alimentation Couche-Tard shares. The tender offer for the remaining shares was announced on Friday by Ipopema Securities, which is acting as the intermediary in the transaction. Alimentation Couche-Tard and Żabka expect subscriptions for the offer to open around 26 August, following a review of the tender document by the Polish Financial Supervision Authority (KNF). The companies foresee the transaction closing by the end of the year. The Canadian company expects Żabka to continue operating independently, under the leadership of its current management team, and to retain its brand. Żabka shares jumped after the announcement, rising from 29.26 zloty to around 31.60 zloty on Friday afternoon, an increase of about 8%. Żabka, which runs Europe’s largest chain of convenience stores, has made its stock market debut in one of Europe’s biggest listings this year. Alex Miller, Alimentation Couche-Tard’s CEO, said the company is “committed to supporting the continued growth of the Żabka business while drawing from its strengths in areas such as food, digital engagement, customer loyalty, private brand, supply chain, logistics and innovation”. Żabka made its debut on the Warsaw Stock Exchange in 2024 in one of Europe’s largest initial public offerings that year, with a valuation of around €5 billion. The company is Poland’s largest convenience store operator, with about 13,000 locations nationwide run by around 11,000 franchisees. It has also expanded internationally, opening its first stores in Romania and reaching 100 outlets there last year.
