World.title: Romania’s Dino Parc Râșnov reaches 4.5 million visitors, estimates EUR 130 mln impact on local economy
World.content:
Dino Parc Râșnov welcomed more than 4.5 million visitors since opening in 2015 and estimates its cumulative contribution to the local economy at over EUR 130 million. The dinosaur park in central Romania is marking its 11th anniversary this year, alongside the recent accreditation of its Forest Museum by the Ministry of Culture.

According to an independent impact study conducted in 2024, Dino Parc generated more than EUR 100 million for the local economy during its first eight years of operation, equivalent to over EUR 12 million annually. Based on this pace and continued growth in visitor numbers, park representatives estimated that its cumulative economic contribution has now exceeded EUR 130 million.

“The 11 years and the more than 4.5 million people who have come through our gates confirm that we have built something lasting," said Dino Parc Râșnov founder and general manager Adrian Apostu.

“We never wanted just a dinosaur park, but a place where children learn with pleasure, almost without realising it, and where families go home with memories and with new things learned. The Ministry of Culture’s accreditation of the Forest Museum is the official recognition of this journey,” he added.

One of the park's latest developments came in May 2026, when its Forest Museum was officially recognized by the Ministry of Culture. The museum houses a collection of more than 1,300 natural exhibits and attracted over 2,500 visitors during its first participation in the Night of Museums event in May.

Dino Parc said it has also adapted its offering to changes in domestic tourism, as families increasingly weigh leisure spending and opt for shorter trips. The park has expanded its attractions, facilities and food areas, while also introducing an overnight experience that allows visitors to sleep in tents inside the park.

“At a time when every leu spent on leisure is weighed carefully, people are looking for experiences that offer more than entertainment. This is the direction family tourism is taking in Romania, and we have prepared for it," Apostu said.

Opened in 2015 near Râșnov Fortress in Brașov County, Dino Parc covers four hectares and features more than 130 life-size dinosaur models, alongside educational and natural history exhibitions.

irina.marica@romania-insider.com

(Photo source: Dino Parc representatives)

World.title: Romania launches new Fidelis government bond offering this week
World.content:
Romania's Finance Ministry will launch the eighth Fidelis government bond offering of 2026 on August 7, with annual interest rates of up to 7.5% for RON-denominated securities and 6.3% for euro-denominated bonds. Subscriptions will remain open until August 14.

For bonds denominated in RON, the ministry is offering an interest rate of 6.3% for a two-year maturity, 6.9% for four years, and 7.5% for ten years.

Euro-denominated securities carry interest rates of 4% for a three-year maturity and 6.3% for a ten-year maturity.

The August edition also includes special tranches for blood donors. Investors who can provide proof of having donated blood since March 1, 2026, can access a 7.3% interest rate on two-year RON-denominated bonds and 5% on three-year euro-denominated securities.

Blood donors also benefit from lower minimum subscription thresholds. The minimum investment is RON 500, compared with the standard RON 5,000, with subscriptions capped at RON 100,000. For euro-denominated securities, the minimum is EUR 100 instead of EUR 1,000, with a maximum subscription of EUR 20,000.

The bonds can be purchased by resident and non-resident individuals aged over 18 through participating banks and brokers and will be listed on the Bucharest Stock Exchange.

Income earned from holding Fidelis government bonds is tax-exempt, while investors can also sell the securities on the stock exchange before maturity.

(Photo source: Facebook/Bursa de Valori Bucuresti)

World.title: Bucharest court suspends five more government decisions at PSD request
World.content:
The Bucharest Court of Appeal has suspended five additional government decisions challenged by Romania’s opposition Social Democratic Party (PSD), bringing to 11 the number of decisions suspended after being referred to the court by the party, the government said on August 3, according to Hotnews.ro.

The government said it would appeal the rulings, which prevent the implementation of measures covering employment bonuses, unpaid fines, external funding, livestock support and staffing at the nuclear regulator.

The five decisions suspended on August 3 concern bonuses for young people upon their first employment, the suspension of permits for unpaid fines, the management of almost EUR 600 million in external funds, support measures for individual livestock breeders and a reduction in the number of positions at the National Commission for the Control of Nuclear Activities.

PSD has challenged 12 government decisions in total. One was subsequently withdrawn by acting prime minister Ilie Bolojan, leaving 11 before the court. The Court of Appeal has now suspended all 11.

The legal proceedings have moved rapidly. PSD referred the decisions to court on July 29, and the Court of Appeal summoned government representatives on the same day. The first group of cases was heard on July 30, while the remaining cases were scheduled for August 3.

The disputes form part of a wider confrontation between PSD and the interim government, which has been operating with limited powers following the collapse of the previous governing coalition.

PSD president Sorin Grindeanu said last week that the party had submitted preliminary complaints against decisions adopted at the government meeting of July 23.

“They all aim to exceed the constitutional and legal limits of the mandate of a dismissed government, because they promote new policies and represent the exercise of ministerial powers after the expiration of the 45-day term,” Grindeanu said.

PSD argues that the interim ministers no longer have the constitutional authority to adopt the measures because their mandate has expired. The government disputes the position and has indicated that it considers the decisions lawful.

The latest court rulings add to uncertainty over the implementation of government measures while Romania remains without a fully empowered administration and political parties continue negotiations over the formation of a new government.

iulian@romania-insider.com

(Photo source: Gov.ro)

World.title: Update: Romania’s Competition Council fines Agrana group over sugar price fixing
World.content:
Update: Lucsor Impex rejected the Competition Council's allegations and said it would challenge the decision in court, arguing that there is no evidence showing an anti-competitive agreement or coordination of commercial policies.

"Throughout the entire period under investigation, Lucsor acted as an independent distributor, not as a producer, offered its customers products at competitive prices and actively competed on the market," the company said in a statement sent to Romania-insider.com. It further argued that its commercial relationship with Agrana was a vertical producer-distributor relationship and that "setting a purchase price cannot be confused with setting resale prices to customers."

The company also challenged the relevance of Agrana's admission of wrongdoing, saying it was made for financial reasons, according to statements during the hearings, and "cannot constitute credible evidence against Lucsor." It further argued that the Competition Council's analysis did not fully reflect the effects of the government's 2023 emergency ordinance limiting commercial markups on basic food products, including sugar.

Initial story: Romania’s Competition Council has fined Agrana Sales & Marketing GmbH, Agrana România SRL and Lucsor Impex SRL a combined RON 52.09 million (EUR 10 million) for an anti-competitive agreement to fix sugar prices on the Romanian market.

Agrana Sales & Marketing GmbH and Agrana România, which the authority considers a single economic unit, were fined RON 42.18 million, while Lucsor Impex was fined RON 9.91 million, Economica.net reported.

Following an investigation, the Competition Council found that the companies had agreed on the selling prices of sugar in Romania. The arrangement involved setting the value of individual components of Lucsor Impex’s selling price, including its commercial margin, which should have been determined independently.

As a result, the selling prices charged by Lucsor Impex to its customers followed the same trend as prices charged by Agrana, the authority said.

The Competition Council concluded that the agreement was intended to increase or at least maintain sugar prices in Romania above the levels that would have resulted from normal competitive conditions.

Agrana Sales & Marketing GmbH and Agrana România admitted the infringement of Romania’s Competition Law and received reductions in their fines as a result.

The Competition Council said the investigation also examined Pfeifer & Langen Romania SRL. However, the authority closed the proceedings against the company after finding insufficient evidence of a breach that would justify sanctions or other measures.

Agrana is one of the major sugar producers operating in Romania and is part of Austria-based Agrana Beteiligungs-AG. The Romanian market has been subject to heightened scrutiny over food prices and competition, particularly amid periods of elevated inflation and pressure on household purchasing power.

The latest sanctions follow the Competition Council’s efforts to investigate agreements that may have restricted competition by influencing retail or wholesale prices. The authority’s findings concern the conduct of the companies during the period covered by its investigation.

iulian@romania-insider.com

World.title: North Macedonia Opposition Blasts ‘Secret Talks’ on Deal With Bulgaria
World.content:
North Macedonia’s Foreign Minister Timco Mucunski. Photo: North Macedonia’s MFA.

North Macedonia’s main opposition party, the Social Democrats, SDSM, accused Foreign Minister Timco Mucunski on Tuesday of holding “secret talks” about the country’s EU future behind the backs of its citizens.

“There is no normal country where a foreign minister says talks on the future of the country are a secret for its citizens,” the SDSM said.

The party accused the centre-right VMRO DPMNE-led government of Prime Minister Hristijan Mickoski of refusing to disclose details of important alleged negotiations.

The accusations came a day after Mucunski, in an interview with the state news agency MIA, said for the first time that the government was pursuing confidential efforts to find a “lasting and sustainable solution” to the long-running dispute with Bulgaria that has blocked the opening of EU accession talks.

“We are working on a solution, but not a solution at any cost, and not one that would prove unsustainable and bring us back to the situation we are in today,” Mucunski said, adding that revealing details could jeopardise the negotiations.

According to Mucunski, Skopje will not cross established “red lines” in these talks and is seeking guarantees from EU member states that its accession process will become more predictable once the current impasse is resolved.

Although he declined to identify those involved in the contacts, Mucunski suggested discussions were also taking place with several European partners behind closed doors in an attempt to break the years of deadlock.

North Macedonia’s accession talks have repeatedly stalled despite the country becoming an EU candidate back in 2005. After resolving a long-running dispute over its name with Greece, Skopje expected to move swiftly toward membership negotiations.

Instead, since 2020, Bulgaria blocked the process, arguing that North Macedonia had failed to address issues related to history, language and the rights of people who identify as Bulgarian.

An attempt to overcome the deadlock came in 2022 through the so-called French proposal, under which North Macedonia agreed to amend its constitution to include Bulgarians among its constitutionally recognised peoples.

However, the VMRO DPMNE-led government, which came to power in 2024, has stressed it will not act unless it receives guarantees that Bulgaria won’t block the country again, further down the line.

Mucunski’s remarks about quiet efforts to achieve a breakthrough come after the EU Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos last month called on North Macedonia again to change its constitution to speed up EU membership, making it clear that EU enlargement is not built on guarantees given in advance.

World.title: Election Race Starts As Bulgaria’s Acting President Seeks Full Mandate
World.content:
Bulgaria’s acting President Iliana Iotova has confirmed she will be running in the upcoming presidential elections scheduled for October.

Iotova, who was previously a low-profile Vice-President to Rumen Radev, assumed office in January after Radev resigned in order to become Bulgaria’s Prime Minister. On July 28 the ruling party, Progressive Bulgaria, and the Bulgarian Socialist Party, where Iotova launched her career, officially endorsed her bid to become the permanent President. Two days later an opinion poll gave her a 50 per cent approval rating from members of the public, enough to give her a landslide win. Other opinion polls have indicated a high, but slightly decreased, support for Radev’s government.

“Iotova has quite a comfortable lead”, Zlatina Zehirova, internal politics editor at Dnevnik.bg, told BIRN. “There are about three months until the elections, in which Iotova's opponents will look for ways to make the most of the power imbalances.” Zehirova said Progressive Bulgaria’s support is both a blessing and a curse, because the shaky politics of Radev’s government might reflect negatively on Iotova's campaign.

World.title: When Propaganda Backfires: Lessons from Orban’s Social Media Defeat in Hungary Election
World.content:
Debunkings went more viral

A notable case was when several young people unfurled a huge Ukrainian flag at the Tisza party’s March 15 national holiday rally. Photos of the protest action were taken and rapidly spread by pro-Fidesz outlets and accounts, portraying the incident as evidence of the opposition party’s pro-Ukrainian alignment.

However, the independent outlet 444.hu quickly reported that the protest action had been coordinated by key staff members of a Fidesz-linked digital campaign agency. It also identified the two minors who had unfurled the flag, one of whom later that day posted an Instagram story showing him with the chairman of the Budapest organisation of Fidelitas, Fidesz’s youth wing.

Repsense examined the content database’s dimensions like viral intensity, which means how fast and how far a narrative spreads – a measure “driven mainly by posting speed (sentences per hour), acceleration, and how big the narrative got in its first six hours relative to its final size”. Regarding the flag issue, the original posts reached 28 points on their “Facebook deep-dive” analysis’ viral intensity scoring, while the exposure scored 44, achieving half of its total reach in under an hour – the fastest spread in their Facebook dataset.

“What the data shows is that Hungarian citizens used the same platforms not as passive consumers of propaganda, but as an active counter-disinformation force. This is a dynamic that echoes the earliest promise of social media as a tool for civic resistance, which brings back memories of the Arab Spring,” says Mykolas Katkus, co-founder and CEO of Repsense. “The information environment had developed an immune response – each new provocation only accelerated its own exposure.”

That the truth behind the flag-unfurling was exposed by an independent media outlet highlights the importance of the free press. “I believe that the report is not fully holistic in the sense that we couldn’t make this government change without independent journalists,” emphasises Kata Horvath, a media researcher at the Department of Media and Communication of Eotvos Lorand University in Budapest.

Horvath believes Hungary’s remaining free press did a tremendous job under very trying conditions, uncovering many corruption cases, the truth behind the flag incident and the paedophile scandal. The latter refers to the 2024 resignation of president Katalin Novak after it emerged that she issued a pardon to the former deputy director of a children’s home who had helped cover up child sexual abuse by his superior.

Bulcsu Hunyadi, head of programs at the Budapest-based Political Capital think-tank, says the active communication by trusted and popular experts also proved important in explaining to the public what was really going on.

Repsense’s data shows similar patterns regarding the divergence between independent pollsters showing the opposition’s advantage and Fidesz-aligned institutes that predicted the governing party would win again. This issue became a narrative thread itself; in the report’s comparison, a poll by the Fidesz-aligned Nezopont Institute scored 15 on the viral intensity index, while the counter-response scored 35.

An AI-generated video featuring a Hungarian father being executed, part of Fidesz’s efforts to frame the vote as a choice between staying out of the war in Ukraine or joining it, scored 28 points, while its counter-narratives got 35. Repsense found that this was one of the most negatively received pieces of campaign-produced content. While these negative reactions could have been towards Ukraine or simply a human reaction, the surrounding discourse, rather than the sentiment score itself, suggests a backlash against the video itself. The most negatively received narrative threads, however, concerned physical attacks on activists.

The pattern was not universal, however: in the widely discussed case of a Ukrainian cash-in-transit seizure that was heavily used for propaganda purposes by the pro-government media, Repsense measured the original narrative and the counter-narrative at the same viral intensity.

World.title: Ticket Out: A Serbian’s Journey from Mercenary in Ukraine to Gangland Hitman
World.content:
For years, Aleksandar Dinic kept a bullet as a souvenir of the war in Ukraine.

Police found it among his belongings in January, when they arrested the 35-year-old Serbian citizen on suspicion of murder.

His alleged victim, a 43-year-old man, was shot dead on January 16 at the foot of Mount Avala, on the outskirts of the Serbian capital, Belgrade.

The dead man is believed to have been part of a Balkan drug cartel and was on trial at the time in Belgrade, accused alongside others of smuggling 324 kilograms of cocaine from South America to Europe.

Organised crime prosecutors in Belgrade suspect that Dinic was hired as a contract killer by the Montenegro-based Kavac criminal clan, according to case files seen by BIRN.

Since 2015, dozens of people have been killed in a gang war between the Kavac and Skaljari clans, which trace their roots to two neighbourhoods of the Montenegrin coastal town of Kotor.

Fighting erupted after 300 kilograms of cocaine vanished from an apartment in the Spanish city of Valencia. Skaljari member Goran Radoman was among the first to die, shot dead in his Belgrade garage.

Since then, the feud has gone global, claiming victims in Montenegro, Serbia, Turkey, Austria, Greece, Spain and other countries.

Dinic had no direct involvement in the gang war, but he did have experience fighting with pro-Russian forces in eastern Ukraine and was on the lookout for some extra cash.

World.title: Wildfires in Greece Blaze for Fourth Day
World.content:
Greek firefighters on Monday battled for a fourth day a fire that started in Viotia, the southern part of Central Greece, and expanded to Western Attica, which has burned homes, livestock and farmland. The fires in Greece have so far claimed the lives of five firefighters.

The Fire Service said the problem is worst in the mountainous area of Kandili and Agia Skepi, residential settlements in Western Attica, and south and southeast of the coastal villages of Psatha and Porto Germeno, where most firefighting forces have been concentrated. Emergency messages were sent to civilians to evacuate their homes.

“Fire Service forces remain very strong in the field and are operating along the entire perimeter to bring this particularly difficult fire under control as quickly as possible,” the Fire Service’s spokesperson, Giannis Artopoios, told state TV on Monday.

A total of 450 firefighters, 22 forest commando teams and 125 fire engines are battling the flames, while 12 helicopters, including two for aerial coordination and 11 aircraft, are assisting from the air.

“The ecological disaster is enormous; thousands of acres of forest and grasslands and especially areas that have been burned in the recent or distant past, all of this has been destroyed, unfortunately,” Panagiotis Margetis, Mayor of Megara, in Western Attica, said on Monday.

Strong ground firefighting forces are operating in Western Attica, including on-site units, water tankers and military and local authority vehicles. Aerial vehicles are continuously dropping water in hard-to-reach areas.

“Our goal is to immediately … return the areas to normality as quickly as possible,” Deputy Minister of Climate Crisis and Civil Protection Kostas Katsafados said on Monday. Katsafados said checks on the affected areas will begin immediately to record the damage to homes, businesses and public infrastructure, and to provide compensation to those affected.

Regarding compensation to farmers, the Agricultural Insurance Organisation will record the damage done to plant capital, while compensation for livestock farmers who have lost animals and assets will also be examined.

So far, five firefighters have lost their lives battling the fires. Two firefighters, a Greek and a Dane, lost their lives on August 2, when a Bell firefighting helicopter collided in mid-air with another helicopter while attempting to extinguish a forest fire that broke out in Psatha, a coastal area in Western Attica.

Two firefighters lost their lives in Krya Vrysi in Rethymno, Crete, on July 30, when they were surrounded by flames, and another firefighter lost his life while on duty in a fire that had broken out in Gytheio, in the Peloponnese.

World.title: Snap Elections Remain Uncertain After Serbia’s No-Confidence Vote
World.content:
Last week, a no-confidence vote was held in Serbia’s parliament in the Serbian Progressive Party-led government.

The motion failed. But for the opposition, it was still an opportunity to speak about the government’s affairs, and for experts, another discussion about when potential snap elections could be held.

Sixty-two opposition MPs submitted a request for a no-confidence motion in February. The first parliamentary session with such a motion on the agenda was scheduled for April – but the ruling majority failed to secure a quorum at two sessions held that month.

Until the no-confidence procedure was concluded, the standard legal process for calling snap elections could not begin.

World.title: Greek Arrests Revive Politically Charged Case of 2010 Bank Arson
World.content:
The case was reopened in July, amid unconfirmed claims of an anonymous tip-off sent by email.

“It doesn’t convince me,” Karagianni told Greek MEGA TV on July 11. Calling for “substantial evidence”, Karagianni said: “We want the perpetrators to be exposed and taken to where they should be taken, which is to prison.”

Thrasivoulos Kontaxis, a lawyer representing 11 injured survivors and relatives of the victims, said he was “cautiously optimistic” of justice being served.

“It will represent mental redemption, that at the end of this journey someone was actually called upon to pay the price by being punished, at least.”

Three people died in the bank fire, caused by a trio of black-clad, masked individuals who set fire to the building on central Stadiou Street during a protest against the austerity demanded of Greece.

Bank employees Epaminondas Tsakalis, Paraskevi Zoulias and Angeliki Papathanasopoulou were trapped by the flames on the third floor and suffocated to death. Papathanasopoulou was pregnant. Twenty-one others were injured.

In 2013, three bank executives were convicted of manslaughter and bodily harm due to negligence; two were sentenced to 22 years in prison and the third to five years and one month.

Then, in 2016, two men were charged with arson but acquitted due to a lack of evidence. The case was closed, reopened again in 2020, reportedly following an anonymous phone call, only to be shelved again.

None of the three suspects have been named. All have denied any wrongdoing.

World.title: Bizarre Medieval “Vampire” Found in Pakrac Cemetery
World.content:
August the 4th, 2026 – An extremely bizarre Medieval “vampire” has been found in a Pakrac cemetery, with archaeologists believing that the particular method of burial was to “prevent the vampire returning among the living”.

Index reports that a very mysterious medieval burial discovered at the Stari Grad Pakrac archaeological site has once again brought attention to ancient beliefs about vampires and the fear of the dead returning among the living. Archaeologists uncovered the remains of a person buried face down, an unusual burial position that experts believe may have been an intentional ritual. According to archaeologist Krešimir Vacek, the way the body was placed suggests that people of the time wanted to prevent the deceased from returning after death.

The “vampire” burial likely dates back to the late 13th century and was found at a medieval cemetery connected with the former settlement around Stari Grad Pakrac. Archaeologists have been researching the site for years, uncovering numerous graves and important historical remains.

This is not the first unusual discovery of its kind at the location. Earlier excavations revealed another so-called “vampire” burial, a skeleton inside a valuable sarcophagus that was missing its human head. Instead, researchers found animal remains believed to be part of a horse skull. Such practices were linked to medieval beliefs that certain people could return from the grave and harm the living.

In medieval Europe, fears of supernatural forces were widespread, and communities sometimes carried out unusual burial practices when they believed someone could become a threat after death. The latest discovery in Pakrac offers another rare insight into the beliefs, fears, and rituals of people who lived more than 800 years ago.

World.title: Animal Rights Group Sparks Debate After Tragic Zagreb Zoo Lioness Death
World.content:
August the 4th, 2026 – A prominent Croatian animal rights group Friends of Animals (Prijatelji životinja) has sparked fresh debate after the tragic death of a lioness at the jaws of a male line at Zagreb Zoo.

Index reports that an ongoing debate over the role and funding of zoological gardens has returned to the public scene in Croatia. It comes after the aforementioned animal rights organisation strongly criticised the way public money is used to support zoos, arguing that people contribute financially even if they never visit them.

The organisation claims that many people are unaware that municipal budgets are used to finance the operation of zoological gardens. According to Prijatelji životinja, taxpayers are effectively contributing to institutions they may never personally use, raising questions about whether public funds should support facilities that keep animals in captivity.

Their criticism focuses on the belief that the traditional zoo model is outdated and that keeping wild animals in enclosed spaces cannot fully meet their natural needs. The group argues that resources should instead be directed towards alternative approaches to animal protection and conservation.

A long-running debate over the purpose of modern zoos

The controversy reflects a much wider global discussion about the role of zoological gardens in the 21st century. Supporters of modern zoos argue that they are no longer simply places where visitors come to see exotic animals. Many contemporary institutions focus on education, scientific research, species protection and breeding programmes aimed at helping endangered animals.

Critics, however, question whether these goals justify keeping animals in captivity. Prijatelji životinja argues that no enclosure can truly replace an animal’s natural habitat and that conservation efforts should focus more heavily on protecting species in the wild.

Public funding remains at the very heart of the discussion

The financial side of the debate has become one of the main points of disagreement.

Prijatelji životinja has previously highlighted examples of cities allocating significant amounts of public money to maintain zoos, arguing that citizens who do not support the concept are still indirectly financing it through taxes. Supporters of zoological gardens, however, point out that these institutions provide educational programmes, contribute to biodiversity awareness and participate in international conservation projects. Modern zoos increasingly present themselves as centres for protecting endangered species rather than simply tourist attractions.

Zagreb Zoo highlights conservation and education

The debate comes at a time when the role of zoos continues to evolve. The Zoological Garden of the City of Zagreb promotes programmes focused on animal care, public education and conservation activities. The institution also offers initiatives such as animal adoption programmes, through which citizens can financially support the care of individual animals while they remain residents of the zoo. The zoo has also highlighted its involvement in international projects aimed at protecting wildlife and raising awareness about biodiversity.

A question with no easy answers…

The disagreement between animal protection organisations and zoo supporters is unlikely to disappear. For critics, the issue is about whether society should continue funding a model based on keeping wild animals in captivity. For supporters, zoos remain important centres for education, research and conservation.

As public discussions about animal welfare become increasingly prominent, the future of zoological gardens will likely depend on how successfully they can balance their traditional role with modern expectations about conservation, ethics and animal wellbeing.

World.title: Croatian High-Tech Trains: The Innovation Transforming Rail Transport
World.content:
August the 4th, 2026 – Croatian high-tech trains are the domestic innovation transforming rail transport as the country enters a new era of railway transport.

As Sinisa Malus reports for Poslovni, that era is being strongly driven by one of the country’s most advanced industrial achievements – modern trains developed and produced by Končar.

Often described as among the most complex technological products created by Croatian industry, these new-generation trains represent a combination of domestic engineering, advanced technology and a push towards greener transport solutions. Over 70 percent of their components are Croatian-made, while key systems and subsystems, including control systems, communication technology, traction transformers and other essential elements, are produced within the Končar Group.

To date, Končar has delivered 70 new-generation low-floor trains to Croatian railways, including 40 units delivered in less than five years. The company has also recently signed new agreements with HŽ Passenger Transport for six battery-electric trains and the construction of a hybrid charging station in Kotoriba, with a total value of 53.6 million euros.

Croatia’s first battery trains enter service

One of the biggest milestones has been the development of Končar’s battery-powered trains, which represent a major technological step for Croatia and one of the first examples of this type of commercial railway technology in Europe.

The battery-electric multiple unit (BEMV) uses fully electric propulsion, powered by onboard batteries as well as existing overhead electrical networks. This makes it particularly suitable for Croatia, where a significant part of the railway network is still not electrified. This type of technology allows the trains to operate on both electrified and non-electrified routes, creating a more sustainable solution for passenger transport across the country.

The train was designed for daily operation of up to 480 kilometres and up to 18 hours of service per day. On non-electrified lines, it can reach speeds of up to 120 km/h using battery power, while on electrified routes it can achieve speeds of up to 160 km/h. Another highly important innovation is the battery motor train (BMV), designed specifically for routes without overhead electrical infrastructure. It can reach speeds of up to 120 km/h and, depending on conditions, can travel more than 200 kilometres during testing on a single charge.

Designed for modern passengers

The new trains are not only focused on efficiency and sustainability but also on improving passenger comfort. They include wheelchair access ramps, dedicated bicycle spaces, accessible toilets, video surveillance, passenger information screens, audio announcements and free Wi-Fi. The trains can also be connected with other new-generation low-floor units already operating in Croatia, allowing increased capacity when needed.

A major investment in greener mobility

The development of these trains is part of the project “Application of Green Technologies in Railway Passenger Transport”, financed through Croatia’s National Recovery and Resilience Plan. Several charging stations have already been opened at railway stations in cities including Split, Osijek, Varaždin, Bjelovar, Virovitica and Pula. Further expansion is planned, with additional battery and hybrid trains expected to enter service in the coming years. A wider project financed through a European Investment Bank loan, worth almost €118 million, includes the delivery of additional trains and charging infrastructure.

New trains to connect Zagreb and Split

Končar is also preparing a new generation of long-distance trains that will connect Zagreb and Split.

The route between the two cities stretches for 429 kilometres, but only around a quarter of the line is electrified. Because of this, the new trains will combine electric and diesel propulsion, allowing them to operate efficiently across different sections of the route. The trains will reach speeds of up to 160 km/h and will be capable of connecting multiple units together to increase capacity. The first six trains are part of a larger agreement between Končar and HŽ Passenger Transport covering 19 new low-floor trains. Additional units are planned to connect cities including Osijek, Rijeka and Pula.

Croatian engineering on the international stage

The latest generation of Končar trains highlights the growing role of Croatian industry in advanced manufacturing and sustainable technology.

From battery-powered rail vehicles to modern mobility solutions, these projects show that Croatian companies are capable of developing complex products that compete in a highly demanding global market. As railway transport across Europe moves towards lower emissions and smarter infrastructure, Croatia’s domestically produced trains are becoming a symbol of innovation, engineering expertise and the country’s ambitions beyond traditional industries.

World.title: Croatian Pizza Prices Spark Debate as Bill Goes Viral
World.content:
August the 4th, 2026 – Croatian pizza prices have sparked fresh debate as a bill of 32 euros issued in Stari Grad on Hvar goes viral across social media.

Debates over prices on the Croatian coast have once again erupted on social media, with a restaurant bill from the island of Hvar becoming the latest trigger for a wider discussion about the cost of summer holidays in Croatia. Poslovni reports that this latest price-related controversy began after a guest shared a receipt from a pizzeria in Stari Grad, where a large pizza cost 22 euros. The post quickly spread online, dividing opinions between two opposing camps.

Some users described such prices as completely unreasonable and a sign of growing greed in the tourism sector. Others argued that restaurants clearly display their menus and prices, meaning guests can see the costs in advance and decide whether they want to order. The fact that another seaside bill became a viral topic highlights how strongly food and service prices continue to shape conversations during every tourist season. The debate has grown beyond the price of one pizza, becoming part of a larger discussion about Croatia’s tourism model.

22 euros is steep compared to a 7.50 euro pizza in italy

Soon, visitors began sharing their own experiences and comparing Croatian coastal prices with those in other popular European destinations. One social media user compared the situation with southern Italy, saying that in a restaurant in Ercolano, near Naples, a pizza cost just 7.50 euros, a beer 3 euros, and a bottle of white wine 10 euros.

Others shared less positive experiences from Croatian islands. One visitor said that while the island of Vis was beautiful, the prices were too high. She described paying €120 per person for a seven-hour speedboat excursion that included visits to three caves and two beaches, but without lunch included. She also pointed out that entering one of the caves cost an additional €15, even for those who chose to swim there themselves.

However, not everyone believes the criticism is justified. Some commenters argued that visitors simply choose where they travel and where they eat according to their own budgets. “Everyone goes where the food and prices suit them,” one comment said, summarising the opinion of those who believe customers have the final choice.

Many also pointed out that high prices will continue as long as there is demand and people willing to pay them.

“While there are people who will gladly pay 22 euros for a pizza, there will be prices like this. But tourism cannot rely on this forever,” one user wrote, warning that the current model may not be sustainable in the long term. Others noted that expensive pizzas are not only found on the coast, mentioning examples from Zagreb as well, expanding the discussion beyond seasonal tourism.

An even more expensive pizza becomes the symbol of the debate

The most attention, however, was attracted by a comment from a man who claimed that he had seen an even more expensive pizza on the island of Brač. “There are also pizzas for 32 euros. If it doesn’t suit you, the door is open for you to leave and go elsewhere,” he wrote.

The comment quickly became a symbol of the argument that prices are ultimately determined by supply and demand, with businesses charging what customers are prepared to pay. Another theory that appeared in the discussion was that some tourists deliberately visit the most expensive restaurants so they can later complain online and share their bills on social media, gaining attention. “They go there on purpose so they can complain about high prices afterwards,” one commenter suggested.

Guests complain, but the spending continues…

Although complaints about Croatian prices return every summer, financial data paints a more complex picture. Examples of expensive bills continue to circulate online, including a case of visitors from neighbouring Bosnia and Herzegovina who reportedly paid more than 50 euros for a jumbo pizza and two coffees near Dubrovnik, as well as a British tourist who paid a whole 42 euros for just two drinks in Split.

However, spending figures show that tourists are still opening their wallets. According to data from Croatia’s Tax Administration, consumer spending during the summer months has continued to grow. In July, the total value of fiscalised receipts increased by almost 24 percent compared with the same month last year, reaching 6.8 billion euros.

The hospitality sector also recorded growth, with more than seven percent more receipts issued and their total value increasing by over 11 percent. Tourism analysts say this shows that visitors continue to spend despite complaints, although they warn that such a trend may not be sustainable forever.

The picture is not the same everywhere

A closer look at the tourism sector shows that success is not evenly distributed. While luxury hotels and high-end campsites are recording strong occupancy and increased revenue, many small private accommodation providers and some restaurants are facing difficulties. June 2026’s figures showed a decline of seven percent in arrivals and six percent in overnight stays compared with the previous year, with the largest drops recorded in Istria, Kvarner and Zadar County.

The data suggests a growing divide within Croatian tourism. Luxury segments continue to perform well, while businesses offering average services at increasingly high prices are finding it harder to attract guests. Tourists appear to be paying closer attention to value for money and are becoming less willing to spend large amounts on experiences that do not match the expected quality.

Market rules apply, but guests are becoming more demanding

Tourism experts have repeatedly warned about price increases that are not matched by improvements in quality. While the government and the Ministry of Tourism have called for more reasonable pricing policies, Boris Žgomba, president of the Croatian Chamber of Commerce’s Association of Travel Agencies, has stressed that prices are ultimately determined by the market and the relationship between supply and demand. Croatia has positioned itself alongside other Mediterranean destinations such as Italy and Spain in terms of pricing, while Dubrovnik regularly ranks among the most expensive cities in the region.

At the same time, travellers are increasingly searching for authentic experiences, local culture and quieter destinations. This could create opportunities for parts of Croatia’s tourism industry that adapt to changing expectations.

If prices continue rising without a corresponding improvement in quality, some tourists may turn towards more affordable destinations such as Albania, which has experienced strong tourism growth by attracting visitors who find Croatia or Greece too expensive. As another busy summer season unfolds, prices on the Croatian coast and islands remain one of the most debated topics in Croatia, raising a continuing question: where is the line between market logic and genuine hospitality?

World.title: Is Spending in July in Croatia Really Breaking Records?
World.content:
August the 3rd, 2026 – Tax Authority data for spending in July in Croatia shows continued growth in fiscalised spending, but the nominal figures need to be interpreted with caution.

Higher receipt totals don’t actually necessarily mean that residents and tourists bought more goods and services, because part of the increase comes from higher prices. Index writes that in order to assess the real trend in consumption it is necessary to remove the effect of inflation. When nominal data are adjusted for price rises, the real growth is noticeably weaker, and in some periods and sectors spending stagnates or even falls.

price increases are largely responsible for nominal growth

According to Tax Authority data on fiscalised spending, food-and-beverage preparation and serving activities as well as the accommodation sector in Croatia recorded strong growth during the summer months, with a clear seasonal jump towards July. The cumulative change compared with the previous period is positive, and growth is also visible in the monthly figures.

In food-and-beverage preparation and serving, fiscalised turnover during the month of July reached 891 million euros nominally, or 860 million euros when adjusted for inflation. In the same month last year the turnover stood at 802 million euros. This means the nominal value of receipts increased by around 11 percent, while real growth after removing the effect of higher prices was about 7 percent.

Cumulatively, from the beginning of the year to the end of July, turnover in hospitality was 11 percent higher nominally than in the same period last year. After correction for inflation the real growth stood at 6.5 percent. In other words, guests and residents did spend more than last year, but the difference is not as large as the nominal figures suggest because part of the rise stems from higher prices of food and drink.

a look at accommodation

Results by county are highly uneven. While some counties recorded real growth in fiscalised accommodation turnover of more than 30 percent, others saw double-digit declines. Most Adriatic counties achieved moderate growth, yet even on the coast the results are not uniform. In some counties turnover rose by only a few percent, while Dubrovnik-Neretva County recorded a slight real decline of 0.6 percent.

Extreme results in individual counties should be interpreted cautiously; they may be the consequence of a low comparative base, changes in coverage or local specifics rather than a dramatic shift in overall tourist activity. During July, fiscalised turnover in the accommodation sector reached 691 million euros nominally, compared with 630 million euros in the same month last year – a nominal increase of 9.7 percent. After removing the impact of inflation this year’s turnover amounts to 667 million euros, meaning it was 5.9 percent higher in real terms than in July last year. Guests therefore left almost ten percent more money for accommodation, but the actual growth in consumption was closer to six percent.

was july 2026 really more successful than july 2025?

The data show that fiscalised turnover in July was higher than last year in both hospitality and accommodation, even after adjustment for inflation. Nevertheless, real growth was significantly weaker than the nominal figures, and results vary considerably between sectors and counties.

It can therefore be concluded that July was better than last year’s according to the indicators examined, but not that the season was dramatically or unequivocally more successful. Tax Authority data are currently the most reliable publicly available indicator of fiscalised spending, yet they do not cover every element of the tourist result. An important methodological change should also be noted: from this year the Tax Authority’s reporting includes payments via transaction accounts. In order to keep the data comparable with the previous year, those payments have been excluded from this analysis.

The conclusion is therefore cautious: nominal spending is rising, but once inflation is taken into account the picture is considerably more moderate. The figures show seasonal growth and large regional differences, but they do not unambiguously confirm that this year’s July was significantly more successful.

World.title: Meet Taljurić, The Strange Croatian Fingerprint Island
World.content:
August the 3rd, 2026 – Taljurić, (or Pijat if you’re local) is a strange formation, it’s a totally flat Croatian island that resembles a human fingerprint and has absolutely zero vegetation on it.

The Adriatic might look calm and alluring during summer, but it’s no stranger to surprisingly violent storms and winds. When they hit, the usually calm Adriatic becomes very choppy and washes over almost its entire surface repeatedly. Putni kofer writes that over countless centuries, these repeated actions have made it appear like a flat stone plate laid carefully in the middle of the open, unforgiving sea.

Wherever you look along Croatia’s heavily indented, rugged and island-laden coastline, something takes your breath away. Be it stunning beaches, pebbles and rocks of every shape, secret coves, water shifting from transparent turquoise to deep blue, shores battered by waves on one side and watched over by powerful mountains on the other… The list goes on. Then there are the 1,000+ islands, small and large, bare and green, low and steep, and some of the most unusual shapes imaginable. Some have been inhabited for thousands of years; others hold only a lighthouse, a lonely chapel or traces of former farming. A few are so tiny and exposed that almost nothing can grow on them. Among these rocky outcrops lie some of the strangest sights on the Croatian coast.

From Galešnjak and Baljenac to… Pijat, (Taljurić)

Some of these islands have gained worldwide recognition. Galešnjak, thanks to its almost perfect heart shape, became known as the Island of Love. Baljenac (also called Bavljenac), seen from the air, resembles a giant human fingerprint – an effect created by the dense, tangled network of dry-stone walls that once enclosed tiny agricultural plots. In this sea of bizarre shapes lies another islet whose appearance is perfectly captured by its name. It is called Taljurić (locally also known as Pijat). Viewed from the sea or from the air, it really does look like a large stone plate carefully placed on the surface of the Adriatic.

Taljurić lies within the boundaries of the remarkable Telašćica Nature Park, on the south-eastern part of Dugi otok, and is regarded as one of the most unusual natural phenomena of this protected area. Official documents list it as a rock (hrid) and rank it among the smallest islands and rocks in the park’s archipelago. It measures about 60 metres in diameter and rises only three metres above the sea.

In essence, it is an almost flat stone slab made of horizontally layered limestone. Its upper surface has been continuously exposed to waves, salt and wind, so the whole islet looks as if the sea has been grinding and levelling it for centuries. During powerful storms the waves can sweep across nearly its entire surface – which explains why no vegetation has ever managed to take hold.

no vegetation manages to take hold on taljurić

Its unusual appearance directly influenced its name. The islet resembles a flat, round board of the kind once used in kitchens, which Venetian sailors called “tagliero” in their dialect. According to Telašćica Nature Park, the name Taljurić, which isn’t frequently used by locals, developed from that word. There are absolutely no trees, bushes or grass on the surface. Although from a distance it looks completely barren, its edge is not lifeless. On the rocks just above the waterline live colonies of barnacles (known locally as brambuljci), tiny marine crustaceans that cling tightly to the stone and withstand the constant pounding of the waves.

Another curiosity lies on the south-western side of Pijat: the remains of a former fossil cave whose roof eroded away over geological time. Today it looks like a cave open to the sky – a stone hollow without a ceiling. The sea around the islet is rich in life, and the wider Telašćica area includes valuable marine habitats such as posidonia meadows, underwater cliffs, reefs and sea caves.

World.title: Stari Grad Pag: The Croatian Town That Cholera Forcibly Relocated
World.content:
August the 3rd, 2026 – Stari grad Pag was entirely planned and constructed, but ended up being completely relocated because of a cholera outbreak that decimated the local population.

Stari grad (Old town) Pag used to be quite a large, fairly wealthy town protected by impressive walls, much like those down in Dubrovnik. Putni kofer writes that all was well until 1852, when a terrible cholera epidemic struck and decimated the local population. It was at that point that plans pivoted, and the entire town ended up elsewhere.

stari grad pag – the town that moved

It’s very well known at this point that the moon-like, rather bizarre looking island of Pag offers an otherworldly landscape of stark stone expanses, centuries-old salt pans that still yield “white gold,” outstanding cheese, and a history stretching back to the Middle Ages. Its main town, Pag, is the ideal base for exploring the island. Highlights include the Gradac viewpoint, the historic core reached via the stone Katina bridge, and the remains of walls and towers.

Few people know that the original Pag actually stood roughly one kilometre further south. Residents moved to the present planned town in the 15th century. Old Pag flourished throughout the Middle Ages thanks to salt production, which sustained the island. On the hilly ground next to the salt pans sat churches, monasteries, a fortified citadel, a palace, large and small loggias, a hospital, and large and small town squares. Along the coastline itself stood salt warehouses and two harbours – Veliki and Mali mul. What remains of Old Pag today are the ruins of the Franciscan monastery and the Romanesque Church of St Mary, which houses a wooden Gothic statue of the Mother of God.

salvation from a deadly disease? maybe…

For a century and a half, every year on the Feast of the Assumption (on the 15th of August), the people of Pag make a pilgrimage from the Old Town to the new Pag, carrying with them the statue of the Blessed Virgin Mary. The votive procession dates from 1855 and has a striking historical background.

The devastating cholera epidemic hit Pag hard in 1852 and took a particularly heavy toll. To stop the spread of the disease, all cemeteries were moved out of the town and local churches. On Assumption Day back in 1855, the townsfolk spontaneously gathered around the statue of the Mother of God in the then Stari grad, praying for deliverance. After they carried the statue on their shoulders to Pag’s Collegiate Church, the last cholera victims were buried on the 16th of August, on the feast of St Roch. The residents then vowed that every single year on that day, they would bring the statue to Pag, where it would remain in the Collegiate Church for a full 22 days, until the Nativity of Mary, so the faithful could give thanks and pray for health, peace and love.

the discovery of remarkable megaliths and an ancient greek settlement

Megaliths and numerous artefacts from antiquity have been found on the site of Stari grad Pag, indicating that a human settlement already existed and functioned there way back during ancient Greek times. The old town was once so rich and economically powerful that it could finance the construction of its own defensive walls.

Its history was also shaped by King Béla IV, who, back in 1244, found refuge on the island while fleeing his enemies. In gratitude for the help he received, he granted Pag a charter as a free royal city. After the relocation in the second half of the 15th century, Stari grad Pag lost its importance and eventually ceased to be an independent settlement. Its only fully preserved building is the Church of St Mary, first mentioned in 1192 and believed to stand on the site of an early Croatian basilica from the 8th century. It was saved from ruin by the Franciscans, who built a monastery nearby and lived there from the 16th until the end of the 19th century.

World.title: Dear Tourists: There Are No Private Beaches in Croatia
World.content:
August the 3rd, 2026 – If someone tells you that there are private beaches in Croatia you can’t enter this summer, you can freely ignore them and carry on swimming.

As Index reports, the basic rule is simple: on almost every beach in Croatia you are allowed to swim, sunbathe and spread out your towel – even if the beach is situated in front of a hotel, campsite, apartment complex or private villa. The sea and the seashore form part of the maritime domain in Croatia. That means they are not private property and are intended entirely for public use. The owner of a house on the first row to the sea does not own the beach in front of it, and a hotel doesn’t become the owner of a beach simply because it is located in front of its building.

swim wherever you like

Signs saying “private beach,” “reserved for guests” or “no entry” do not automatically mean swimming is forbidden. If the beach is part of the maritime domain, then you are allowed to be there. A hotel, restaurant or concessionaire may charge for sunbeds, umbrellas, drinks, food or other services. However, they cannot charge you simply for being on the beach or entering the sea and swimming. You do not have to rent a sunbed, order a drink or be a hotel guest in order to swim there. You are free to bring your own towel, food, drinks and portable cooler.

sun loungers cannot occupy the entire beach

Empty sunbeds must not be used to reserve the beach. Just because someone rents out sunbeds does not mean they can occupy the whole beach in the morning and leave only a narrow path to the sea for other bathers. The same applies to towels left overnight – a towel does not reserve a spot for the next day. Anyone who wants a place on the beach has to come to the beach. Access to the shore may be restricted in military zones, special-purpose ports, shipyards, parts of harbours, or places where it is regulated for safety reasons.

there are exceptions with very special rules…

A very small number of beaches still operate under older concessions that allow special access rules. There are 15 such beaches in Croatia; better-known examples include Kostabela in Rijeka, Valalta in Rovinj and the beaches in front of Hotel Alan in Starigrad. These are exceptions. Under the 2023 Maritime Domain and Sea Ports Act, new sea beaches may not be fenced off, entrance fees may not be charged, and they may not be excluded from general public use except in strictly defined cases (for example, beaches belonging to public health institutions or designated nudist beaches).

the beach and the path leading to it are very different things

It is important to distinguish the beach itself from the path leading to it. The beach may be public, but the way to reach it can cross private land. If the only path to the beach goes through someone’s yard, garden, olive grove or fenced property, the owner can refuse you passage if there is no public path or right of way. The fact that it is the shortest or only land route does not give you the right to cross private property. In such cases you can reach the beach from the sea – by boat, kayak, SUP or by swimming. Once you have arrived legally, the owner of the house by the sea cannot forbid you from staying on the beach itself.

what if someone tries to kick you off a beach?

Don’t get into an argument. Ask on what basis they are forbidding you to stay. Photograph the sign, fence, padlock or the situation on the ground. If someone threatens you or tries to remove you physically, call the police on 192. If someone is fencing off the shore, locking access to the sea or illegally occupying a beach, you can report it to the harbour master’s office, municipal wardens or maritime inspectors.

The bottom line is simple: in Croatia, a beach in front of a hotel, campsite, restaurant or private villa is, as a rule, not private. You may swim, sunbathe and stay there. Just don’t try to reach it by cutting through someone else’s private garden.

World.title: Tallinn's beloved Old Thomas symbol takes center stage in Sõru Museum exhibit
World.content:
At the Sõru Museum on Hiiumaa, it is possible to explore items bearing the motif of Tallinn's symbol — the weather vane Old Thomas — from the private collection of Eero Kööp.

At the Sõru Museum, Old Thomas is depicted on very different kinds of objects. Collector Eero Kööp said he has found, bought and received these items as gifts over roughly ten years.

"I don't remember how the interest started. Maybe it began with one wall plaque. Many items were left out of this exhibition," Kööp said.

Tallinn's guardian Old Thomas, or Vana Toomas in Estonian, will soon be celebrating a major anniversary.

"The Old Thomas weather vane was placed on the [Tallinn Town Hall] tower when the year was 1530. But according to one legend, he was named Thomas later," Kööp said.

It is also unknown who the author of the first Old Thomas — now held at the Tallinn City Museum — originally was. And in broad terms, Old Thomas has retained his appearance over five centuries.

"But he has been stylized in several different ways. For example, once we had a sister city, Schwerin, and they made him into a complete clown. At the request of restaurants, Old Thomas looks a bit different. But mostly he is still the same — the flag is always on one side," Kööp said.

Most of the Old Thomas items on display at the exhibition date back decades. The best‑known object is perhaps the former Estoplast factory's Old Thomas table lamp from the Soviet era. But today's so‑called modern Old Thomases have a completely different story.

The weather vane now turning atop the Tallinn's Town Hall is the present‑day Old Thomas. Source: Siim Lõvi /ERR

"Modern Old Thomases are made in China. Our souvenir sellers order their products from China," Kööp noted.

And the reason such an exhibition was set up on Hiiumaa at all is very simple and practical.

"Here at the Sõru end, Eero Kööp had a few Old Thomases, and over ten years he collected more. Then the time came when he needed to do renovations at home. And then he came to the museum and asked whether an exhibition could be made. And that's how it started to branch out," said Sõru Museum director Eve Ellermäe.

World.title: Estonia's new ambassadors take up their posts
World.content:
At the beginning of August, several Estonian ambassadors to foreign countries took up new postings, including the ambassadors to the United States, Canada and NATO.

Hannes Hanso succeeded Kristjan Prikk as Estonia's ambassador to the United States, based in Washington. Since 2022, Hanso had served as Estonia's ambassador to China, as well as to Vietnam, Mongolia and Thailand.

Prikk, who had served as Estonia's ambassador to the United States since 2021, in turn succeeded Jüri Luik as Estonia's permanent representative to NATO.

Marje Luup was appointed Estonia's ambassador to Kazakhstan, based in Astana.

Estonia's previous ambassador to Kazakhstan, Jaap Ora, resigned on December 9 last year after drawing criticism from Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna (Eesti 200) and Foreign Ministry Secretary General Jonatan Vseviov over President Alar Karis' state visit to Kazakhstan. Ora has since challenged his dismissal in court.

Luup previously served as Estonia's ambassador to India, as well as to Bangladesh and Sri Lanka. She was succeeded in New Delhi in August by Kristi Karelsohn.

Ambassadors were also replaced in Canada, Ukraine, Albania, Hungary, Ireland, Spain, Portugal and Brazil.

Gert Auväärt succeeded Margus Rava as Estonia's ambassador to Canada, based in Ottawa.

Tiina Intelmann succeeded Annely Kolk as Estonia's ambassador to Ukraine, based in Kyiv.

Piret Urb succeeded Karin Rannu as Estonia's ambassador to Albania, based in Athens.

Jana Vanamölder succeeded Raul Toomas as Estonia's ambassador to Hungary, based in Budapest.

Kairi Saar-Isop succeeded Kairi Künka as Estonia's ambassador to Ireland, based in Dublin.

Lembit Uibo succeeded Andres Rundu as Estonia's ambassador to Spain, based in Madrid.

Katrin Kivi succeeded Moonika Kase as Estonia's ambassador to Portugal, based in Lisbon.

Estonia also opened new embassies this year in Yerevan, the capital of Armenia; Chișinău, the capital of Moldova; Baku, the capital of Azerbaijan; Brasília, the capital of Brazil; and Nairobi, the capital of Kenya.

Former Ambassador to Portugal Moonika Kase was appointed Estonia's first ambassador to Brazil, based in Brasília.

Tiina Nirk was appointed Estonia's ambassador to Azerbaijan, based in Baku.

Siiri Königsberg was appointed Estonia's ambassador to Moldova, based in Chișinău.

Several diplomatic rotations are still to come.

Daniel Erik Schaer will take up his post as Estonia's ambassador to Kenya, based in Nairobi, on August 31.

Estonia's ambassador to Latvia, based in Riga, will change on December 1, when Celia Kuningas-Saagpakk succeeds Eerik Marmei.

Kuningas-Saagpakk had previously served as Estonia's ambassador to the Holy See, based in Tallinn. She was succeeded by Minna-Liina Lind.

World.title: Estonia ramps up defenses against invasive pests as warming climate hikes risks
World.content:
A combination of a warming climate and international trade and mobility have meant invasive species and threats once unheard of in Estonia are now threatening to arrive here.

From plant-eating, flying beetles, to parasites which themselves attach to beetles and other bugs, to those species which can affect wooden items, such as pallets, there is a range of potential pests which could devastate Estonia's forests and gardens.

This would be particularly poignant given Estonia has for over 20 years held the EU's rare protected zone status, which means strict restrictions on plants entering the country from other EU member states and the use of "plant passports."

Alien species rarely reach Estonia of their own accord. Instead, they arrive with the aid of human activity. Global supply chains, timber imports and busy international travel all provide ideal pathways for insects and plant diseases to spread. The authorities' watchlist now has nearly 500 different threats.

Speaking to radio program "Ökoskoop," Ülle Metsmann, plant health adviser at the state Agriculture and Food Board (PTA), stressed how critical prevention is, starting at Estonia's borders.

"One of the most important plant health measures is barring new pests from reaching Estonia via trade. Border crossing areas are naturally high-risk locations for surveillance, where it would make sense to set traps and monitor trees and shrubs," she said.

Changing weather conditions have also been leading to an expansion of the workload facing customs inspectors, and also plant health inspectors, particularly the milder winters and longer warm periods, which have allowed species from more southerly climes to survive more easily than they could previously.

As a result, many pests and bacteria that would have perished during the Estonian winter are increasingly successfully overwintering, for instance in the Estonian soil or beneath tree bark.

"Climate change is definitely affecting the spread of plant pests as a warmer climate favors their survival. The warmer it gets, the more suitable the conditions get for species that have not previously established themselves here," Metsmann noted.

One of the greatest concerns has been the emerald ash borer, a beetle native to northeastern China which is responsible for the rapid destruction of native ash trees. It has not been found in Estonia yet, but it is making steady progress into the EU more broadly.

Like many species of beetle, the emerald ash borer can fly. Source: USDA-APHIS / Wikimedia Commons

After getting established in Ukraine some years ago, this tiny species of beetle somewhat unexpectedly began moving further towards Central Europe, and has now also been detected in the EU nations of Hungary and Slovakia.

"Given the current situation, you can imagine how little capacity Ukraine's national plant protection service has to monitor this pest. Unfortunately, it has now reached the European Union, which means a great deal of additional work for the countries where it has been found," the adviser said.

In addition to the bug being found to Estonia's south, it has also turned up to the east as well, and close to Estonia. Four years ago, a viable population of the pest was discovered near St. Petersburg, just 150 kilometers from the Estonian border, putting local specialists on high alert.

As a beetle, the species can fly too, of course. "It is an insect with excellent flying ability, so its arrival here from the St. Petersburg area is highly likely. At some point it will make that journey. Our task is to detect it as early as possible so we are prepared," Metsmann explained.

The emerald ash borer measures just 1.4 centimeters in length, maximum, so is extremely difficult to spot in the wild with the naked eye. To improve early detection, the state maintains 90 special sticky traps along the eastern border and along major highways, replacing them every couple of weeks.

Another invasive pest is the Japanese beetle, which often travels long distances by hitching rides on human transport, hence the precautions taken at major highways and the border.

"The Japanese beetle is indeed one of the species we monitor because it is what we call a hitchhiking insect that can arrive on vehicles. It can hide in aircraft cargo holds, which is why we conduct extensive surveillance around airports," the adviser went on.

As to why it is of concern, the beetle targets any ash trees which have already been severely weakened by ash dieback, a chronic fungal disease. Once beneath the bark, its larvae bore through the tree's nutrient-carrying layer, eventually causing the tree to dry out completely and die.

Ash trees are not the only plants requiring protection from the Japanese beetle either. Many ornamental and fruit trees are also threatened by the Japanese beetle, which has an enormous appetite for the leaves and flowers of grapevines, apple trees, maples and roses.

After feeding through the summer, the beetle burrows into the soil to spend the winter, where as noted it has more scope for doing so in a milder climate. Once underground, its larvae feed on plant roots and damage grasslands.

Alongside flying beetles, specialists also monitor even smaller, often microscopic threats. Another major concern is the pine wood nematode, which is completely invisible to the naked eye. In addition comes the tiny roundworm, mainly found in Portugal and parts of Spain and which has recently spread into France's conifer forests.

Ash trees are susceptible to several types of invasive pests. Source: ERR

To colonize new areas, the nematode secretes itself inside longhorn beetles, which themselves travel between countries in international wooden packaging material. Once the large beetle begins feeding on conifer trees at its destination, it delivers its hidden passenger directly into the living tree's vascular system.

The dangerous Asian longhorn beetle spreads in a similar way and has already been discovered several times in wooden pallets arriving at Estonia's border.

Ensuring the safety of wooden pallets used in global trade requires constant and strict inspections. Although their quality has improved over the years in eastbound trade, exporters still do not treat shipments thoroughly enough, allowing destructive wood pests to move freely between countries.

"There are many other threats as well, especially those associated with wooden packaging material, because it is used so widely and many countries fail to comply with the established requirements. We have to remain extremely vigilant at the border and everywhere else because these packages circulate around the world so extensively," Metsmann said.

A fourth major threat neither flies nor tunnels through wood, but spreads as a bacterium. Fire blight, a destructive bacterial plant disease caused by Erwinia amylovora, is considered the world's most destructive disease affecting plants in the rose family.

Since 2005, Estonia has held the EU's rare protected zone status, imposing strict restrictions on plants entering the country from other member states.

"There are very few protected zones left — only Finland, Latvia and Lithuania. In the case of this bacterium, we can protect ourselves by ensuring that plants come only from safe areas," Metsmann went on.

To maintain this protective barrier, all host plants crossing the border — including pear, apple and rowan trees — must originate entirely from disease-free nurseries. The requirement applies to every shipment without exception.

The system relies on official documentation certifying plant safety. "Every single plant, regardless of how many an individual or landscaper brings in, must be accompanied by a plant passport confirming that it is safe for a protected zone," Metsmann stressed.

Official inspections alone, however, are not enough, so the authorities are increasingly relying on the public to detect new threats. Gardeners are also encouraged to monitor fruit trees and report browned branches or shoots bending downward to specialists. Forest visitors, meanwhile, can use the PlutoF Go app to map living ash trees and carefully inspect larval tunnels beneath the bark.

Only through joint monitoring can Estonia continue to keep these potentially dangerous unwelcome guests out of its natural environment.

World.title: Tallinn weighs extending late-night public transport hours to airport
World.content:
Tallinn is considering extending late-night public transport to the airport after even restored tram service left some early-morning air travelers without a direct option.

Direct tram service to the airport resumed in August, serving lines from both Kopli and Tondi. The two airport lines also serve the Ülemste City business district, where according to the city, about 6,000 people commute by tram each day.

The first trams reach the airport shortly after 5:30 a.m., while the last departures leave around 12:45 a.m. Despite the early hour, 5:30 still isn't early enough for passengers catching the earliest flights of the day.

Deputy Mayor Joel Jesse (Center) said the city is reviewing demand before deciding whether to extend service, but noted that the city considers it a priority to ensure public transport is available during peak travel times.

"We have to take passengers' needs into account," Jesse said. "First we get the lines up and running; people will need time to readjust to using them."

Extending late-night service is a broader issue, he continued, as Tallinn Airport serves travelers from across Estonia, not just Tallinn.

"Those passengers are more spread out, many with large suitcases," the deputy mayor said. "These tram lines really only serve those staying in hotels or who live along the route."

Depending on demand, however, the city could instead extend one of Tallinn's night bus routes to the airport.

Major roadwork winding down

Jesse also said the city's major summer roadwork projects remain largely on schedule, even despite occasional delays caused by unexpected archaeological finds and underground utility lines that didn't match up to construction plans.

Traffic capacity is expected to improve by September as summer vacation travel winds down, he added.

While some major projects, including the intersection at Hipodroomi, will continue into next year, roadwork on Lauteri tänav is due to finish by the end of August, and the overhaul of Peterburi tee is expected to be completed in November.

World.title: Gallery: Estonian exhibition takes new look at machines in Soviet-era art
World.content:
A new exhibition in Pärnu looks back at how Estonian artists of the 1960s-80s imagined technology, progress and humanity's changing place in the world.

Opened Saturday at Avangard Gallery, "Dialogue with the Machine" features Soviet-era Estonian graphic works that portray machines not just as tools, but as symbols of society, industry and human ambition.

Curator Marian Grau said the exhibition highlights the technical skill and conceptual range of the era's artists, whose works combined geometric forms, architecture, electronics, semiotic systems and visual experiments.

"In some works, the machine is depicted as an almost heroic representation of progress and faith in the future," Grau said. "In others, it becomes a mirror of humanity or a symbol of alienation."

She noted that modern audiences will undoubtedly view these works in a different light, through the lens of algorithms, digital systems and artificial intelligence, sparking a dialogue between past visions of the future and today's reality.

'Moscow censorship would have never allowed it'

Speaking at the opening Saturday, art historian Harry Liivrand said machines have been a major inspiration for avant-garde artists since the early 20th century, and that the exhibition shows the diversity of approaches taken by Estonian artists during the Soviet occupation period.

"This gives an indication of the opportunity that existed during the Soviet era to create highly modern art that Moscow censorship would have never allowed, but which was possible in Estonia as a smaller Soviet Socialist Republic," Liivrand said.

During that period, he added, Estonian art was of international caliber.

Curated by Marian Grau and Jan Leo Grau, "Dialogue with the Machine" features works by Vello Vinn, Peeter Ulas, Leonhard Lapin, Evald Okas, Illimar Paul, Olev Soans, Allex Kütt, Renaldo Veeber, Evi Tihemets and Epp Marguste.

It will remain open at Avangard Gallery through August 31.
