The discussion also featured criticism of the People’s Party of Kazakhstan for its proposal to impose penalties on schools with low PISA scores.

Respublica candidate Nurgul Tau argued that penalizing teachers would fail to address structural inequalities between rural and urban schools. Instead, she called for creating equal educational opportunities.

World.title: Kazakhstan to Become One of Eurasia’s Leading Logistics Hubs, Tokayev Says
World.content:
ALMATY – Kazakhstan has unveiled a new phase of its transport infrastructure strategy, launching construction of the Beineu–Saksaulsk highway and announcing the expansion of two additional road corridors as part of a broader effort to reposition the country as a key logistics hub linking Europe and Asia.

Speaking at an Aug. 3 ceremony, President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev said the projects are designed not only to improve domestic connectivity but also to increase transit capacity, shorten cargo routes between China and Europe, and strengthen Kazakhstan’s role in Eurasian supply chains.

According to him, Kazakhstan’s long-term objective extends beyond building roads to creating an integrated transport network capable of supporting growing Eurasian trade flows.

“Our main goal is to transform Kazakhstan into one of the leading logistics hubs connecting Europe and Asia,” Tokayev said.

The new highway, which President Tokayev proposed naming the Aral-Caspian Highway, will directly connect border checkpoints with China to the Caspian ports of Aktau and Kuryk, reducing freight routes between China and Europe by nearly 1,000 kilometers and shortening delivery times by up to three days.

Moving beyond traditional transport routes

The announcement reflects a broader shift in Kazakhstan’s transport strategy. The latest projects aim to complement old networks with new East-West corridors that align with growing trade between China, Central Asia, the Caspian region and Europe.

In parallel with the Beineu–Saksaulsk project, Tokayev announced the expansion and reconstruction of the Kyzylorda–Saksaulsk and Ulgaysyn–Saksaulsk highways, covering a combined 774 kilometers.

According to him, domestic companies will lead construction, creating more than 10,000 jobs, while annual freight volumes along the corridor are expected to increase 2.5-fold to 13.2 million tons after completion.

“Undoubtedly, these projects will contribute to the development of the national economy and tourism, as well as to improving the welfare of the population. Each of these projects is seamlessly integrated into the transportation system of Kazakhstan. The historically established vertical transportation networks are now complemented by horizontal connections,” Tokayev said, instructing that all projects should be completed no later than 2029.

Building a logistics economy

The road projects form part of a wider effort to transform transport into one of Kazakhstan’s principal growth sectors. According to Tokayev, freight transportation reached nearly 37 million tons in 2025, a 6% increase from the previous year.

Road transport has become one of the fastest-growing segments of the sector. Cargo volumes transported by road have doubled over the past five years, while revenues reached 1.5 trillion tenge (US$2.9 billion) last year, approaching the scale of Kazakhstan’s traditionally dominant railway sector.

In addition, Kazakhstan currently sits on eight international transport corridors, with approximately 35,000 vehicles crossing them every day. The country’s infrastructure expansion has accelerated accordingly. In 2025, authorities built or rehabilitated 13,000 kilometers of roads, with 6,000 kilometers already commissioned. Customs checkpoints along international highways are also scheduled to undergo full reconstruction by 2027, marking the first comprehensive modernization of border road crossings since independence.

Rail development is advancing simultaneously. Construction of the Moiynty–Kyzylzhar and Darbaza–Maktaaral railway lines is expected to finish this year, followed by completion of the Bakhty–Ayagoz railway in 2027.

More than roads

Tokayev argued that Kazakhstan’s transport ambitions now extend beyond physical infrastructure. Rather than simply expanding highways, he said the country must build a modern digital transport ecosystem, supported by a forthcoming national program for domestic freight carriers and the local automotive industry.

The combination of new infrastructure, digitalization and logistics services is intended to increase Kazakhstan’s competitiveness as Eurasian supply chains continue to diversify. The key indicators to watch over the coming years will include cargo volumes on the Aral-Caspian corridor, transit times between China and Europe, utilization of the Caspian ports of Aktau and Kuryk, and the modernization of border checkpoints and digital freight systems.

When completed, the new transport corridors would reshape the country’s position within Eurasian logistics, strengthening its role as a transit hub linking China, Central Asia, the Caspian region and European markets.

World.title: Kazakhstan Meets Renewable Energy Goal Ahead of Schedule. What Comes Next?
World.content:
ALMATY – Kazakhstan exceeded its national target for renewable electricity generation in 2025, marking another milestone in the country’s green energy transition. But while record output underscores the success of years of investment in wind and solar power, the figures also point to the next phase of the transition: integrating a rapidly growing share of intermittent renewable energy into the country’s electricity system.

According to the Kazakh Energy Ministry, renewable energy facilities generated 8.6 billion kilowatt-hours of electricity in 2025, accounting for 7% of the country’s total electricity production. Compared with 2022, when renewable generation stood at 5.11 billion kWh and represented 4.5% of the electricity mix, output has increased by more than 1.7 times, exceeding a target of increasing renewable electricity production by 1.5 times.

The ministry attributed the growth to continued government support for the sector, including renewable energy auctions, investment attraction and the commissioning of new generating facilities. In 2025 alone, Kazakhstan commissioned nine renewable energy projects with a combined capacity of 503.5 megawatts (MW). This year, authorities plan to add another 10 projects totaling 245 MW, including four wind farms, five solar power plants and one hydropower station.

Wind continues to lead renewable expansion

International data show Kazakhstan’s renewable sector continues to expand steadily, although growth remains concentrated in a limited number of technologies.

According to the International Renewable Energy Agency’s (IRENA) Renewable Capacity Statistics 2026, Kazakhstan increased its installed renewable energy capacity from 5,561 MW in 2024 to 6,084 MW in 2025.

Most of the increase came from wind power, whose installed capacity rose from 1,520 MW to 1,909 MW. Solar capacity also continued to expand, albeit at a slower pace, increasing from 1,229 MW to 1,325 MW.

Despite the growth, renewables’ share in Kazakhstan’s total electricity generation capacity increased only marginally from 22.4% to 22.8%, highlighting that expanding installed capacity alone does not immediately transform the country’s overall power system.

While Kazakhstan remains one of the region’s leading renewable energy markets, neighboring countries are also expanding clean energy deployment, reflecting growing efforts across Central Asia to diversify electricity generation and reduce dependence on fossil fuels.

Looking ahead

Kazakhstan’s immediate priority remains maintaining investment momentum. The planned commissioning of 10 additional renewable projects in 2026 will further expand generating capacity and help diversify the country’s electricity mix.

At the same time, the rapid growth of wind and solar is expected to shift attention toward broader questions of power system management, including transmission infrastructure, energy storage and grid flexibility.

Having exceeded its renewable generation target ahead of schedule, Kazakhstan’s next challenge may no longer be how quickly it can build renewable energy facilities, but how effectively it can integrate them into a stable, reliable and increasingly low-carbon electricity system.

World.title: Wondering Where to Go in Mangystau This Summer? Start With These Ten Places
World.content:
ASTANA – From canyons and chalk-white cliffs to underground mosques and windswept Caspian shores, Kazakhstan’s Mangystau Region offers some of the country’s most striking landscapes and a growing draw for summer travelers seeking culture, adventure and the unexpected.

Stretching from the shores of the Caspian Sea to the vast Ustyurt Plateau, Mangystau is home to some of Kazakhstan’s most distinctive geological formations. Much of the region was submerged beneath the ancient Tethys Ocean millions of years ago, leaving behind chalk cliffs, colorful canyons, salt flats and fossil-rich landscapes that continue to attract geologists, photographers and adventure travelers from around the world.

Leading the list is Bozzhyra, one of Kazakhstan’s best-known natural landmarks. Located on the Ustyurt Plateau around 300 kilometers from Aktau, the valley is famous for its towering white limestone cliffs and dramatic rock formations shaped by millions of years of erosion. Visitors can explore panoramic viewpoints, hike through the surrounding terrain or join off-road jeep expeditions to experience one of Central Asia’s most spectacular desert landscapes.

Another geological wonder is Torysh, commonly known as the Valley of Balls. Hundreds of perfectly rounded stone spheres, some measuring several meters in diameter, are scattered across the steppe. Scientists believe the formations developed naturally through the cementation of mineral sediments, although local folklore has long surrounded the mysterious stones with legends.

The Airakty–Shomanai Mountains, often nicknamed the Valley of Castles, feature weathered cliffs and rock towers that resemble ancient fortresses. The mountains were formed from limestone deposits on the floor of the ancient Tethys Ocean some 40 million years ago. Tectonic shifts later pushed the terrain upward as the sea retreated, exposing layers of rock that wind and rain gradually shaped into the striking formations seen today. The site is particularly popular among photographers and travelers seeking panoramic views of Mangystau’s rugged terrain.

For those looking to explore more remote landscapes, the Karynzharyk Depression offers one of the region’s most striking panoramas. Its lowest point lies around 75 meters below sea level. At its heart is the Kenderli salt flat, which dries into a cracked white plain in summer but can turn into a mirror-like expanse after rainfall. The area is especially popular for camping, jeep tours and sunrise or sunset photography.

Nature lovers can also visit Tamshaly, a small oasis where freshwater springs trickle down rocky cliffs, creating lush vegetation in the middle of the arid steppe. It is located on the Tupkaragan Peninsula near Fort Shevchenko, around 130 kilometres from Aktau. The shaded gorge provides a welcome retreat from the summer heat and has become a favorite destination for picnics, short hikes and family outings.

The Mangystau Region is also Kazakhstan’s gateway to the Caspian Sea. The beaches of Aktau attract thousands of visitors every summer with sandy shores, modern resorts and a wide range of recreational activities, including swimming, boating, jet skiing and paddleboarding. The city’s waterfront promenade has become one of the country’s most popular seaside leisure destinations.

Alongside its natural attractions, the region is home to important cultural and religious heritage sites. The Beket-Ata Underground Mosque, carved into limestone in the 18th century, remains one of Kazakhstan’s most significant pilgrimage destinations. Built by the revered Sufi scholar Beket-Ata, the mosque welcomes thousands of pilgrims and tourists annually who come to learn about the country’s spiritual traditions while admiring the unique underground architecture.

Among the Mangystau Region’s most recognizable geological monuments is Bokty Mountain, whose nearly symmetrical conical shape resembles a giant yurt rising from the surrounding plains. The 165-meter-high isolated formation also resembles a pyramid from one angle and an overturned ship from another. Located in Mangystau Region’s Karakiya District, Bokty is a state-protected natural monument. The nearest city Zhanaozen is around 90 kilometers away, while the mountain lies roughly 20 kilometers from the unpaved road linking Zhanaozen with the Beket-Ata mosque. Layers of red, yellow and white sedimentary rock create striking patterns that become especially vivid during sunrise and sunset, making the mountain a favorite stop for photographers.

The region’s spectacular scenery continues at Tuzbair, a vast salt flat bordered by towering white chalk escarpments, located around 270 kilometers northeast of Aktau. Formed when the ancient Tethys Ocean retreated millions of years ago, Tuzbair offers visitors dramatic landscapes unlike anywhere else in Kazakhstan. Off-road expeditions, eco-tourism, camping and landscape photography are among the area’s most popular activities.

Completing the list is Kyzylkup, widely known as the Tiramisu Canyon because of its distinctive layers of red, white and golden sedimentary rock that resemble the famous Italian dessert. It is located around 20 kilometers from Bozzhyra and right near the Bokty Mountains. The colorful hills, created through millions of years of geological processes, have become one of the country’s most photographed natural attractions and are increasingly featured in international travel publications. The site is located around 300 kilometers from Aktau. Much of the route follows paved roads, but the section beyond Zhanaozen is unpaved and can be loose or slippery.

With its combination of spectacular natural monuments, ancient spiritual sites and the country’s only Caspian Sea coastline, the Mangystau Region offers visitors an opportunity to experience one of Central Asia’s most diverse and remarkable landscapes, making it an increasingly popular choice for summer travel.

Aktau city is the main gateway and it can be reached by air from major cities in Kazakhstan, including Astana and Almaty, and from abroad, as well as by train and long-distance road connections. While some attractions are accessible on day trips from Aktau, many of Mangystau’s best-known sites lie hundreds of kilometers apart in remote desert terrain. Roads are often unpaved or may be absent altogether, making a high-clearance four-wheel-drive vehicle essential for most routes. Travelers without substantial off-road experience are often advised to join an organized tour or hire a local guide and driver rather than undertake the journey independently.

World.title: Diaspora youth: Patriots or ‘information soldiers’? The hidden mission of camp in Azerbaijan
World.content:
Zangilan diaspora youth camp in Azerbaijan

Zangilan diaspora youth camp in Azerbaijan. More than 120 young people from 64 countries gathered in Zangilan under the slogan “Reviving Cities”. Officials told participants they should defend Azerbaijan’s achievements and push back against what they described as “biased campaigns”.

Against the backdrop of protesters calling Ilham Aliyev a “dictator” in Berlin, that message raises another question: is the state seeking to foster independent thinkers or “information soldiers” who will promote its official narrative abroad?

What was discussed at the 7th Diaspora Youth Summer Camp?

The 7th Diaspora Youth Summer Camp, which opened in Zangilan on 2 August, is officially presented as a platform for “patriotic education”, learning about “the realities on the ground” and rejuvenating the Azerbaijani diaspora. More than 120 young people from 64 countries are spending a week visiting reconstruction projects in the territories retaken by Azerbaijan, meeting government officials and learning what organisers describe as “Azerbaijani realities”.

A closer look at the speeches by Fuad Muradov, chairman of the State Committee for Work with the Diaspora, and other officials, however, reveals a more pragmatic objective. The government appears to see young people living abroad not simply as members of the diaspora with ties to their homeland, but as active participants in the information battle.

Muradov said the participants should be able to “respond with well-founded arguments to biased campaigns”. He said they should “represent” Azerbaijan’s interests with dignity in their countries of residence, on international platforms and within their own communities.

Another message struck an even tougher tone. Officials said that although their number was small, some people living abroad who called themselves Azerbaijanis did not welcome Azerbaijan’s successes. They urged participants to know who these people were, be familiar with their statements and respond to them with well-reasoned arguments. Officials also said “black PR”, “distortion of facts” and “organised campaigns” were unacceptable. At the same time, they said they remained open to “well-founded criticism”.

Elvin Aslanov, a representative of the Heydar Aliyev Foundation, acknowledged that defending Azerbaijan abroad was “far from easy”, saying it required confronting double standards and disinformation. According to him, the young participants’ mission is to “convey the truth accurately and objectively”.

From the authorities’ perspective, such rhetoric may appear defensive and entirely legitimate. However, the broader context allows for another interpretation. Critics argue that the programme goes beyond patriotic education and instead systematically prepares “information soldiers” – young people expected to promote the official narrative on social media, in online discussions and in international debates. In other words, they see it as an attempt to build a state-directed “soft power” network.

What happened in Berlin, and why does it matter in this context?

The timing of these appeals is no coincidence. During Ilham Aliyev’s official visit to Germany on 21 July, Azerbaijani expatriates gathered on the streets of Berlin and chanted: “Dictator!”

Around the same time, Germany-based exiled blogger Alemdar Bunyatov approached Foreign Minister Jeyhun Bayramov and presidential aide Hikmet Hajiyev on a street in Berlin. He questioned them about political prisoners and allegations of torture.

Official media immediately described the incident as a “provocation” and portrayed Bunyatov as someone “known for his close ties to the Iranian intelligence services”. Responding to his questions, Bayramov dismissed the allegations of torture as “a personal opinion”.

Hajiyev, for his part, questioned Bunyatov about his sources of funding, his legal status in Germany and his reasons for leaving Azerbaijan. He stressed the importance of sovereignty and national security. The incident triggered a strong reaction in pro-government media, which portrayed the blogger’s questions as “provocative”.

The events in Berlin further illustrate the practical meaning of the messages delivered in Zangilan. In the official narrative, criticism is often framed as a “biased campaign”, “black PR” or the result of “external influence”.

As a result, the authorities themselves largely determine the line between “well-founded criticism” and a “biased campaign”. Young people, in turn, are expected to accept that distinction and challenge those whom the state places on the other side of it.

A method of training trolls?

Opposition figures and independent observers have long described such camps as a form of “troll factory”. Critics argue that their purpose is not to encourage independent thinking but to prepare young people to defend the official position on social media, in online discussions and before international audiences. They say that, under the banner of patriotism, organisers cultivate emotional attachment and ideological loyalty while encouraging participants to view critical voices as “hostile”.

Every country seeks to use its diaspora as a tool of soft power, and Azerbaijan is no exception. The problem, critics argue, is that the shrinking space for domestic criticism places a disproportionately heavy burden on young Azerbaijanis abroad to “defend” the official line. They must adapt to societies where freedom of expression is a fundamental principle while remaining loyal to Baku’s official narrative. For many young people, that contradiction can create genuine tension.

Muradov says, “We are open to dialogue”, while also insisting, “We will not tolerate black PR.” This raises an obvious question: what qualifies as “well-founded criticism”, and what counts as a “biased campaign”? If official media portray the questions and slogans heard on the streets of Berlin as a provocation, where is the line for young people who raise the same issues in international media or at academic forums?

Zangilan diaspora youth camp in Azerbaijan

World.title: Armenia’s new parliament holds first session as opposition, as expected, makes its presence felt
World.content:
First session of Armenia’s ninth parliament

Armenia‘s newly elected parliament convened for the first time on 2 August. Three political forces won seats in the ninth National Assembly: the Civil Contract, Strong Armenia and Armenia factions. During the opening session, lawmakers managed only to appoint members of the Counting Commission. Heated exchanges between the ruling party and the opposition prevented them from addressing the rest of the agenda.

The opposition’s main grievance was the absence of the Catholicos from the opening session. The authorities did not invite him, and he did not bless the work of parliament. Opposition lawmakers described this as an unprecedented event in the history of independent Armenia.

Under the constitutional law governing the National Assembly’s rules of procedure, both the president and the Catholicos of All Armenians have the right to deliver opening remarks at parliament’s first session. This time, however, only President Vahagn Khachaturyan addressed lawmakers. Earlier, the Mother See of Holy Etchmiadzin said it had received no invitation for the Catholicos. When journalists asked Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan about Garegin II’s participation, he replied: “I do not know such a Catholicos.” The incident reflects the long-running dispute between the Armenian authorities and Catholicos of All Armenians Garegin II. More than two years ago, Prime Minister Pashinyan called for the Catholicos to step down. He initially argued that Garegin II could not lead the Armenian Apostolic Church because he had broken his vow of celibacy and fathered a daughter. Pashinyan later accused him of links with foreign intelligence services. The ruling Civil Contract party also included the removal of “the de facto head of the Church” in its election manifesto.

Lawmakers also fiercely debated the nomination of Ruben Rubinyan, the ruling party’s sole candidate for speaker of parliament.

Opposition MPs repeatedly referred to his research work at Istanbul Policy Center in Turkey in 2017–18. They asked whether he had interacted with local residents and even questioned what they looked like.

“Ask me directly whether I met representatives of the Turkish intelligence services in Turkey and whether they recruited me. Ask me: ‘Is that true?’ And I will answer: ‘No,'” Rubinyan said.

Parliament resumed its first session today. Lawmakers have already settled one of the main items on the agenda. In a secret ballot, they elected Ruben Rubinyan as speaker with 63 votes in favour and 28 against.

The opposition Armenia bloc boycotted the secret ballot. MPs from the second opposition force, the Strong Armenia faction, voted against Rubinyan’s nomination.

In the previous parliament, Rubinyan served as deputy speaker. Between 2022 and 2026, he also acted as Armenia’s special envoy for the normalisation of relations with Turkey. A few days ago, Rubinyan said he would be unable to continue in that role if parliament elected him speaker. The ruling party has not yet announced who will succeed him.

“Where is the Patriarch?” Opposition MPs visit him to receive his blessing

On the opening day of the session, opposition MPs began chanting, “Where is the Patriarch?” after the president’s address. During the oath-taking ceremony, they pointedly refused to stand or recite the oath. They said they were protesting the Catholicos’s absence. However, they signed the written text of the oath, allowing them to take office formally.

At the end of the first working day, MPs from both opposition factions visited the Catholicos’s residence.

The Mother See’s information service said Garegin II blessed the opposition lawmakers. He spoke of an “alarming situation and serious problems” facing the country. He also criticised what he described as the authorities’ “illegal and unconstitutional actions” against the Church.

Catholicos receives opposition MPs at the Mother See

The Catholicos praised what he described as the opposition MPs’ “devotion and filial love for the Church”. He said their stance was especially important at a time when “the authorities continue their campaign of repression, while national benefactor Samvel Karapetyan remains under arrest for speaking out in defence of Holy Etchmiadzin”.

In June last year, Armenian authorities opened a criminal case against Russian businessman and billionaire Samvel Karapetyan. Prosecutors accused him of publicly calling for the seizure and usurpation of power. In an interview with local media, Karapetyan discussed the escalating conflict between the government and the Church. He said he supported the Church and added: “If Armenia’s political forces fail to resolve this situation, we will have to intervene in the campaign against the Church in our own way.” His supporters founded the Strong Armenia party after his arrest, and he has remained under house arrest since December last year.

105 MPs in the new parliament

The three political forces that entered the National Assembly secured the following number of seats:

The ruling Civil Contract party – 64 seats

The Strong Armenia faction – 29 seats

The Armenia bloc – 12 seats

Strong Armenia leader and businessman Samvel Karapetyan did not enter parliament. During the election campaign, his allies confidently predicted victory and even said Karapetyan would become prime minister. However, he is ineligible to serve either as an MP or as prime minister. Under Armenia’s constitution, anyone holding citizenship of another country cannot hold either office. Karapetyan holds Armenian, Russian and Cypriot citizenship.

Former President Robert Kocharyan headed the electoral list of the Armenia bloc, making him its candidate for prime minister. However, Kocharyan declined to take up his parliamentary seat. His son, Levon Kocharyan, who also ran on the bloc’s list, accepted a mandate and has already joined parliament. He also served as an MP for the Armenia bloc in the previous legislature.

“I will do everything to ensure our children never experience war”

Rubinyan thanked the more than 700,000 voters who backed Civil Contract. He said they had given the ruling party “a mandate to continue Armenia’s democratic reforms and peace agenda”. According to Rubinyan, those voters had defended the country’s sovereignty and independence.

He said the time had come for Armenians to enjoy peaceful lives, have children and raise them without fear.

“My son, who is almost two years old, and children of his age have never experienced war. I will do everything to ensure that my children, your children and all our children never have to learn what war is,” he said.

Rubinyan also thanked those who voted for opposition parties out of conviction rather than in exchange for election bribes.

“It is time to change the political discourse,” Rubinyan says

Addressing opposition MPs, Rubinyan raised the issue of the tone of parliamentary debate. He said society, political circles and journalists had formed a common view of parliament in recent months. According to him, many now see the National Assembly as a place for pointless arguments, slander and insults.

“They say this parliament will be even worse than the previous one in that respect. It seems everyone expects exactly that from us. I want to propose that we break this curse together,” the speaker said.

He argued that the opposition factions had largely stayed away from the work of the previous, eighth convocation of parliament.

“All we saw here was political confrontation, shouting and radical speeches. It is time to change the narratives that have dominated Armenian politics over the past six years. I propose that we make this parliament a place for vigorous but respectful debate that never crosses the boundaries of decency.”

At the same time, he warned that if the opposition rejected his proposal and continued “down the well-trodden path”, the ruling party was ready to respond “in the toughest possible way”.

“Why did we take our seats?” Opposition MPs explain

Ishkhan Saghatelyan, an MP from the Armenia faction, argued that neither the opposition nor the ruling party had truly won the election.

He again claimed that the authorities had used administrative resources during the campaign and imprisoned opposition figures.

“This parliament has a serious legitimacy problem. We are here to organise political struggle and advance national goals. We are here to raise the concerns of Armenia’s citizens, speak about the prisoners held in Baku and Armenia’s occupied territories, and, yes, defend the people of Artsakh’s right to a collective return.”

Hayk Farmanyan, an MP from the Strong Armenia faction, echoed that message.

“We accepted our mandates to remain true to our Armenian identity, to fight for our national values, and to defend our dignity, our identity and our Church.”

Comment

Political analyst Lilit Dallakyan shared her impressions of the new parliament’s opening session on social media:

“Well, I ‘congratulate’ the Armenian people on the start of work by a new, high-quality, substantive parliament that is supposedly ready to tackle Armenia’s complex challenges.

The daily exchange of ‘Your father is a murderer’ [directed at MP Levon Kocharyan, son of former President Robert Kocharyan] will now gain a new, equally substantive argument: ‘Your uncle is a Russian oligarch’ [directed at MP Narek Karapetyan, nephew of Strong Armenia leader Samvel Karapetyan]. That will, in turn, prompt the reply: ‘You are Turkish dictators’ [directed at the authorities].

The only positive aspect is that this season of the series is unlikely to interest anyone or distract people from the real problems that are rapidly emerging.

At a time of profound change across the world, Armenian society and every individual will have to look for solutions to their own problems. Ultimately, that will bring about the changes the country needs.”

First session of Armenia’s ninth parliament

World.title: Opinion: ‘Abkhaz diplomacy must become more flexible – and more assertive’
World.content:
Against the backdrop of the Pacific island nation of Nauru withdrawing its recognition of Abkhazia’s independence, prominent Abkhaz public figure Akhra Bzhania reflects on what Abkhazia’s foreign policy doctrine should look like.

Nauru, a small island nation in the Pacific region of Micronesia, recognised Abkhazia’s independence in 2009 but withdrew that recognition in late July 2026. The move reduced the number of countries recognising Abkhazia’s independence to four. Abkhazia’s foreign ministry said Nauru had come under “unprecedented pressure”.

Akhra Bzhania said: “Around 230,000 irregular migrants crossed the EU’s borders in 2025–26 alone. All of them fled countries that enjoy broad international recognition.

Why didn’t they stay in Morocco, Mali or Afghanistan? Presumably because having a flag outside the UN headquarters does not automatically mean you live in a genuine state – one where you can influence public life, where your voice matters and where your dignity will never be trampled.

Being a recognised country and being a country where people want to live and are willing to die for it are two different things.

You may achieve the first and never attain the second. But if you have the second, then you have accomplished the most important task: building a country that belongs to its citizens. That is what defines a modern state. And that is precisely what should become the main instrument for Abkhazia’s integration into the international community.

Bzhania continued: “We must send a clear message to the international community that, despite sanctions, isolation and the threat of war, the people of Abkhazia have built a society based on the rule of law and freedom. Without being members of international institutions, we have incorporated the core principles of international conventions on civil and political rights into our system of governance.

We see ourselves as part of the international community and believe we deserve our rightful place within it. To achieve that, our diplomacy must become more flexible – and more assertive. It should focus not on waiting for or preserving acts of recognition, but on consistently demonstrating our statehood and expanding our international contacts.

No one else is obliged to do this for us. By recognising our sovereignty, Russia effectively made Abkhazia a subject of international law. But it cannot solve our problems on our behalf.”

Bzhania continued: “We must use every tool at our disposal to achieve our goals: the resources of the diaspora, cultural, trade and sporting ties, personal connections, migration policy and regional logistics. In this game, we need to keep raising the stakes.

Today, there is a window of opportunity for such an active policy. It is no secret that relations between Georgia and the West are at their lowest point since the 1990s. Those on whom Tbilisi relied to promote its anti-Abkhaz agenda have become disillusioned with Georgia, and we should take advantage of that. That includes reviving the active dialogue with European countries that existed in the late 1990s. After all, the hopes the West once placed in Georgia as a bastion of the free world in the Caucasus have, to a greater extent, been realised in Abkhazia.

Another key asset, which has remained almost entirely outside our foreign policy efforts, is the Circassian diaspora. Four million people spread across 50 countries represent a powerful resource we can genuinely rely on. More importantly, we should offer them the prospect of political cooperation.

Abkhazia can and should become the centre of the Circassian world as the only independent state of this sub-ethnic group. Our country can become the same kind of homeland for Circassians worldwide that Israel has become for Jews. If every Circassian, wherever they live, knows they will find protection and support for their interests in Abkhazia, it will create a strong foundation for advancing our shared interests.”

Bzhania concluded: “It will probably not happen tomorrow, no matter how much effort we put in. But it can happen within a foreseeable future if those efforts remain consistent and systematic.

In 2017, I had the honour of welcoming a delegation from Nauru’s parliament to Abkhazia on behalf of the Abkhaz parliament. They were wonderful, warm people. Unfortunately, ships at sea do not only meet – they also part ways. Today, Nauru has set a course away from Abkhazia, apparently believing it to be the safer option. I wish them well. As for us, we will continue on our own course.”

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

Nauru’s withdrawal of recognition of Abkhazia

World.title: “For safe and strong Georgia”: Saturday march in Tbilisi. Georgia protests video blog
World.content:
612th day of protests in Tbilisi

“For a Safe and Strong Georgia” was the main slogan of the traditional pro-European Saturday march held in Tbilisi on 1 August 2026.

Before the march began, participants observed a minute’s silence in memory of a teenager who was recently killed in central Tbilisi and who would have turned 18 today.

Hundreds of people gathered once again in Avlabari Square for the 612th consecutive day of protests. With construction work continuing on Rustaveli Avenue, the march followed an alternative route for the second Saturday in a row, starting at Avlabari metro station and ending outside the parliament building.

For more than a year and half – since November 2024 – continuous protests have been taking place in Georgia, with demonstrators demanding that the country return to the path of European integration. Every evening thousands, and often tens of thousands, gather in Tbilisi and several other cities. Over this time dozens of participants have been detained, many have faced criminal charges, and some have been sentenced to prison terms. For the first time in the history of independent Georgia, the country has up to 150 prisoners of conscience, including women. Among them is Mzia Amaglobeli, founder of the popular outlets Batumelebi and Netgazeti. In 2025 she was sentenced to two years in prison for slapping a police officer. Protesters demand the release of all political prisoners, new parliamentary elections – as they do not recognize the results of the 2024 vote – and the repeal of all anti-democratic laws adopted over the past two years. To suppress the protests, the ruling Georgian Dream party has increasingly tightened repression against civil society and the media. However, protests in various forms continue.

612th day of protests in Tbilisi

World.title: South Ossetia presidential election: Meet the seven contenders
World.content:
Presidential contenders in South Ossetia

Registration of candidates for South Ossetia‘s snap presidential election, scheduled for 18 September 2026, has closed, with seven contenders set to run.

Yet, even before the campaign has begun, many in South Ossetia believe the outcome is already decided. Most see acting President Marat Kambolov – a senior Russian official appointed from Moscow – as the clear frontrunner and the likely winner.

Candidates

Marat Kambolov

The initiative groups have nominated acting President and Prime Minister Marat Kambolov, former KGB officer Kazbek Kodoyev, and Eduard Gabarayev, a member of the extra-parliamentary Iron party and a former defence ministry official.

***

Murat Valiyev

Several political parties have also nominated their own candidates. Khoh Chochiyev, a former State Protection Service officer, has been nominated by the extra-parliamentary Iry Farn party. Another security official, Murat Valiyev – a serving officer in the presidential State Protection Service and a former KGB officer – has been nominated by the Patriots of Alania party.

***

Zurab Kokoyev, chairman of the Unity party, which has previously been in power, has also announced his intention to run, despite having earlier backed Kambolov’s nomination.

***

Fatima Khugayeva

Finally, the only woman in the race and a newcomer to South Ossetian politics is Fatima Khugayeva, a retired lieutenant colonel in Russia’s Interior Ministry – making her yet another candidate with a security background.

She has been nominated by the Development Party. Although she was born in Moscow, Khugayeva has South Ossetian roots. After retiring, she returned to her ancestral homeland, got married, and now works as a deputy headteacher while teaching history.

Dropouts

In a surprise development, Georgiy Kabisov, leader of the Iron party, a former head of the Information and Press Committee who previously served a prison sentence for fraud, abandoned his earlier plans to run for president. His party now appears set to throw its full support behind its other nominee, Eduard Gabarayev. Vladimir Kelekhsayev, leader of the Unity of the People party and a former member of parliament, has also decided not to run. His party is likely to back one of the remaining contenders.

Following the close of registration, the Central Election Commission will review the documents submitted by the registered contenders to ensure they meet all legal requirements. Only then will they officially acquire candidate status, allowing them to open campaign accounts and begin collecting signatures. Some contenders may still be eliminated at this stage if irregularities are found in their paperwork.

Frontrunner, ‘supporting cast’ and ‘independent players‘

Of the seven contenders, only Prime Minister Marat Kambolov appears to have a realistic chance of winning. A Moscow official dispatched from the Kremlin just a few months ago, he has no prior ties to South Ossetia but enjoys unprecedented political backing. Even the territory’s main opposition forces have effectively thrown their support behind him, opting not to contest the election so as not to stand in his way.

Zurab Kokoyev

Kazbek Kodoyev

Most of the remaining candidates are viewed by analysts as technical candidates whose role is largely to fill out the ballot rather than mount a serious challenge.

This includes Kazbek Kodoyev and Zurab Kokoyev.

***

Murat Valiyev is a political newcomer whom the Patriots of Alania party appears to have nominated primarily to give him electoral experience. The campaign will also provide the party, founded only in 2023, with an opportunity to raise its profile. At the same time, the party’s chairman, Dzambolat Tedeyev, has urged voters to back Marat Kambolov.

Khoh Chochiyev

Analysts regard Khoh Chochiyev and Eduard Gabarayev as the more independent contenders.

Eduard Gabarayev

In this context, “independent” means that neither politician is regarded as a technical candidate or as someone willing to run merely to benefit the frontrunner. However, both are backed by different groups of current and former officials, as well as opposition figures.

***

Fatima Khugayeva, meanwhile, is widely seen as a candidate backed by local business interests. The Development Party, which nominated her, is led by businessman and restaurateur Albert Valiyev, who is friends with Khugayeva’s husband, a producer of alcoholic beverages.

However, Khugayeva is not merely being put forward because of her husband’s connections. She has political experience of her own: she remains a member of the Russian party Communists of Russia and has frequently taken part in protest rallies.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

World.title: Russian woman faces prison after calling Armenians ‘rat-like’ people
World.content:
Russian calls Armenians ‘rats’

A criminal case has been opened in Armenia against Russian national Nadezhda Pirozhkova. A blogger who has lived in Armenia for the past year and a half, Pirozhkova came under fire after criticising Vardavar, the Armenian tradition of pouring water over one another on the holiday. She described the custom as an act of aggression. In another video, she referred to Armenians as a “rat-like people”.

Armenia’s Investigative Committee has initiated criminal proceedings against Pirozhkova under the article on “public statements aimed at inciting hatred and discrimination through the use of the internet”. Armenia’s Criminal Code provides for a prison sentence of up to four years under this article. If Pirozhkova is found guilty in court, she could therefore face imprisonment.

For now, however, she has been banned from leaving her place of residence as a preventive measure. The blogger may leave Yerevan only with written permission from a prosecutor or a judge.

Vardavar is one of the principal feasts of the Armenian Apostolic Church, celebrating the Transfiguration of Jesus Christ, although its origins date back to pagan times. It is virtually impossible to stay dry on the streets that day, but taking offence is not customary, as drenching someone with water is considered a way of congratulating them on the holiday. The water is believed to bring health, good fortune and purification.

Pirozhkova’s Instagram posts sparked outrage among social media users—not only Armenians, but also fellow Russians.

Many have not only criticised Pirozhkova but have also called on law enforcement authorities to punish her as severely as possible or deport her from the country.

Political commentator Artyom Yerkanian did not rule out the possibility that certain actors interested in damaging Armenia’s image as a tourist destination were behind the spread of such videos. He pointed to the large number of Russian tourists visiting Armenia. In the first half of 2026 alone, Armenia received 1.042 million foreign visitors, around 40% of whom were from Russia.

“It’s interesting, isn’t it? On the one hand, the Russian government imposes trade restrictions [on imports of Armenian products and goods], while on the other, Russians happily travel to Armenia, enjoying its nature, its people and, why not, its traditions,” Yerkanian said.

What else Pirozhkova said

In a video about Vardavar, the Russian blogger said that the holiday made her want to leave Yerevan more than anything else. She described the tradition of pouring water over one another as “the height of tactlessness”. In her view, Armenians do not understand the concept of “personal boundaries” and routinely violate them.

Pirozhkova argued that splashing passers-by with water was disrespectful towards those who did not wish to take part in the celebration.

“If I’m in your country, I’m not obliged to follow your traditions. This is a direct manifestation of aggression.“

Following the video, Pirozhkova has periodically posted about the wave of online abuse directed at her. She has also publicly apologised several times, saying:

“I understand that many people saw it as disrespect towards the Armenian people. And I’m truly sorry. That was never my intention, and it still isn’t.”

At the same time, the blogger has acknowledged that she is using the controversy to promote her Instagram page.

“People recognise me now. Why shouldn’t I make use of something I’ve been through after putting in so much effort? I’ve worked hard for this. Why shouldn’t a person take advantage of circumstances and situations they have rightfully earned? I just want to change my life.“

Foreign nationals are required to respect Armenia’s national customs and traditions

The legal status of foreign nationals in Armenia is governed by the Law on Foreigners. Article 5 of the law states that foreigners in Armenia enjoy the same rights, freedoms and obligations as Armenian citizens. At the same time, it stipulates that “foreigners in the Republic of Armenia are obliged to respect the Constitution and laws of the Republic of Armenia, other legal acts, as well as national customs and traditions.”

The same article also provides that foreign nationals bear the same legal responsibility as Armenian citizens while in Armenia.

Armenia’s Criminal Code provides for penalties for “public statements aimed at inciting or promoting hatred, discrimination, intolerance or hostility against an individual or group of persons on the grounds of race, nationality or ethnicity, as well as the dissemination of materials or objects for that purpose.”

The available penalties include fines, community service, restriction of liberty and imprisonment.

Under Article 329, offences committed “through publicly displayed works, the mass media, or information and communication technologies” are punishable by one to four years’ imprisonment

Commentary

Political commentator Artyom Yerkanian said in an interview with a local television channel::

“After the Russian blogger publicly apologised, this story could have ended there. But some social media users continued calling on the Armenian law enforcement authorities to examine Nadezhda Pirozhkova’s actions and determine whether they amounted to a criminal offence. The authorities decided to respond to those calls.

Perhaps there was no need to be so severe. The court will, of course, take all mitigating circumstances into account.

Perhaps we should not politicise everything. It is obvious that the aim was not to incite ethnic hatred but simply to increase her audience through provocative videos.

In two weeks, the video attracted more than 250,000 views and over 5,000 comments. As a result, the number of followers on her page increased more than fifteen-fold.

In other words, this blogger simply found a ridiculous and foolish way to grow her audience.

Nevertheless, perhaps such cases should be monitored more closely, because this is not an isolated incident.

In recent weeks, there have been several similar cases in which foreign bloggers, particularly Russians, have made remarks discrediting Armenians and damaging Armenia’s reputation as a tourist destination.

There was one case in which a young woman accused an Armenian taxi driver of attempting to rape her. I also recall another similar incident, and there are probably many more. But what is more important?

Notably, these videos are deliberately amplified by non-existent users. An army of fake accounts is spreading this material in pursuit of a specific objective.

It cannot be ruled out that certain forces are behind these fake accounts and are interested in ensuring that Armenia is not perceived as a safe destination for tourists.

Every tourist who enjoys visiting the country indirectly becomes its ‘agent of influence’. Perhaps that is exactly what some people dislike.

I don’t know whether it is a coincidence, but it was precisely during those days that the Russian Foreign Ministry added Armenia to its list of countries where Russians cannot feel safe, citing the possibility that the Armenian authorities could extradite them to third countries. Perhaps it is a coincidence—or perhaps it is not.”

Social media reaction

“If, after a year and a half of living in Armenia, she still allows herself to speak like this, it cannot be dismissed as an accident or naivety.”

“The police should investigate her actions. She’s a planted agent.”

“She should be fined heavily and deported.”

“She should be tried and deported from our country. It’s a matter of the nation’s dignity.”

“If an Armenian had behaved like this in Russia, he would already have disappeared.”

“Foreign visitors are obliged to obey the law, respect the country and its people, and behave like guests.”

World.title: Meet Nitsa, Elvis and Oliver: Pine martens at Tbilisi Zoo. Video
World.content:
Nitsa, Elvis and Oliver are young pine martens and the newest residents of Tbilisi Zoo. A local resident found the orphaned cubs alone in an attic and took them home after discovering they had no mother.



However, pine martens are wild predators with powerful teeth and strong natural instincts. Once the cubs had grown up, releasing them back into the wild was no longer an option. Contact with humans had altered their natural behaviour, leaving them unable to survive on their own. Their rescuer therefore turned to Tbilisi Zoo for help.

Konstantin Pkhakadze, head of the zoo’s exotic animals department, said the pine martens arrived at Tbilisi Zoo about a month ago. He said such cases are quite common. People often assume that young animals found alone have been orphaned and need rescuing, but that is not always the case.

In most instances, the mother is nearby, hunting, searching for food or moving her young to a new location. Pkhakadze said intervening at that stage is the biggest mistake people can make. They should not even approach the cubs, as the mother may detect the scent of humans, see it as a threat and never return to her offspring.

Tbilisi Zoo currently has very limited capacity to take in new animals. Its existing site is overcrowded, while most of its resources are being directed towards the construction of a new zoo.

Nitsa, Elvis and Oliver were initially housed in the zoo’s exotics pavilion. However, the small enclosed space was unsuitable for such active and energetic animals. Zoo staff therefore built a temporary outdoor enclosure, giving the pine martens more space, fresh air and room to move freely.

Tbilisi Zoo‘s history spans nearly a century. It was founded on 10 February 1927 on the basis of the Caucasian Society for the Acclimatisation of Animals, which had been keeping wild animals since the early 20th century, though without official zoo status. The zoo was originally built on 70 hectares in the Vere River gorge. Over the years, the expansion of the capital — and later the devastating flood of 13 June 2015 — significantly reduced the territory of the old zoo. Today, it covers five hectares and is home to around 1,500 animals, each with its own story. In this video series, we will introduce you to the residents of Tbilisi Zoo. We will show how their day unfolds, how they interact with other animals and people, and how their behaviour changes depending on the weather and the season. Get ready to hear many fascinating stories.

Pine martens at Tbilisi Zoo

World.title: Georgia’s opposition launches campaign to restore voting rights for emigrants
World.content:
In Georgia, the opposition alliance Coalition for Change and the Strategy Aghmashenebeli party have launched the Emigrant’s Vote campaign, calling for the restoration of Georgian citizens’ right to vote from abroad in parliamentary and municipal elections.

Under the new Election Code, approved by the ruling Georgian Dream party on 17 December 2025, emigrants are no longer allowed to vote from abroad. Instead, they must travel to Georgia to cast their ballots.

One of Coalition for Change’s members, Tengo Tevzadze, announced the launch of the campaign, saying the initiative would culminate in a constitutional challenge seeking to restore emigrants’ right to take part in elections.

According to Tevzadze, the campaign aims to demonstrate that allowing emigrants to vote is consistent with Georgia’s constitution and that every Georgian citizen, regardless of where they live, should be able to take part in elections.

Tevzadze noted that Georgian Dream won just 13.4% of the overseas vote in the disputed 2024 parliamentary election, which the opposition says was rigged. He argued that this was why the authorities later moved to strip emigrants of their voting rights.

Tevzadze argues that depriving emigrants of the right to vote violates Georgia’s constitution and is unfair to a group of citizens that makes a significant contribution to the country’s economy.

The campaign’s organisers have set out two main demands: restoring emigrants’ right to vote and creating an electoral system that allows Georgian citizens living abroad to cast their ballots.

“We need as many emigrants as possible to sign the petition so that, alongside political efforts, we can also challenge the regime through legal means. Through a constitutional lawsuit, we will clearly demonstrate that emigrants’ participation in elections and their voting rights are protected by the constitution, and that Georgians, both at home and abroad, must be able to take part in free and fair elections,” Tengo Tevzadze said.

Voting rights for Georgian emigrants

World.title: Three lions die at Japanese zoo amid extreme temperatures
World.content:
Three lions have died of suspected heat stroke at a zoo in Tokyo after soaring mid-summer temperatures across Japan.

Over the past week at Tokyo's Tama Zoological Park, three female lions, aged three to 15, have become the first heat-related deaths among the facility's lion population in its 62-year history.

The lions, all born in the zoo, showed signs of severe dehydration and multiple organ failure in post-mortem examinations; however, the exact cause of death is still under investigation, the zoo said in a press release this week.

As temperatures in Tokyo suddenly spiked in mid-July, the majority of the zoo's 16 lions began losing their appetite and became lethargic to the point of requiring treatment, the zoo said.

While some lions recovered, others deteriorated to develop severe symptoms including the inability to stand and loss of consciousness, it said.

"No other animals have shown any signs of illness, but the staff are managing the animals more carefully than before," an official at the Tama Zoo said.

Treatment such as water-spraying and medicating through intravenous drips continues, the zoo said.

Zoo officials suspended public viewing of the lions on July 23 as their condition deteriorated.

It is not yet clear when the exhibit will reopen to the public.

A zoo representative, Miwa, Kosaka, told the BBC it was the first time the zoo had experienced heat-related deaths.

"Last year was also hot, but none of our lions fell ill like this," Miwa, Kosaka said.

The BBC reported the timeline of the deaths starting with the youngest of the three lions named Mugi.

The zoo said the three-year-old lion lost its appetite and a day later was unable to stand up.

Tama Zoo staff said ventilation and water were provided to cool her down, and later subcutaneous fluids, liver tonics and vitamins were administered.

She died on 28 July.

Ichigo, an 11-year-old female lion, died on July 31.

Luena, a 15-year-old female lion, died on Sunday, the BBC reported.

Temperatures in the area rose to nearly 39 degrees Celsius in mid-to-late July, triggering heat stroke warnings.

Lions are native to sub-Saharan Africa where they are accustomed to arid heat rather than Tokyo's combination of heat and high humidity, which makes it difficult for them to thermoregulate.

REUTERS/ ABC

World.title: 'Zip': Hanson has no answers for challenges facing Australia, says Rudd
World.content:
Former prime minister Kevin Rudd says One Nation leader Pauline Hanson would have no concept of how to govern Australia and is merely trading off the politics of division.

Speaking to 7.30 from London, Mr Rudd gave his views on the rise of Senator Hanson, Australia's AUKUS agreement, Chinese leader Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump.

Not for the first time this year Senator Hanson's One Nation party has seen its primary vote eclipse Labor, this time in a Redbridge poll, where Prime Minister Anthony Albanese remained preferred PM.

Mr Rudd, who is now the global president of US-based think tank the Asia Society, told 7.30 Senator Hanson's act had not changed in all the years she had been in parliament.

"It's very easy to play the politics of protest," Mr Rudd said.

"It's very hard to do the grinding business of government, which looks after practical problems of national security ... of the economy and growing it, environmental sustainability ... and delivering basic services for the Australian people, including housing affordability, which has been eating away so badly at people's standard of living over a long period of time.

"The hard business of government is to come up with practical responses to each of those challenges.

"The easy business of politics is simply to act as a protest vector and then lace it and spice it with the politics of race.

One nation leader Paiuline Hanson has been enjoying a boost in popularity throughout 2026. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

"That's what Ms Hanson's been doing ever since she emerged in my fair state of Queensland, a quarter of a century ago.

"Her script hasn't changed.

"Ask this question of yourselves. What single answer does she have to any of the list of problems and challenges which I went through before?

" Zip, is the answer to that. "

Concerns about China's naval might

The former prime minister has long been a student of China. Fluent in Mandarin he was conferred a Doctorate of Philosophy from Oxford in 2022 for his thesis on Chinese President Xi Jinping.

As president Mr Xi has overseen China's economic and military evolution but the latter has come with flashpoints.

Kevin Rudd did a university thesis on President Xi Jinping at Oxford in 2022. (Reuters: Tingshu Wang)

China been involved in a number of incidents at sea, with other Asian nations, in the Indo-Pacific region.

Mr Rudd told 7.30 that China has an enhanced and growing submarine fleet, which was one reason he supported Australia acquiring nuclear submarines under the AUKUS agreement.

"This will be a great addition to the Royal Australian Navy's capabilities set in terms of our ability to maintain Australia's own sovereign interests in the Indo-Pacific," Mr Rudd told 7.30.

"China now has 60 to 75 submarines of which 15 to 20 are nuclear-powered. And a number in addition to that are ballistic missile submarines that are nuclear-armed.

"They are currently at size when compared boat-for-boat against the size of the US Pacific submarine fleet.

"And the Chinese surface fleet is already at some 370 boats, larger than the US surface fleet, of some 290 operational ships as we stand.

The Jiangkai-class frigate Hengyang was among the Chinese flotilla sailing east of Sydney. (Department of Defence)

"So it's important that Australia has its own naval capabilities given the changes to the strategic and military balances, which are occurring within our wider region."

While Mr Rudd said he believed Australia is well within its rights to acquire those submarines, not everyone agrees.

Earlier this year Victor Gao, the vice-president of the Center for China and Globalisation (CCG), issued Australia a warning, on 7.30, over acquiring the nuclear-powered subs.

Victor Gao is the vice-president of the Centre for China and Globalisation. (ABC News)

Mr Rudd said that behaviour was expected but that China itself did not like the AUKUS agreement.

"Mr Gao is a professional provocateur on the part of the Chinese, let's call it political establishment," Mr Rudd told 7.30.

"If you look at official statements through the Chinese media and since AUKUS first came into being, obviously the Chinese system doesn't like it because these are formidable assets.

"That's why Australia is acquiring them.

"We need greater naval capabilities in order to sustain our own national interests. And that's where these assets of ours are important additions to Australia's overall defence capabilities."

Rudd's Taiwan 2028 theory

Mr Rudd has in the past espoused a theory that the year 2028 could see an emboldened Mr Xi finally look to take Taiwan by force.

Mr Rudd is uniquely positioned when it comes to understanding both the Chinese and US presidents. (AAP: Mick Tsikas)

Mr Rudd said a number of factors come into play:

Mr Xi's almost inevitable return to General Secretary of the Communist Party in October 2027, the January 2028 Taiwanese presidential elections and "the robustness of President Trump's posture on deterrence by the United States against China over Taiwan".

Mr Xi's own recent language has also played a part.

The Chinese leader recently told Mr Trump that this is a very dangerous issue which could result in collision and conflict.

Mr Rudd said the choice of words was concerning.

"That's the first time I've heard Xi Jinping use that sort of absolutely direct language with a US president in the context of a formal bilateral summit," Mr Rudd told 7.30.

"Xi Jinping is laying down his own markers.

Donald Trump and Xi Jinping met in Beijing, in May. (Reuters: Evan Vucci)

"President Trump's language in response to that has been criticised in the United States for being less than robust, pointing out that Taiwan was a long way away from the United States.

"It's both Xi Jinping's statement and Donald Trump's response, which has given rise to further concerns about the maintenance of peace and stability [in Taiwan] through to the end of 28."

Asked if anyone knew how Mr Trump would respond to a Chinese move on Taiwan, Mr Rudd said he could not say but that the presence of the United States military in the area was of great importance.

"What we can observe is the continuing posture of the United States Pacific Command led by Admiral (Camuel) Paparo," he said.

"These are the folks who are in the front line and they, under Admiral Paparo, every day of the week, every week of the year, are sustaining the posture of US deterrence over Taiwan.

" The political language will therefore come and go ... but where the actual substance of US deterrence posture lies is in the capabilities set represented by US Pacific Command. "

Watch 7.30, Mondays to Thursdays 7:30pm on ABC iview and ABC TV

World.title: Shark Bay crash killed grandfather taking family on holiday
World.content:
More details are emerging of a horror crash near Shark Bay that killed a 60-year-old grandfather and seriously injured his partner and their 12-year-old grandson on Monday.

The family's vehicle and caravan collided head-on with a Toyota LandCruiser utility on the North West Coastal Highway.

The 45-year-old driver of the LandCruiser also died at the scene.

The highway is gradually reopening after a lengthy shutdown. (Supplied: Josh Osgood)

The 12-year-old boy and his grandmother, aged in her 50s, suffered life-threatening injuries and were flown to hospitals in Perth where they remain in a stable condition.

The crash closed the highway south of the Overlander for more than 24 hours during the peak of the tourist season, blocking travellers and truckers from heading north to the Pilbara.

The crash occurred on a highway used by many tourists who travel north during winter. (ABC News)

Officers from the Major Crash Investigation Section are investigating the circumstances surrounding the crash.

Horrific scene

Sandy Winkle was at the scene moments after the crash and did her best to help those involved.

"In the distance, I could see a little bit of dust and then obviously there was a caravan in the bush," she said.

"I just pulled out my first aid kit and ran down there with bandages and stuff like that."

Two dead, child critical in WA crash Two people have died, and a 12-year-old child has been critically injured after a utility struck a vehicle towing a caravan near Shark Bay in WA's Gascoyne.

Ms Winkle comforted one of the drivers in his final moments.

"He was in a lot of trouble and I thought, 'He doesn't want to be here by himself,'" she said.

" So I hung with him to just try and console him that there was help coming on the way. "

Ms Winkle was returning to Dunsborough from a family holiday in Shark Bay.

"It was pretty traumatic, to be honest with you, but the message is, like, these sort of things happen in an instant," she said.

"I had a very restless night thinking about all the things that I possibly should have done.

"That will stay with me for quite some time."

As of Tuesday afternoon, the North West Coastal Highway is gradually reopening between the Overlander and Billabong roadhouses.

World.title: Kath Pettingill, the mother of the Walsh Street police killers, dies
World.content:
The mother of one of Melbourne's most notorious crime families responsible for the Walsh Street police killings has died, aged 91.

Kath Pettingill's death was confirmed by a family member, who declined to comment to the ABC.

Among her many children, Pettingill was the mother of Trevor Pettingill and Victor Peirce, who were charged with two other men over the 1988 murder of two young police officers in Walsh Street in South Yarra.

Underworld figure Victor Peirce was one of Pettingill's 10 children. (ABC News)

Constables Steven Tynan and Damien Eyre were ambushed and killed after being called to investigate a dumped stolen car.

The double shooting was said to be a revenge attack after the Armed Robbery Squad shot dead close friend of the Richmond-based family, Graeme Jensen.

All four were later acquitted by a jury.

Crime matriarch Kath Pettingill, pictured at the 2002 funeral of her son, Victor Peirce, has died. (ABC News)

Peirce's wife, Wendy, was meant to have been a key witness in the trial.

But after 18 months in witness protection, costing $2 million, she changed her mind and refused to give evidence.

After Pierce was later shot dead in Bay Street in Port Melbourne in an underworld hit, she told media that her husband had indeed planned and carried out the murders.

Two police officers were killed in Walsh Street, South Yarra in October 1988. (ABC News)

Among Pettingill's other children were her eldest son, drug dealer Dennis Bruce Allen, who was known as Dr Death.

He was a suspect in more than 10 murders.

He died in jail.

Another son, Peter Allen, was a convicted heroin dealer.

Pettingill's family was the inspiration behind the 2010 Australian movie Animal Kingdom, in which actor Jacki Weaver played matriarch Janine Cody.

Jacki Weaver starred as a character inspired by Pettingill in the 2010 Australian film, Animal Kingdom. (www.imdb.com)

In an interview with News Corp in 2011, Pettingill did not give a glowing review of the movie or Weaver's portrayal.

"Jacki Weaver and I have only one thing in common, neither of us can act," she told the Sunday Herald Sun shortly after the film's release.

"I've seen the movie and I'm not impressed. She's supposed to have read books about me and studied me for the part, but it doesn't come off," she said.

Pettingill had a glass eye, reportedly as a result of being shot in the 1970s as she and Dennis Allen tried to repay a debt on behalf of a daughter.

World.title: Aboriginal community police sue NT Police for alleged racial discrimination
World.content:
A group of current and former Aboriginal police officers in the Northern Territory are suing the Territory government in the Federal Court, claiming they experienced decades of racial discrimination, abuse and vilification while working for NT Police.

The group members claim they were subject to offensive and derogatory language and received less pay than their non-Indigenous colleagues for similar work.

The class action follows an unsuccessful complaint made by the Aboriginal community police officers (ACPOs) to the Australian Human Rights Commission (AHRC) in September 2024.

Aboriginal police officers detail allegations of 'racist culture' A human rights complaint alleges "countless" examples of racism within NT Police.

Earlier this year, the AHRC terminated that claim after the parties failed to reach a resolution, giving the officers 60 days to take legal action.

One of the three lead applicants, Shawn Lewfatt, who has been a serving member of the NT Police Force (NTPF) in Darwin for almost 30 years, said the lawsuit was a last resort.

"It's been a long journey," Mr Lewfatt said.

"We tried to fight it internally for decades, but we had no voice.

" I felt it was our only option. "

Mr Lewfatt, who first joined the police force in 1998, said he pursued a career in policing to have a positive impact on his community, but claimed he struggled with the culture within the force.

Shawn Lewfatt has been a member of the police force for almost three decades. (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

"I've experienced many incidents of direct and indirect racial discrimination and I know my fellow Indigenous employees have also experienced it," he said.

Officers seeking compensation, apology

The applicants are being represented by Melbourne-based law firm Gordon Legal.

Partner at the firm, Seb O'Meara, described the allegations made by the three officers as "deeply concerning".

"They concern almost three decades of unchecked racist abuse and unequal terms and conditions of employment," he said.

"[Our clients] allege systemic racial vilification and abuse, both directed at them personally, but also directed to others — including community members — by members of the NT Police Force, in their presence."

Mr O'Meara said the officers were seeking compensation for the "loss and damage" suffered, as well as an apology from NT Police.

Seb O'Meara says the officers are seeking compensation and an apology. (ABC News: Matthew Holmes)

"They think that change is really important, and that is what is motivating them," the lawyer said.

Mr O'Meara estimated the class action could grow to include hundreds of current and former ACPOs.

Claimant wants 'safer, fair work environment'

NT Police has been subject to intense scrutiny over recent years since damaging allegations of racist behaviour within the force were aired during the coronial inquest into the 2019 shooting death of Kumanjayi Walker.

'That is confronting': NT police executives acknowledge racism within force An NT Police executive says there remain ongoing disciplinary issues in the force involving "incidences where we are dealing with racism".

The NT coroner, Elisabeth Armitage, found "clear evidence of entrenched, systemic and structural racism within the NT Police" and that examples of racism were ignored by the then-commissioner, Michael Murphy.

In the wake of the inquest findings, NT Police released an anti-racism strategy which included a commitment to provide anti-racism training for all employees.

Mr Lewfatt said he wanted a "safer, fair work environment for Aboriginal employees" but that he was also seeking accountability.

The NT Police Force has committed to ensuring all staff undertake anti-racism training. (ABC News: Hamish Harty)

"It's all well and good that the department are moving forward," he said.

" But I think it's also important they acknowledge the past, the hurt, the trauma that many Indigenous employees have had to endure. "

In response to news of the class action, an NT Police spokesperson said the force was "aware of the ongoing legal proceedings" and it would be "inappropriate for the NTPF to comment further".

The case is set to go before a court for the first time later this month, with the applicants' lawyers seeking to have the matter progress to a trial in 2027.

World.title: Minns government rejects hate speech advice it fought to keep secret
World.content:
The Minns government has rejected key advice from a review it commissioned, which recommends hate speech laws be extended to protect more members of the community.

As a result, inciting hatred against people based on sexual orientation, disability, gender identity, religion and other characteristics will not be made illegal under the Crimes Act.

Inciting hatred based on race will remain a criminal offence.

For months, the government refused to release the review by former Supreme Court judge John Sackar KC, which was completed in November last year.

The government clashed with upper house MPs who were seeking to force the document's release, resulting in the parliamentary suspension of Labor frontbencher John Graham.

On Tuesday afternoon, the government released the review along with a statement rejecting its key recommendation.

Mr Daley says the government believes expanding the laws would raise "complex questions". (AAP: Bianca de Marchi)

"The NSW government has decided not to expand the existing criminal offence of inciting racial hatred to apply to additional protected attributes," Attorney-General Michael Daley said.

"The government's view is that expanding the racial hatred offence to cover other attributes raises complex questions about freedom of expression, freedom of religion, and the consistent application of the criminal law across the community."

Pressure to protect

It is already illegal to incite violence against someone based on characteristics like race, religion, sexual orientation, intersex status or HIV status.

But in 2025, following a spate of antisemitic incidents, the Minns government announced it would amend the Crimes Act, making it illegal to incite hatred as well.

This went against the NSW Law Reform Commission, which recommended against changing the existing laws.

The new laws tackling antisemitism in NSW Laws designed to curb racial hatred in NSW were the first pieces of legislation introduced to state parliament this year. Here's everything you need to know about them.

But, Labor's new legislation only covered hate speech based on race, prompting some other vulnerable groups, including disability and LGBTIQA+ advocates, to argue for the same protections.

The government commissioned Mr Sackar to assess whether the hate speech protections should be extended to other vulnerable groups.

His report recommended greater uniformity between the groups protected against incitement to violence and those protected against incitement to hatred.

He said the inconsistency was "detrimental to social cohesion".

"Both offences ought to protect the same groups to prevent any perception of a 'hierarchical, two-tier model of protection'," he said.

He also recommended that disability be added as a protected attribute, against incitement to both hatred and violence.

Other recommendations called for better reporting and education around hate-based conduct, as well as specialised training for police.

The government said it would "continue to consider" the remainder of the report.

However, Mr Daley said a NSW Law Reform Commission review into anti-discrimination laws would also help guide government policy, along with the recommendations of the royal commission into antisemitism.

"There is no place for hatred in New South Wales," Mr Daley said.

"Everyone deserves to feel safe, respected and free from intimidation, regardless of their background, faith, sexuality or identity."

Greens slam 'secrecy'

Dr Cohn says the Minns government has engaged in "months of secrecy". (ABC Sydney: Andrew Whitington)

The Greens have accused the government of childish tactics in seeking to suppress the report.

Upper house MPs made repeated attempts to force the government to hand over the Sackar review, but Labor argued it was a cabinet document.

Greens MP, Amanda Cohn, said marginalised groups were experiencing "worsening hatred and division", after the government engaged in "months of secrecy".

"This report has been sitting on the government's desk since November last year," she said.

"More than half of its recommendations don't require legislative change.

"The Minns Labor government 'continuing to consider' the remaining recommendations after seven months is kicking the can down the road on critical matters of safety and inclusion."

World.title: Clarkson happy with handshake to extend contract as North set to miss finals
World.content:
North Melbourne coach Alastair Clarkson is unfazed going into the final year of his contract, saying he just needs a "handshake".

As Clarkson comes towards the end of his fourth season in charge, North will spend a 10th-straight year without experiencing finals action.

Speculation has started to mount that Kangaroos hierarchy might consider letting Clarkson go at the end of his current five-year deal, signed in late 2022 in what was a massive coup for the club.

Although North have improved this year, they are yet to beat a team above them on the ladder and will fall short of a wildcard berth.

AFL round 21 Saturday live updates Josh Fraser's bid to become Carlton's next full-time coach receives a massive boost as the Blues record a thumping win over the Brisbane Lions.

"Old school" Clarkson will not be pushing for a contract extension beyond 2027 this off-season and is happy to wait it out.

"All I require is a handshake and a wink and a nod, and that'll do me," the four-time Hawthorn premiership coach said on Tuesday.
