"We'll work our way through whatever we need to do.

"I'm really here to serve the footy club … it's not just me, but those that are in leadership positions at the club have done a really good job stabilising the footy club.

"We're really keen to progress and get ourselves up the ladder, but all we do know is that that's done best when you've got stability."

Clarkson drew on examples of Brisbane Lions, Fremantle and Adelaide of clubs who were patient with their coaches and find themselves in powerful positions on the field.

"I've been in the caper for a long time, so that's a bit of water off the duck's (back)," he said of speculation about his future.

"The best examples are the reigning premiers (Brisbane) who took a while to get going and then Adelaide with 'Nicksy' (Matthew Nicks) and Fremantle with Justin Longmuir.

"The governance and administration of the club just sticking to the path and sticking to the course, and we're going to be no different."

Clarkson's record at North is 19-1-59, a far cry from his glory years with the Hawks.

The Kangaroos face a challenging run home, starting with the Western Bulldogs at Docklands on Thursday night.

They have long losing streaks against the Bulldogs, and their final two opponents, Geelong and Sydney.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

Clarkson bristled when asked how important it would be to beat one of those teams to finish off this season.

"You're just searching, searching for a headline," he said.

"Teams that have been in the bottom four or five on the ladder haven't beaten the top teams very often in the last five or six years.

"That's the reason why they've been in that position on the ladder."

AAP

World.title: Trial date set for man accused of murdering 14-year-old girl
World.content:
A man accused of murdering a Tasmanian teenager will face trial in April next year, almost four years after her death.

Scottsdale man Christopher Mark Jordan, who has pleaded not guilty to murdering 14-year-old Shyanne-Lee Tatnell, appeared in the Supreme Court in Launceston via video link from Risdon Prison today.

Justice Michael Brett told the court the trial date has been listed for April 19 next year, four years after the Burnie teenager went missing while staying at a Launceston youth hostel.

Following an extensive search, her remains were found almost three months later, off a dirt track at Nabowla, north-east of Launceston.

Mr Jordan was arrested the next day.

He was charged with murder and pleaded not guilty in 2024.

The trial is expected to take five weeks and will be heard by Justice Brett.

Another directions hearing, in which parties are expected to discuss any pre-trial issues, has been listed for November 27, 2026.

World.title: From deadline to details: The six things you need to know to handle the census
World.content:
PoliticsFederalCensus From deadline to details: The six things you need to know to handle the census Shane Wright August 4, 2026 — 7:31pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When is census night, how do you fill it out, and do you need to be at home? Census night this year is August 11. But, as more than 1.2 million households have already done, you can complete your census form before that date. If you complete your census form before August 11, you need to fill it out as if you were home on that day. If a member of a household is away from home on the special night, you can include them as if they were home. If you are visiting someone, make sure you’re included in their household form. But make sure you’re counted only once. Your personal details are confidential – but your descendants could ask for them in 99 years. Tanya Macheda



For those travelling or staying at hotels, caravan parks and registered campgrounds, operators should have census forms for you to complete. If you happen to be free camping or staying at a remote location, various visitor information centres will have census forms. If that doesn’t work, you can get a census number from the ABS so you can complete your form when you have access to the internet. Why do we have the census? Since the Babylonians in 3800 BC, governing bodies have sought to count the number of people under their control. The census that features in the Gospel of Luke was conducted by authorities for taxation and administration reasons as Rome brought the province of Judea under its control.



Related Article Census In 1947, the census asked if you had a flushing toilet. This is what it will ask this year Outside of tax, censuses have been used to plan for services such as schools and cemeteries, while in many countries they are central to the allocation of electorates in parliaments. The first official census in this country was in 1828. It was termed a “muster” and held in NSW to help align the number of people in the colony with its food supplies. Colonial headcounts were carried out until the mid-1880s. In 1905, the federal government passed the Census and Statistics Act. The Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) was created the following year. The first national census was held on April 2, 1911. That census counted 4.45 million people (excluding the nation’s Indigenous population).



Some of the questions used in that census have disappeared. We are no longer asked if we live in a wagon or if the family home is made from spinifex or calico. But others have remained constant, though maybe the answers change. In 1911, 79 people said their religion was Callithumpian, while another 32 described their belief as “wowser”. At the 2001 census, almost 70,000 people said they were Jedi. What happens if you don’t complete the census? Completing the census is compulsory, and has been since the first count in 1911.



If a household does not complete and submit a census form, the ABS will contact you and ask for it to be done. If a household continues to hold out, it can be served a formal direction to complete the census, which is a legal instruction. At this point, if you continue to refuse to fill out the form, you can be prosecuted and fined up to $364 a day. What is a census field officer, how are they chosen, and how much are they paid? The census is one of the nation’s largest one-off job opportunities. The ABS is employing more than 16,000 field officers – the people who go around to households with forms and then pick them up – through the census period. It’s a job that appeals to seniors or those looking for some casual work, and the pay starts around the $33-an-hour mark.



Related Article Census A decade after the last census disaster, the security of this year’s count is at risk There are thousands of other positions that require more specialist skills or being in particular parts of the country, such as isolated regions. What has changed in Australia because of the census? One of the most important discoveries in health was uncovered by Australian statistician Oliver Lancaster. He used the 1911, 1921 and 1933 censuses – which asked a question on deaf-mutism – to establish for the first time the link between rubella and congenital problems in unborn children.



More recently, housing experts noticed a drop in the number of home owners between the 1996 and 2001 census. This continued into the national headcounts of 2006, 2011, 2016 and 2021. This decline in ownership rates, particularly across people in their 20s and 30s, has been highlighted by advocates for changes in housing policy, including taxation policy. The Treasury analysis contained in this year’s federal budget, which contained changes to negative gearing and capital gains tax, referenced this census data. What happens to your data, and is it a privacy concern? Some people are concerned about their personal data as the census form collects names and addresses.

World.title: The best public schools in HSC maths, ranked – and how one non-selective surprised everyone
World.content:
NationalNSWHSC The best public schools in HSC maths, ranked – and how one non-selective surprised everyone Christopher Harris and Nigel Gladstone August 4, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Balgowlah Boys, Fairvale High and Killarney Heights High recorded the highest average marks in advanced mathematics of any non-selective public schools in last year’s Higher School Certificate. A Herald analysis of average marks in the subject shows the 43 students at Balgowlah Boys who enrolled in the advanced course achieved an average mark of 90.3 – stronger than all but four selective schools. For the Mathematics Standard 2 course, fully selective school Merewether High in Newcastle had the best average marks, followed by Manly selective and then Balgowlah Boys. Oliver Yang, Leo Robinson, and Luke Macfarlane scored top mathematics results in the HSC last year for their school, Balgowlah Boys. Sitthixay Ditthavong



Balgowlah’s head of mathematics, Chris Hickford, traces its HSC success back to year 7 and teachers’ focus on building strong algebra skills, an ability to think formulaically and interpret critical information in written questions. Related Article HSC We re-ranked schools by HSC averages. This is what the most precise data reveals “We do have, I suppose, a traditional approach to maths teaching here at the school,” he said. A typical lesson contains teacher-led examples, student questioning, followed by a “gradual release” for the students to work independently. Or, in teacher parlance, it is an “I do, we do, you do” approach. Many students took up mathematics because they aspired to work in a trade and could see the value of numeracy skills to real life, he said, while other students wanted to take mathematics-based university courses. Others simply enjoy the subject because they’re good at it.



“The explicit nature of the subject appeals to the boys … seeing a clear result and an answer that very rarely can be ambiguous or misinterpreted. I think that clarity of it really appeals to the boys,” Hickford said. It is easy to slip behind during the fast-paced year 11 and 12 courses, so the teachers focus on “ensuring the students are actually doing the work” with rigorous checks. “We find just keeping the students to account for actually getting their work done makes a huge difference,” he said. Eddie Woo, Professor of Practice at the University of Sydney, said there was no single method to improve mathematics results but successful schools often closely analyse results data provided by the NSW Education Standards Authority.



“It gives super granular data. We can drill down to individual classes and items in an exam,” he said. Schools could detect areas of weakness and learn from their teachers whose classes had produced excellent results in certain topics, such as discrete random variables. Another key to success was structured mentoring and purposeful skill development for teachers, which included pairing new teachers with experienced ones so they could see how they approached teaching the mathematics course. “Some schools do it extremely well and other schools have constraining factors, so that means it doesn’t happen as much,” Wu said. “Just because you can do the content yourself is not the same as being able to teach it ... anyone who has taught someone how to drive can attest to this. It’s a whole different set of skills.”



Most private schools do not publish subject averages, though the high-ranking selective Sydney Grammar School reported an average of 87.7 for advanced maths. Girls school Roseville College reported a mean of 83.2. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Red flags: A tech company claims it can identify Australia’s most at-risk children
World.content:
Exclusive TechnologyAI Red flags: A tech company claims it can identify Australia’s most at-risk children David Swan August 4, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

An Australian company founded by a survivor of childhood abuse is bringing a machine-learning system to childcare centres to flag children who may be at risk of harm, as the sector grapples with balancing young people’s privacy against a need to keep them safe. The warning system’s rollout in daycares across the country comes as the sector undergoes its biggest safety overhaul since the national quality framework began. SAFE chief executive Ruby O’Rourke. The company says its eponymously named SAFE system is already in use in more than 1000 early childhood services. Educators log everyday observations – a bruise, a missed meal, a parent affected by drugs at pick-up – and the machine-learning model turns those fragments into a live picture of which children may be most at risk. Parents are not asked to opt in; the company says consent is given when families enrol their kids to a daycare and agree to its professional systems. Chief executive Ruby O’Rourke, a longtime children’s rights campaigner who ran for federal parliament in 2019, built the company after a childhood shaped by forced adoption, domestic violence and abuse that, she says, culminated in a family member holding her under the water at a Melbourne creek. Passersby revived her. The family member was never charged.



Her argument is that none of it was invisible. “The schools, the Brownies, the Girl Guides, all of these signals were missed,” she said. Neighbours told her years later that they had heard her scream, and done nothing. “If I’m going to leave my life with anything,” she said, “it’s knowing the next generation has this layer of SAFE sitting under the surface” – what she calls a “flight control tower” for children at severe risk. SAFE co-founder David Salajan. O’Rourke began building childcare software in the mid-2000s; the predictive layer started in 2012 with NICTA, the country’s former information and communications technology research centre that is now part of the CSIRO. Co-founder David Salajan describes SAFE as a machine paired with human reviewers.



“It’s just an observation, no matter how big or small,” he said. The software returns a risk score and guidance on whether a concern meets the mandatory reporting threshold; every case is then reviewed by former child protection workers. A national dashboard, seen by SAFE’s team rather than the daycare centre staff, triages every case so they can see which children are at highest risk. Related Article Exclusive

Child abuse Thousands of NSW children are being abused. Police say it has become an epidemic The pitch lands at a volatile moment for the childcare sector. Changes to national laws governing the industry took effect on February 27, making children’s safety the paramount legal consideration, creating a workers’ register and mandating carers to attend child safety training by August 27. A $226 million government package also funds a national CCTV trial. The overhaul follows recent abuse cases such as that of Queensland worker Ashley Paul Griffith, jailed for life in 2024 over 307 offences against 73 children. In Sydney, daycare worker Hamish Alexander Edward Tait was arrested last month, facing more than 320 charges over his alleged abuse of 150 children under his care. Those cases involved alleged abuse at childcare centres though, rather than abuse elsewhere detected by an educator. The SAFE system also raises privacy concerns: a private company holds a live, prioritised register of children it deems most at risk, plus behavioural records on about 200,000 workers in the childcare industry.



The Office of the Australian Information Commissioner would not comment on SAFE, but a spokesperson said behavioural information about a child in a care setting may count as personal – and sometimes sensitive – information under the Privacy Act, carrying obligations to collect only what is necessary, keep it secure and not reuse it. Whether an enrolment agreement amounts to valid consent depends on how it is worded, the spokesperson said, adding that consent should be “informed, current, specific and voluntary”, especially for children’s information. The regulator is also drawing up a Children’s Online Privacy Code, due by December 10, expected to cover most online services used in early childhood settings. It would require information to be handled in a child’s best interests, with a parent’s consent necessary for children under 15. Carol Matthews, NSW/ACT branch secretary of the Independent Education Union, which represents early childhood care staff, said for-profit software was “no substitute for a comprehensive focus on child safety at every centre”. The union backed the regulatory reforms over the past year, but was wary of the technology. “Machine learning takes the risk of a privacy breach to a whole new level,” Matthews said, warning that many services may not be equipped to safeguard the data. She urged employers to consult staff before rolling out any such platform. O’Rourke dismissed concerns that the machine-learning system could entrench bias given the data it’s working with is based on childcare workers’ observations. SAFE does not identify children by ethnicity, socioeconomic background or disability, she said, and its signals are “continuously reviewed by child protection experts to identify and prevent bias, not enshrine it”. However, the observations that feed the warning system are human judgments.



Related Article Child abuse ‘This doesn’t happen to us’: Family’s horror after Sydney day care abuser unmasked She likens it to a blood test: the machine records the markers, but a qualified professional interprets them, and no action follows until her review team validates the case. A NSW parliamentary inquiry this year recommended a database to track problematic staff behaviour in childcare centres and foster stronger intelligence-sharing between regulators, police and screening bodies – which is close to what SAFE is pitching. But the same committee was wary of technological fixes, warning that CCTV “should not be relied upon” and was no substitute for staffing and supervision. Tamara Hughes, head of safeguarding at Save the Children, said Australia’s problem was not a lack of knowledge about cases but sustained action. “A child’s safety should not depend on where they live, who they come into contact with, or their background,” she said. For O’Rourke, the bottom line is simpler. While the childcare industry homed in on early childhood education standards, care and safety were left as an afterthought. “We’ve got the priority wrong.”



Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732). Anyone affected by sexual, domestic or family violence can also access 24/7, free and confidential trauma-specialist counselling through Full Stop Australia (1800 385 578). World.title: Mystery powerbroker emerges from Gaza deal
World.content:
WorldMiddle EastIsraeli-Palestinian conflict Mystery powerbroker emerges from Gaza deal Paul Nuki August 4, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

London: Of all those involved in getting the tortuous Gaza disarmament negotiations over the line, the most intriguing is Mohammed Dahlan. Sources close to the negotiations said the exiled Palestinian politician, who has a reputation as something of a modern-day Machiavelli, played a crucial role in securing the deal. Mohammed Dahlan (left), with Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas in 2005, has been a powerful figure on the periphery of Palestinian politics for decades. AP Specifically, he is said to have been instrumental in convincing the Islamist militant group that only through disarmament could its political flame burn on. “Over the past two days, he actually did play a major role,” a well-placed source at the heart of the negotiations said.





He now resides in exile amid the gleaming towers of Abu Dhabi, where he is the right-hand man of Sheikh Mohammed bin Zayed Al-Nahyan, ruler of the petro-rich state and president of the United Arab Emirates (UAE). Dahlan is a wealthy businessman in his own right and is said to be influential in security relationships that Abu Dhabi has established in the Balkans, North Africa and Sudan. ‘Hamas has reached a point where they understand that this is not going anywhere [militarily]. So they need to be smart.’ Palestinian source In 2016, it was said that Turkey placed Dahlan on its “most wanted terrorist list”, offering a $US700,000 ($997,000) bounty, accusing him of involvement in the failed 2016 Turkish coup attempt. Middle East specialists say there are several converging “timelines” that explain the deal coming to fruition, one of those being Dahlan’s and the UAE’s political ambitions in the region.



First, the negotiators were getting tired. The talks had been going for almost a year and, in June, the Egyptians were said to have run out of patience, issuing Hamas with an ultimatum. Mohammed Dahlan is said to have an eye on the forthcoming Palestinian elections – if they go ahead. AFP “The Egyptians [said] either you give us a ‘yes’ or you don’t come back,” said a source privy to the negotiations. “It was very direct.” After that, the process was said to have moved swiftly, with all but two clauses – clause 5 on compensation and clause 8 on disarmament – quickly agreed via the Egyptians two weeks ago. The disarmament clause was sealed after Hamas secured a commitment that its debts to “suppliers, contractors and other parties” would be honoured up to $US400 million in clause 5, said the source.



These debts include payments due to civil servants and others, and in some instances date back 20 years. Paying them is a matter of honour, security and patronage. Diplomatic boost US President Donald Trump’s timeline was also pivotal. The White House, after more than 150 days of war with Iran, was in urgent need of a diplomatic boost, said experts – one that would play well with its battered allies in the Gulf as well as at home. Despite the announcement of a ceasefire, Israel has continued to strike targets in Gaza. Getty Images



“Trump wanted to point to something, wanted this wrapped up, wanted to be able to declare a win,” said Hugh Lovatt, a senior policy fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations. But it was the Palestinian elections to be held in the Israeli-occupied West Bank on November 28 that may have been the most important factor of all, experts said. If they happen – a big if, given Israeli settler violence in the territory – they will be the first held in more than 20 years and will reshape the Palestinian Legislative Council, the legislature of the Palestinian Authority, for decades to come. It was this pivotal election that Dahlan is said to have his eye on, and which explained his intervention with Hamas to get the deal over the line, sources said. Like Hamas, his faction of the Palestinian national movement, Fatah, stands against the regime headed by Abbas and is aligned with Marwan Barghouti, the popular Palestinian politician who has spent the past 24 years in an Israeli jail.



“Dahlan put pressure on Hamas to make the final concessions, and to agree to the text in exchange for having this sort of potential political alignment going forward,” one source told London’s Telegraph. On the principle that “the enemy of my enemy is my friend”, he was saying to Hamas that now is the time to disarm and join the political fight for the future of the Palestinian movement, a second source said. Related Article Opinion

Trump's White House Trump’s entered a new phase: the unmaking of his presidency Bruce Wolpe Senior fellow at the US Studies Centre and former political staffer They added: “Hamas has reached a point where they understand that this is not going anywhere [militarily]. So they need to be smart. If you want to stay as a political movement, that’s the way to do it now, by changing and joining others.” The extent to which Dahlan represents the UAE as well as himself in these dealings is not clear, but experts said he would not risk his position in Abu Dhabi, which has made him a rich and powerful man.



Others point out that both Dahlan and Abu Dhabi have provided substantial sums in humanitarian aid to Gaza and the West Bank over the past two years, thereby cementing relationships and patronage there. “If you look at the numbers, the UAE is the biggest humanitarian donor over the past few years for Gaza … And everyone knows that [Dahlan] is influencing this,” the source close to the negotiations said. The one timeline that does not seem to have been considered as regards the Gaza deal is Israel’s. Benjamin Netanyahu is facing a tricky election run-in, with some polls suggesting his opponents will erode his position. AP The stipulations that the Israel Defence Forces withdraw from the strip, stop shooting and be replaced by a Palestinian-run bureaucracy and security apparatus are the last thing Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu needs before the Israeli election, scheduled for October 27.



Already, even normally friendly Israeli media commentators are getting stuck in. “‘I will tell them no.’ That’s what Netanyahu reportedly told his ministers days before flying to Washington, in response to reported US pressure for a “series of withdrawals” across Syria, Lebanon and Gaza, wrote Israeli journalist Amit Segal on Friday. “He later denied the issue even came up in the meeting – a denial that now appears to have been a lie.” Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: How Roosters sought approval from adidas’ German HQ to change jersey
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 How Roosters sought approval from adidas’ German HQ to change jersey Christian Nicolussi August 4, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Senior executives at adidas’ German headquarters have given the Sydney Roosters rare permission to alter the colours of their famous three white stripes on their Indigenous Round jersey. In an Australian sporting first, the Roosters’ playing strip to be worn against the Bulldogs on Friday will switch the iconic white stripes to red, yellow and black – the colours of the First Nations’ flag. The Roosters’ Indigenous Round jersey, worn by Connor Watson, will feature adidas’ famous three white stripes being changed to red, black and yellow, the colours of the Aboriginal flag. The Roosters are in the first year of a four-year deal with the athletic apparel giants, but when it came to their Indigenous wish, which was designed by former player Craig Salvatori’s daughter, Kaylie, club officials needed to get top-brass approval. It’s not unprecedented as adidas has allowed Germany to change the white stripes on their national football jerseys, as well as powerhouse clubs like Liverpool, whose away strip in the English Premier League this season will feature three red stripes.



Officials from adidas in Australia passed on the Roosters’ wishes to their chiefs in the Bavarian town of Herzogenaurach – and they were more than happy to agree to the request because of the “profound cultural or community significance”. Related Article State of Origin What Matt King’s NSW coaching contract means for Ivan Cleary “We’re incredibly proud to have worked collaboratively with the Sydney Roosters, designer Kaylie Salvatori, and our product team in Germany to create the 2026 First Nations Jersey,” said Rachel Howard, general manager of adidas Pacific. “It was important that this jersey reflects the stories, cultures and communities it represents, ensuring the design is both authentic and deeply connected to the local community. “Any change to the adidas three stripes is reserved for moments of profound cultural or community significance.



“Changing the three stripes to the colours of the Aboriginal Flag is a proud reflection of this.” Roosters chief operating officer Jarrod Johnstone said the club reached out to adidas towards the end of last year so they had ample time to assess their request. Cody Ramsey, Connor Watson and Blake Steep model the latest strip, which is a nod to former player and proud Indigenous man, Craig Salvatori. Sydney Roosters “We’re delighted adidas were open to the design, and they put the wheels in motion to get global approval – significant changes like altering the white stripes needed that [permission] from their headquarters,” he said. Proud Gamilaroi man and Roosters utility Connor Watson loved the latest jersey, which features paintings by Salvatori, and the red, yellow and black stripes down the side. The Roosters have for several seasons dedicated their Indigenous jersey to former First Australians’ players.



It will be the last time Watson wears the Indigenous jersey at Bondi before he joins St George Illawarra next year ahead of his 2028 move to the PNG Chiefs. He was also aware he could have easily been playing against the Roosters on Friday after meeting with Phil Gould about a move to the Bulldogs ahead of the 2024 season. “It was pretty serious, it got pretty close, and that was when it didn’t look like there was going to be any room for me here; it’s a bit of a sliding-doors moment,” Watson said. A second Roosters’ Indigenous player, Cody Ramsey, only discovered his First Nations’ heritage when he moved to Sydney when he was 17, and was keen to learn more about his past.

World.title: A litany of sordid allegations against Alan Jones stripped bare
World.content:
Analysis NationalNSWAlan Jones trial A litany of sordid allegations against Alan Jones stripped bare Jacqueline Maley August 4, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Warning: graphic content The specificity was described with calm legalese, in clinical tones removed from the subject matter. “How long was that happening, where your penises were in contact with each other?” prosecutor Georgina Wright, SC, asked the man known to the court as complainant “J”. Alan Jones has been a man of many titles, but now he is reduced to just one: defendant. Peter Rae “It was ... between five and 10 seconds,” he replied, appearing live via video link.



Alan Jones has been a man of many titles, but now he is reduced to just one: defendant. He sat in court for the second day of what is scheduled to be months of hearings into the indecent assault and sexual touching charges against him. He was pristine in a sky-blue blazer and aubergine trousers, his walking cane resting beside him, notepad and pen at the ready. He watched the screen intently. “It was skin on skin, in that moment,” “J” continued.



Related Article Graphic content

Alan Jones trial ‘I just want justice’: Complainant’s emotional testimony in Alan Jones trial He paused. “I will just replay it. I was not fully erect at that time, it was slightly, if you go flat …” He gestured with his hand to convey the angle. Prosecutor Wright thought that gesture conveyed about a “135-degree angle”, but Judge Glenn Walsh demurred.



“I would have said 45-degree angle,” he said. The details of indecent assault involve a lot of what theatre people call “blocking”. The level of detail about the former broadcaster’s alleged offending has been described in calm legalese. Sam Mooy Whose hand was where, and where did it move to? How many seconds did a kiss last? Who took the underpants off, or were they already down when the touching started? The Jones trial is no different. The choreography of the alleged offending is of utmost importance, and the second day of evidence from “J” involved extremely graphic detail.



It was invasive and undignified, and in the context of the court, it was stripped of all emotion. “J”, recounting the occasion Jones allegedly invited him to his luxury Fitzroy Falls estate, said that during dinner, his host told him: “There is only one rule – there are no rules”. ‘He opened it [the robe] up and he looked at me and said: “I said, the robe and nothing else”.’ “J” gives evidence at Alan Jones’ trial No rules, sure. But some orders were to be obeyed, according to the evidence of “J”. After they finished eating, “J” alleged Jones told him to go shower and change into a robe “and nothing else”.



As “J” left the room, Jones reiterated his command, calling after him: “The robe and nothing else!” Jones was around 63 years old at the time. “J” was about 18 or 19. He changed into the robe but kept his underpants on. Later, on the lounge, when Jones went to touch “J”’s penis, he reproached him. Loading “He opened it [the robe] up and he looked at me and said: “I said, the robe and nothing else.”



“J” was contrite. “I said ‘I’m sorry’,” he told the court. That’s when Jones indecently assaulted him, for the second time that evening, according to “J”. This time, “J” spoke up and told his benefactor he “wasn’t comfortable with that”. Jones stopped. Relieved, “J” went to bed, only to hear a tapping on his door, minutes later.



Related Article Analysis

Alan Jones trial Alan Jones used to talk for a living. He sat silently as a young man detailed his alleged crimes Jones, who vehemently denies all charges, showed no sign of shame or humiliation as “J” detailed what he alleged happened next – a hug, a buttock squeeze and then an alleged act of parallel masturbation. “J” remembered the shadow Jones cast as he moved around the bed, through a shaft of light, to get to him. “It was another trapped moment. I was completely frozen,” “J” said. “I thought, ‘If I just do this, and I do this myself, it’s just going to be over. I can get to the shower and clean myself up’. I could prevent him from being near me or from touching me.”



“J” gave his evidence cogently and with detail. He recalled which hand the defendant held a glass of wine in. He remembered the “smart” white shoes he bought after Jones lambasted his appearance and thrust cash in his hand to go buy something decent. He remembered the stress of a credit card bill, and Jones telling him he would pay it. “Your problems are my problems,” Jones reassured him, “J” said. He remembered having a hit on the Fitzroy Falls tennis court with a fellow guest, who thrashed him.



“I just thought he was some guy who was hitting winners,” he said. ‘What the defendant was doing was wrong. I know it was wrong.’ “J” on why he came forward to police It turned out the guy, who was named in court, was “one of the greatest tennis players we have ever produced”. “J” did have some memory troubles, occasionally stopping to ask if he could close his eyes to envision the scene he was being prompted to recall. “I try to really focus as much as I can,” he told the court.



“I close my eyes and I take myself all the way back.” The second day of evidence from “J” involved extremely graphic detail. Sam Mooy When defence counsel Gabrielle Bashir, SC, began her cross-examination of “J”, she seemed to be leading evidence to show his memory was, indeed, faulty. She directed him to 2023 news reports in The Sydney Morning Herald about allegations against Jones which contained similar details to the ones “J” gave when he contacted police the following year. “J” denied his memory had been tainted. He said he had not read much about the Jones allegations because he was trying to “distance” himself from the matter.



Related Article Alan Jones trial Alan Jones trial as it happened: Complainant’s cross-examination begins after court told he feared he owed $110,000 to former 2GB broadcaster “I haven’t seen or read or seen any of the specifics and I still haven’t,” he told Bashir. “I don’t know anything about these people.” Earlier, at the conclusion of his evidence in chief, “J” was asked by Wright why he decided to come forward to police in 2024, after Jones’ arrest, more than a decade after he cut him off financially and they had ceased contact. He paused for several seconds before speaking.



“I’m going to be 100 per cent honest. I feel like I’m here because I haven’t been able to say no and stand up for the right thing and do the right thing,” he told the court, with emotion. “I’m a father now. I am a proud dad, and I want to teach my daughter right from wrong. What the defendant was doing was wrong. I know it was wrong.” The defendant, sitting in court, was not watching the complainant on screen as he said that. He tilted his chin upwards and stared into the middle distance. Jones, who is now 85, vehemently denies all the charges. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Woman urged to hand herself in after running over man while stealing his car
World.content:
NationalVictoriaCrime Woman urged to hand herself in after running over man while stealing his car James Costa and Alexander Darling August 4, 2026 — 7:29pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Police are urging a woman to hand herself in after she ran over a man who was trying to stop her from stealing his car in Heidelberg West. As the 68-year-old man continues to fight for his life in hospital, police have released more CCTV of the woman in the moments before the crime on Saturday night, and the black Honda CRV which remains missing. Loading Detective Acting Inspector Paul Lineham said on Tuesday that the man had undergone surgery and remained in a critical condition.



“I’ve spoken to the family this morning, and they are absolutely traumatised by the events,” he said. “I’ve got no doubt she knew she ran this victim over. The time for panic is over,” he said, addressing the culprit directly. “It’s time for you to hand yourself in right now, and if you’re truly remorseful, and have any shred of decency at all, hand yourself into police.” “They’re incredibly angry this happened and that the father got left on the road with these life-threatening injuries.” The additional CCTV footage released on Tuesday shows the car left running with a door open in the driveway and a woman in a dark beanie, white hooded puffer jacket, leggings and white sneakers, watching the car and looking around before approaching the driveway. Detective Acting Inspector Paul Lineham urged the offender to surrender. Chris Hopkins



Lineham said police had information that the woman, Caucasian and in her 40s, had been walking around the area before the incident. He said she had been loitering, walking into properties and looking over fences as if searching for an opportunity to steal something. He said the victim and his family did not know the culprit. “The community would be rightly outraged about this.” The fresh footage follows chilling CCTV released the day after the incident. In that vision, the woman can be seen staking out the street before crossing the road and entering the driveway of a property, just after the man pulled the Black 2018 Honda CRV into his driveway for a short stop. He left his car running while he went inside. Loading



The confrontation happens off camera: A few seconds after the woman walks up the driveway, setting off a pilot light, more women’s voices begin to shriek: “Somebody help!” “Get out of the car!” Then a man angrily joins in: “Get the f--- out of the car”, he roars several times. Half a minute later, footage then shows the man on the back of the SUV as it hurtles backwards out of the driveway. He falls off and appears to be driven over. The man’s wife then rushes from the driveway to his aid, while the car is backed into a driveway across the road and speeds off as the wife’s screams fill the night air. World.title: Melbourne and Alan Richardson to go their separate ways
World.content:
In today’s AFL Briefing, your wrap of footy news: Melbourne football boss to depart at season’s end.

Essendon’s poor performances and horror fixture is set to hurt them financially.

Tim Watson backs former rival’s appraisal of beleaguered Bombers.

Richmond’s Nathan Broad pulls pin on AFL career.

The Tasmania Devils have unveiled their new head of development. Melbourne and football boss Alan Richardson are parting ways after seven seasons with the veteran official at the helm. Richardson joined the Demons in 2020 after he finished up as St Kilda coach and was a key figure in Melbourne’s drought-breaking premiership in 2021. Melbourne coach Steven King (left) and football boss Alan Richardson (right). Getty Images Two competition sources with knowledge of the situation, but who spoke on condition of anonymity, confirmed Richardson was leaving at the season’s end.



He informed key football department personnel in the past week that this season would be his last at the club. Richardson was part of the group who told Simon Goodwin he was being sacked as coach last August after the Melbourne board decided to move on the coach. The Demons then appointed a new coach, Steven King, and Ned Guy joined the football department as chief of football and innovation. The club has surged under their leadership, defying pre-season expectations to sit in sixth spot of the ladder. Tom McDonald will retire at the end of the year. Getty Images The club had to apologise this year to the partner of premiership player Steven May after Richardson, then club CEO Paul Guerra and King held an online meeting with players’ partners to discuss his potential departure from the club.



They released a statement after settling the matter with May’s partner Sachi Dade after she had complained to the club and initiated legal action. “In February 2026, the Melbourne Football Club leadership team divulged personal and sensitive information about Ms Dade. We acknowledge that this was inappropriate and constituted a serious invasion of her privacy. “… Our senior leaders, including the board, the incoming CEO and our leaders in the football department, are committed to taking all steps necessary to ensure this does not happen again. We sincerely apologise to Ms Dade and her family for the hurt, distress and impact our actions have caused.” Also on Tuesday, Demons premiership player Tom McDonald announced his retirement, effective as of the end of the season. He has played 256 matches, including last week’s win over Gold Coast, after being selected with pick No.53 in the 2010 national draft.

- Peter Ryan How the Bombers’ season from hell stands to affect their bottom line



Andrew Wu Essendon’s dwindling crowds could cost the club a low six-figure sum in revenue as the effects of their poor season come back to bite. An industry source with knowledge of how crowd figures affect Essendon’s bottom line, speaking on the condition of anonymity, told this masthead the recent low crowds from a horror fixture could cost the Bombers about $200,000 across the year. There were plenty of empty seats for Essendon’s game against GWS in round 19. Getty Images Bombers supporters have dropped off in alarming numbers lately, plummeting to levels not seen since 2016 when 34 players were suspended for the drugs saga, and their faith will be further tested in final rounds of the season.



The crowd of 14,601 for the Bombers’ shock win against GWS three weeks ago was the club’s lowest home attendance since round 21 in 1991, against the Brisbane Bears when the Dons still called Windy Hill home. The turnout for the round 19 win against the Giants is one of the Bombers’ lowest crowds at home since the start of the AFL era in 1990. That figure was only marginally higher than the 14,463 who watched the Bombers take on the Giants in round 13 of their ruinous 2016 season when the club claimed its first wooden spoon since 1933. Only 20,518 turned up for the Bombers’ 72-point hammering by Adelaide at Marvel Stadium on Sunday. That figure is the lowest for games between those clubs at Docklands, including the 2021 season, when crowd restrictions were in place due to the COVID-19 pandemic. The Bombers refused to be drawn on the extent of the financial fallout but told this masthead any downturn in crowds at the end of the season were offset by strong attendances earlier in the year.



The Bombers drew 71,384 for their opening game of the season against Hawthorn, which was billed as a grudge match after former skipper Zach Merrett’s failed trade to the Hawks. Marquee games like the Anzac Day blockbuster and the King’s Birthday eve clash against Carlton were also their home matches. Those crowds are a major reason the Bombers’ average home crowd of 44,505 is in the top six in the league, behind Collingwood, Carlton, ladder leader Fremantle, Adelaide and West Coast. Essendon’s draw for the floating part of the fixture has not been kind commercially. With four of their final five games at home and against non-Victorian clubs, the Bombers were vulnerable to having their drawing power affected significantly by on-field performances. The Bombers have won just two of their past 33 games. They were banished from the prized Thursday and Friday-night slots and dealt three home games in the dreaded late Sunday-afternoon graveyard shifts, including the two matches against the Giants and Crows. Their run home features another late Sunday-afternoon game, against Sydney at the MCG next weekend, before a season finale against lowly Port Adelaide on a Sunday at 12.20pm.

- Andrew Wu



Bombers great Watson takes aim at former club Jon Pierik Essendon’s coaching exodus has continued with another assistant coach about to leave the club, while Bombers great Tim Watson has taken aim at his former club for “dobbing” in Leigh Matthews for his comments about the club’s coaching process. The Bombers confirmed on Tuesday that forwards coach Cam Roberts would leave the club at the end of the 2026 season, just like football department general manager Dan McPherson, whose departure was announced five days earlier. Essendon great Tim Watson has defended one-time Hawthorn rival Leigh Matthews over his comments about the Bombers’ coaching race. Joe Armao



They join senior coach Brad Scott, assistant Ben Jacobs and head of psychology Ben Robbins among those departing the club this year. Related Article AFL 2026 ‘I wouldn’t be going to Essendon’: Matthews slams Bombers; Lyon again eyeballs reporters in presser It was Matthews’ comments about the Bombers’ search for Scott’s replacement that lit a fuse on Saturday. The four-time premiership coach – one of the AFL’s most respected voices – told 3AW he would have “no confidence” to coach the Bombers under the current administration, adding: “If I was a coach, I wouldn’t be going to Essendon”. The Bombers were privately upset with Matthews’ comments on Saturday when contacted by this masthead, given the Australian Football Hall of Fame Legend is a Brisbane Lions club director, but they went a step further on Sunday when chief executive Tim Roberts sent a transcript of Matthews’ comments to the AFL, as reported by Seven’s Agenda Setters. Bombers president Andrew Welsh also contacted Lions chairman Andrew Wellington for an explanation of Matthews’ comments.



Three-time premiership great Watson, speaking on SEN on Tuesday, said Matthews, the former Hawks hard nut who clashed against the Bombers in three grand finals in the 1980s, was within his rights to comment. “Leigh is very considered and has powerful conversations from time to time, and he’s very direct in what he has to say,” Watson, the former Bombers skipper, told SEN. “He’s not somebody that goes out there looking for clickbait, he’s not a hot-taker. There’s enough evidence around to suggest that what he’s saying not completely untrue, either. It didn’t last long – only a few minutes – but the fight on the outer wing during the first quarter of the 1985 VFL grand final had its bitter moments. While Matthews and Watson (far left) declared a truce, three other bouts were in full swing. The Age archives “I don’t know whether I would have gone to that degree, had I been at Essendon, that I thought, ‘OK, I need to go to the AFL and get some sort of comment from them’.”



The AFL will not take action against Matthews, insisting it’s a club-based issue. When asked if there was an insecurity at the bottom-placed Bombers, Watson said: “I think there’s a lot going on at the club at the moment. “They’re staring down the wooden spoon, they haven’t got a coach. I would have thought you’ve got much bigger things to worry about than dobbing someone in about what they’ve said. “I would think the best thing you can do in this business is point at the scorecard. At the moment, their scorecard looks miserable, but when it looks better you can point at it and say this is where we’re at. But they’ve got a long way to go before they are at that point.” Andrew Welsh, James Hird and Matthew Lloyd in their playing days at Essendon in 2004. Getty Images



A Bombers spokesman said on Tuesday the club had dealt with the Matthews matter on Saturday afternoon. Cam Roberts’ stint at Essendon lasted seven seasons, starting as a development coach for the 2020 campaign. “When I first arrived, I simply wanted to contribute and help people improve. To have had the chance to work alongside such committed players, coaches and staff over the past seven seasons has been a privilege,” Roberts said. Jacobs and Robbins quit in May in solidarity with Scott, while McPherson confirmed last week he would step down at the end of the season.



Tim Roberts thanked Cameron Roberts for his contribution. Related Article Opinion

AFL 2026 I wish Hill and Stengle well, but the game must learn lessons from their exits Mathew Stokes AFL columnist “We appreciate that prior to appointing a senior coach there is always a level of uncertainty at AFL clubs. While we’re disappointed to see him leave, we completely respect his decision and thank him for everything he’s contributed to Essendon,” the CEO said. The Bombers’ hunt for a new senior coach has been reduced to four candidates: club legend James Hird, Fremantle assistant Jaymie Graham, Sydney assistant and former Bomber Mark McVeigh and Adelaide director of coaching Murray Davis, a former long-time Brisbane Lions assistant. Caretaker coach Dean Solomon, a friend and former teammate of Hird and McVeigh, will this week have his first formal discussions with club hierarchy about the full-time job. But Solomon has publicly remained tight-lipped on whether he’ll seek the head coaching role.



Welsh, Tim Roberts, football director Ted Richards, vice president and ex-Victory chairman Anthony Di Pietro and Essendon’s general manager of people and culture, Caroline Monzon, are on the selection panel. Melbourne Victory great and former coach Kevin Muscat, and long-time opposition analyst at Collingwood and Hawthorn John Wardrop have supported the panel, challenging the candidates on their leadership credentials and game style. Formal interviews are continuing this week, the Bombers hoping to confirm their appointment by the end of next week as they restructure their football department, including the men’s and women’s programs. Broad calls time a Tigerland Three-time Richmond premiership defender Nathan Broad has decided to retire, rather than accept an on-field leadership role at West Coast. Broad, who has played 189 games for Richmond, told his teammates on Tuesday of his plans to bow out.



Nathan Broad has experienced life at both ends of the ladder in his career at Richmond. AFL Photos His departure leaves just six Tigers left at Punt Road from their grand final-winning teams in 2017, 2019 and 2020. The 33-year-old’s final AFL match will be in round 23 against St Kilda, leaving the Tigers without him for the final match of the season a week later in Geelong. Originally from Western Australia, Broad will relocate with his family back to his home state after he finishes up at Richmond. View post on X



Already planning to move back to WA, Broad was weighing up the idea of continuing playing at the Eagles, where former Richmond caretaker coach Andrew McQualter is in charge. Former Tigers Liam Baker, Tylar Young and Jack Graham are already at West Coast. Broad did not make his debut until he was 23 after being taken by Richmond as a mature-aged recruit, but he enjoyed immediate success, and by 2020 he became the quickest player in VFL/AFL history to win three premierships, achieving the feat in just 70 games. With Broad exiting, the only premiership players left at Richmond from Damien Hardwick’s sides will be Nick Vlastuin, Toby Nankervis, Dion Prestia, Jayden Short, Tom Lynch and Noah Balta. Broad hoped the Tigers, who have endured a difficult three seasons under coach Adem Yze, will recover quickly.



“The culture here is our competitive advantage, but it does not just happen, it has taken years to build,” he told teammates. “It can also be lost in a matter of moments. Continue to water and feed this culture because it is our biggest strength.”

AAP Lappin on Tassie’s shore Greg Dundas The Tasmania Devils have landed another key off-field recruit, luring Nigel Lappin away from Geelong to be their head of development and work alongside senior coach Ken Hinkley.



Geelong assistant Nigel Lappin is heading to Tasmania to be the Devils’ head of development. AFL Photos A triple premiership player at the Brisbane Lions, Lappin spent 18 years in various roles at Geelong, most recently head of development. He first assisted Mark Thompson before becoming a key lieutenant to his former Brisbane Lions teammate Chris Scott. The Cats won AFL premierships in 2009, 2011 and 2022 while Lappin was at the club, and he was widely respected for helping develop players. Unlikely recruits such as Mark Blicavs, Tom Stewart, Tom Atkins, Mark O’Connor and Oisin Mullin were among those who benefited from his tutelage. “Nigel is one of the most respected development coaches in Australian football,” Devils CEO Brendon Gale said. View post on X



“The role of head of development is exceptionally important to the build of the club’s football lists, [and] we are confident that Nigel’s experience, humility and values make him an outstanding fit for what we’re creating. “With the recent appointment of Ken Hinkley and now Nigel, I am confident that we are building a team that will lay the most solid of foundations for us to build upon.” Hinkley worked with Lappin at Geelong in 2009 and said he was thrilled with the appointment. “He’s got a wealth of experience from both his playing and coaching career, but what stands out most is the way he connects with people and helps players get the very best out of themselves,” the coach said. Loading



The Devils trumpeted their signing about the same time Geelong announced Lappin’s departure. “I leave with mixed emotions,” Lappin said in a statement released by the Cats. “I’m incredibly grateful for the opportunities this club has given me and the stability it has provided my family over the past 18 years.” “While leaving is difficult, I’m excited for a new challenge – the opportunity to help build something at a foundation club, in a football-obsessed state with strong personal ties, and in an area of the game I’m deeply passionate about.” Geelong’s football boss Andrew Mackie congratulated their outgoing development boss. “We’re excited for Nigel and this new opportunity in his career,” Mackie said.



“Nigel has worn plenty of hats in his 18 years at the Cats and has been a constant source of support for our players, coaches and staff.” Lappin will continue his role at Geelong until the end of the season. Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: Recent cases show exactly why suppression law must change
World.content:
NationalVictoriaCourts Editorial Recent cases show exactly why suppression law must change The Age's View Editorial August 4, 2026 — 7:45pm

August 4, 2026 — 7:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

This week the public learnt the identity of a rapist. The man, Ralph Carr, was convicted last week by a jury of one count of sexual assault and two of rape dating back to 2023. Carr had pleaded not guilty. He had sought and been granted a suppression order on his name. Thus, for three years, as the case went through the courts, the public had no idea of his identity, his age, or the industry in which he worked. He was only a well-known Melbourne businessman. On Monday, a judge ordered the suppression order be lifted after Carr said he would not be seeking its continuance. His lawyers say he will be appealing his conviction. Ralph Carr outside court in June 2024. Jason South Carr’s is not an isolated case in relation to those applying for and being granted a suppression order. As the Open Courts Act section 18 stands at present, he and his legal team were merely using one line in it. Tom Silvagni and his legal team used the same method to suppress his name while his rape case went through the courts. Silvagni was found guilty of rape last year, and his identity was revealed. He is appealing. On Tuesday, a doctor accused of filming women and children at a public pool could finally be identified after two rounds of legal wrangling after claiming his child’s mental health would suffer if he were named. That case continues.



While section 18 covers several reasons that an order should be given for the proper administration of justice, (1) C states that an order should be considered “to protect the safety of any person”. This is the hole in the dyke from which a flood of suppression orders has been sought and granted. In Victoria, 477 orders, in various forms, were given last year. The highest number were issued on the basis of safety for the accused, including their mental health. While the mental health of anyone is a legitimate concern, justice must be seen to be done. It beggars belief that the grounds for these orders were so compelling as to be granted. Suppression should not be a shield against such disclosure, nor a blind from witnessing the open administration of justice. Related Article Opinion

Courts I’m a retired Supreme Court judge. Tom Silvagni should not have been prosecuted in secret Betty King Retired Supreme Court judge The state government is reviewing suppression orders. Last March, The Age and other media outlets wrote to Attorney-General Sonya Kilkenny calling for the (1) C line to be revised. Kilkenny said she was looking into the issue “with some urgency”. The word “some” seems to be the fulcrum on which Kilkenny’s urgency swings. Following this week’s decision on Carr, shadow attorney-general James Newbury said Victorians were sick of living in the “suppression order capital of Australia”. The opposition, if elected, would restrict suppression orders to genuine physical safety reasons. The new premier, Ben Carroll, has been quick to stamp his mark on the government, and perhaps this issue is another opportunity.



Robert Clark, who as attorney-general, introduced the Open Courts Act in 2013, has criticised the way lawyers and defendants have used the legislation. “The safety ground for a suppression order was about protecting people from threats of violence or similar, not about claims of psychological distress,” he has said. We agree. Jason Bosland, an associate professor at the University of Melbourne’s law school, recently wrote in The Conversation of the need to tighten suppression orders “being made to prohibit the publication of an accused’s identity based on the mental health consequences of publicity (as in the Silvagni case). Such orders fall short of public expectations. They create a perception (if not a reality) that those with the financial means to hire expensive lawyers and to pay for psychiatric reports obtain special treatment in our courts”. Special treatment is anathema to the justice system. If, as a society, we are to uphold the principle that all are equal before the law, then it follows that this suppression loophole must be closed. Urgently, if you don’t mind, minister. Get a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own.

World.title: From deadline to details: The six things you need to know to handle the census
World.content:
PoliticsFederalCensus From deadline to details: The six things you need to know to handle the census Shane Wright August 4, 2026 — 7:31pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When is census night, how do you fill it out, and do you need to be at home? Census night this year is August 11. But, as more than 1.2 million households have already done, you can complete your census form before that date. If you complete your census form before August 11, you need to fill it out as if you were home on that day. If a member of a household is away from home on the special night, you can include them as if they were home. If you are visiting someone, make sure you’re included in their household form. But make sure you’re counted only once. Your personal details are confidential – but your descendants could ask for them in 99 years. Tanya Macheda



For those travelling or staying at hotels, caravan parks and registered campgrounds, operators should have census forms for you to complete. If you happen to be free camping or staying at a remote location, various visitor information centres will have census forms. If that doesn’t work, you can get a census number from the ABS so you can complete your form when you have access to the internet. Why do we have the census? Since the Babylonians in 3800 BC, governing bodies have sought to count the number of people under their control. The census that features in the Gospel of Luke was conducted by authorities for taxation and administration reasons as Rome brought the province of Judea under its control.



Related Article Census In 1947, the census asked if you had a flushing toilet. This is what it will ask this year Outside of tax, censuses have been used to plan for services such as schools and cemeteries, while in many countries they are central to the allocation of electorates in parliaments. The first official census in this country was in 1828. It was termed a “muster” and held in NSW to help align the number of people in the colony with its food supplies. Colonial headcounts were carried out until the mid-1880s. In 1905, the federal government passed the Census and Statistics Act. The Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) was created the following year. The first national census was held on April 2, 1911. That census counted 4.45 million people (excluding the nation’s Indigenous population).



Some of the questions used in that census have disappeared. We are no longer asked if we live in a wagon or if the family home is made from spinifex or calico. But others have remained constant, though maybe the answers change. In 1911, 79 people said their religion was Callithumpian, while another 32 described their belief as “wowser”. At the 2001 census, almost 70,000 people said they were Jedi. What happens if you don’t complete the census? Completing the census is compulsory, and has been since the first count in 1911.



If a household does not complete and submit a census form, the ABS will contact you and ask for it to be done. If a household continues to hold out, it can be served a formal direction to complete the census, which is a legal instruction. At this point, if you continue to refuse to fill out the form, you can be prosecuted and fined up to $364 a day. What is a census field officer, how are they chosen, and how much are they paid? The census is one of the nation’s largest one-off job opportunities. The ABS is employing more than 16,000 field officers – the people who go around to households with forms and then pick them up – through the census period. It’s a job that appeals to seniors or those looking for some casual work, and the pay starts around the $33-an-hour mark.



Related Article Census A decade after the last census disaster, the security of this year’s count is at risk There are thousands of other positions that require more specialist skills or being in particular parts of the country, such as isolated regions. What has changed in Australia because of the census? One of the most important discoveries in health was uncovered by Australian statistician Oliver Lancaster. He used the 1911, 1921 and 1933 censuses – which asked a question on deaf-mutism – to establish for the first time the link between rubella and congenital problems in unborn children.



More recently, housing experts noticed a drop in the number of home owners between the 1996 and 2001 census. This continued into the national headcounts of 2006, 2011, 2016 and 2021. This decline in ownership rates, particularly across people in their 20s and 30s, has been highlighted by advocates for changes in housing policy, including taxation policy. The Treasury analysis contained in this year’s federal budget, which contained changes to negative gearing and capital gains tax, referenced this census data. What happens to your data, and is it a privacy concern? Some people are concerned about their personal data as the census form collects names and addresses.

World.title: The best public schools in HSC maths, ranked – and how one non-selective surprised everyone
World.content:
NationalNSWHSC The best public schools in HSC maths, ranked – and how one non-selective surprised everyone Christopher Harris and Nigel Gladstone August 4, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Balgowlah Boys, Fairvale High and Killarney Heights High recorded the highest average marks in advanced mathematics of any non-selective public schools in last year’s Higher School Certificate. A Herald analysis of average marks in the subject shows the 43 students at Balgowlah Boys who enrolled in the advanced course achieved an average mark of 90.3 – stronger than all but four selective schools. For the Mathematics Standard 2 course, fully selective school Merewether High in Newcastle had the best average marks, followed by Manly selective and then Balgowlah Boys. Oliver Yang, Leo Robinson, and Luke Macfarlane scored top mathematics results in the HSC last year for their school, Balgowlah Boys. Sitthixay Ditthavong



Balgowlah’s head of mathematics, Chris Hickford, traces its HSC success back to year 7 and teachers’ focus on building strong algebra skills, an ability to think formulaically and interpret critical information in written questions. Related Article HSC We re-ranked schools by HSC averages. This is what the most precise data reveals “We do have, I suppose, a traditional approach to maths teaching here at the school,” he said. A typical lesson contains teacher-led examples, student questioning, followed by a “gradual release” for the students to work independently. Or, in teacher parlance, it is an “I do, we do, you do” approach. Many students took up mathematics because they aspired to work in a trade and could see the value of numeracy skills to real life, he said, while other students wanted to take mathematics-based university courses. Others simply enjoy the subject because they’re good at it.



“The explicit nature of the subject appeals to the boys … seeing a clear result and an answer that very rarely can be ambiguous or misinterpreted. I think that clarity of it really appeals to the boys,” Hickford said. It is easy to slip behind during the fast-paced year 11 and 12 courses, so the teachers focus on “ensuring the students are actually doing the work” with rigorous checks. “We find just keeping the students to account for actually getting their work done makes a huge difference,” he said. Eddie Woo, Professor of Practice at the University of Sydney, said there was no single method to improve mathematics results but successful schools often closely analyse results data provided by the NSW Education Standards Authority.



“It gives super granular data. We can drill down to individual classes and items in an exam,” he said. Schools could detect areas of weakness and learn from their teachers whose classes had produced excellent results in certain topics, such as discrete random variables. Another key to success was structured mentoring and purposeful skill development for teachers, which included pairing new teachers with experienced ones so they could see how they approached teaching the mathematics course. “Some schools do it extremely well and other schools have constraining factors, so that means it doesn’t happen as much,” Wu said. “Just because you can do the content yourself is not the same as being able to teach it ... anyone who has taught someone how to drive can attest to this. It’s a whole different set of skills.”



Most private schools do not publish subject averages, though the high-ranking selective Sydney Grammar School reported an average of 87.7 for advanced maths. Girls school Roseville College reported a mean of 83.2. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Red flags: A tech company claims it can identify Australia’s most at-risk children
World.content:
Exclusive TechnologyAI Red flags: A tech company claims it can identify Australia’s most at-risk children David Swan August 4, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

An Australian company founded by a survivor of childhood abuse is bringing a machine-learning system to childcare centres to flag children who may be at risk of harm, as the sector grapples with balancing young people’s privacy against a need to keep them safe. The warning system’s rollout in daycares across the country comes as the sector undergoes its biggest safety overhaul since the national quality framework began. SAFE chief executive Ruby O’Rourke. The company says its eponymously named SAFE system is already in use in more than 1000 early childhood services. Educators log everyday observations – a bruise, a missed meal, a parent affected by drugs at pick-up – and the machine-learning model turns those fragments into a live picture of which children may be most at risk. Parents are not asked to opt in; the company says consent is given when families enrol their kids to a daycare and agree to its professional systems. Chief executive Ruby O’Rourke, a longtime children’s rights campaigner who ran for federal parliament in 2019, built the company after a childhood shaped by forced adoption, domestic violence and abuse that, she says, culminated in a family member holding her under the water at a Melbourne creek. Passersby revived her. The family member was never charged.



Her argument is that none of it was invisible. “The schools, the Brownies, the Girl Guides, all of these signals were missed,” she said. Neighbours told her years later that they had heard her scream, and done nothing. “If I’m going to leave my life with anything,” she said, “it’s knowing the next generation has this layer of SAFE sitting under the surface” – what she calls a “flight control tower” for children at severe risk. SAFE co-founder David Salajan. O’Rourke began building childcare software in the mid-2000s; the predictive layer started in 2012 with NICTA, the country’s former information and communications technology research centre that is now part of the CSIRO. Co-founder David Salajan describes SAFE as a machine paired with human reviewers.



“It’s just an observation, no matter how big or small,” he said. The software returns a risk score and guidance on whether a concern meets the mandatory reporting threshold; every case is then reviewed by former child protection workers. A national dashboard, seen by SAFE’s team rather than the daycare centre staff, triages every case so they can see which children are at highest risk. Related Article Exclusive

Child abuse Thousands of NSW children are being abused. Police say it has become an epidemic The pitch lands at a volatile moment for the childcare sector. Changes to national laws governing the industry took effect on February 27, making children’s safety the paramount legal consideration, creating a workers’ register and mandating carers to attend child safety training by August 27. A $226 million government package also funds a national CCTV trial. The overhaul follows recent abuse cases such as that of Queensland worker Ashley Paul Griffith, jailed for life in 2024 over 307 offences against 73 children. In Sydney, daycare worker Hamish Alexander Edward Tait was arrested last month, facing more than 320 charges over his alleged abuse of 150 children under his care. Those cases involved alleged abuse at childcare centres though, rather than abuse elsewhere detected by an educator. The SAFE system also raises privacy concerns: a private company holds a live, prioritised register of children it deems most at risk, plus behavioural records on about 200,000 workers in the childcare industry.



The Office of the Australian Information Commissioner would not comment on SAFE, but a spokesperson said behavioural information about a child in a care setting may count as personal – and sometimes sensitive – information under the Privacy Act, carrying obligations to collect only what is necessary, keep it secure and not reuse it. Whether an enrolment agreement amounts to valid consent depends on how it is worded, the spokesperson said, adding that consent should be “informed, current, specific and voluntary”, especially for children’s information. The regulator is also drawing up a Children’s Online Privacy Code, due by December 10, expected to cover most online services used in early childhood settings. It would require information to be handled in a child’s best interests, with a parent’s consent necessary for children under 15. Carol Matthews, NSW/ACT branch secretary of the Independent Education Union, which represents early childhood care staff, said for-profit software was “no substitute for a comprehensive focus on child safety at every centre”. The union backed the regulatory reforms over the past year, but was wary of the technology. “Machine learning takes the risk of a privacy breach to a whole new level,” Matthews said, warning that many services may not be equipped to safeguard the data. She urged employers to consult staff before rolling out any such platform. O’Rourke dismissed concerns that the machine-learning system could entrench bias given the data it’s working with is based on childcare workers’ observations. SAFE does not identify children by ethnicity, socioeconomic background or disability, she said, and its signals are “continuously reviewed by child protection experts to identify and prevent bias, not enshrine it”. However, the observations that feed the warning system are human judgments.



Related Article Child abuse ‘This doesn’t happen to us’: Family’s horror after Sydney day care abuser unmasked She likens it to a blood test: the machine records the markers, but a qualified professional interprets them, and no action follows until her review team validates the case. A NSW parliamentary inquiry this year recommended a database to track problematic staff behaviour in childcare centres and foster stronger intelligence-sharing between regulators, police and screening bodies – which is close to what SAFE is pitching. But the same committee was wary of technological fixes, warning that CCTV “should not be relied upon” and was no substitute for staffing and supervision. Tamara Hughes, head of safeguarding at Save the Children, said Australia’s problem was not a lack of knowledge about cases but sustained action. “A child’s safety should not depend on where they live, who they come into contact with, or their background,” she said. For O’Rourke, the bottom line is simpler. While the childcare industry homed in on early childhood education standards, care and safety were left as an afterthought. “We’ve got the priority wrong.”



Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732). Anyone affected by sexual, domestic or family violence can also access 24/7, free and confidential trauma-specialist counselling through Full Stop Australia (1800 385 578).
